source: cross-examiner verdicts from the research fleets (one agent per contested claim, both lenses)

verdicts.dateTest: Restated as: MoD/DGDE listed 62 Cantonment Boards including Khasyol on 2023-03-20, and listed 61 without Khasyol on a page last updated 2025-10-21. The dates fit. PIB 1942023 (24 Jul 2023, a Rajya Sabha written reply by RRM Ajay Bhatt) says: "One Cantonment namely, KhasYol has already been de-notified w.e.f. 27.04.2023." That date falls after the 20 Mar 2023 list and before the 2025 page, so both lists were accurate on their own dates. Press reports say MoD notified the excision of Khasyol's civil areas on 19 Jan 2023. The 20 Mar 2023 reply still counts Khasyol, which matches a Board that existed until the 27 Apr 2023 de-notification.
verdicts.identityTest: Every source names the same entity: "Khasyol" (PIB 2023, HP row 10), "KhasYol" (PIB 2012 command-wise list and PIB 24 Jul 2023), also written "Khas Yol Cantonment Board" (Yol, Kangra district, near Dharamshala, HP). The DGDE page lists 61 by command: Central 24, Eastern 4, Northern 1, Southern 19, Western 12, South Western 1. I counted these myself. Khasyol is absent and the page text says "There are 61 Cantonments in the country". Using the DGDE node as both s and t is fine for an inventory note.
verdicts.baseRate: Khasyol is 1 of 62 Boards (about 1.6%), and it was the first ever de-notified. It is also not a one-off. The same 24 Jul 2023 reply says the modalities for excising civil areas in 58 more cantonments were sent to state governments. The count difference is a deliberate policy change, not an anomaly. The claim accuses nobody, so there is no symmetry control to apply. It names no person, no unpublished budget and no operational detail, so there is no reason to kill it.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable, because the claim makes no accusation. MoD itself confirms the mechanism: PIB 24 Jul 2023, https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=1942023, "One Cantonment namely, KhasYol has already been de-notified w.e.f. 27.04.2023."
verdicts.innocentReading: The innocent reading is confirmed, not just likely. Khasyol was de-notified with effect from 27 Apr 2023 as the pilot of MoD's policy of excising civil areas from cantonments. Its civil population (about 16,000) was merged into the gram panchayats of Rakker, Baghni, Tangroti Khas and Narwana Khas (Outlook; APAC News; Deccan Herald). The record's caveat "the gazette record was not opened" is now out of date: a primary MoD statement fixes both the mechanism and the date.
verdicts.reason: All three sources say what the claim says. PIB 1908805 (20 Mar 2023) prints 62 Boards state-wise, with Khasyol under HP. PIB relid 90277 (10 Dec 2012) prints "List of 62 Cantonment Boards (Command wise)", which includes KhasYol. The DGDE page says "There are 61 Cantonments" and its list leaves Khasyol out. The comparison holds and the chronology is clean. The one weakness is the claim's own hedge that the mechanism is unconfirmed. That hedge is wrong: MoD's 24 Jul 2023 Rajya Sabha reply documents the de-notification w.e.f. 27.04.2023. That meets the record's own upgradeIf condition ("a DGDE notice is opened"), since a ministry statement in Parliament is primary. The claim survives and should be raised from analytic to documented, with the PIB 1942023 source added.
verdicts.corrections: (1) tier/pred: change analytic to documented. (2) srcs: add ["PIB 2023-07-24 — Moving away from the British-era concept of cantonment towns (RS written reply; 'One Cantonment namely, KhasYol has already been de-notified w.e.f. 27.04.2023'; excision modalities for 58 cantonments sent to states)", "https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=1942023"]. (3) text: replace "Innocent reading: one de-notification/merger; the gazette record was not opened" with "Khasyol was de-notified w.e.f. 27.04.2023 (MoD RS reply, 24 Jul 2023); its civil areas were merged into four gram panchayats. It was the first de-notification, and modalities for 58 more have been circulated to states." (4) innocentReading: change it from a hypothesis to the documented mechanism, and remove "the official notification was not opened here". (5) upgradeIf: mark as met. Optionally add the 19 Jan 2023 excision notification as reported (press). (6) DGDE node d-list: note that the change from 62 to 61 dates to 27 Apr 2023, so "61 (DGDE, 2025-10)" and "62 (RS reply 2023-03-20)" do not conflict. (7) Optional: the 2012 PIB list's inclusion of KhasYol is now confirmed (the record says it was "only partly read").

verdicts.dateTest: The claim restated: DGDE lists 61 notified cantonments (page last updated 2025-10-21), and RGI projects population as on 1 March 2026. Both dates are current and they line up. The 61 against the 62 in the PIB 2023 RS list is explained by Khasyol (HP), which was excised in 2023, so HP's count of 6 is right for the present. The causal clause is a claim about when cantonments were created, and the cited sources don't cover that: each record note says "notification date not printed on either list". DGDE's own historical-perspective page (https://dgde.gov.in/en/about-department/historical-perspective/) does cover it: "Out of 61 Cantonments, six were created after Independence." and "In 1962, Ajmer was the last to be notified as a Cantonment." So none was created by any government after 1962, and the date test passes for the "not present allocation" reading. That page is not in srcs.
verdicts.identityTest: The node is force:dgde, which is correct: DGDE is the MoD inter-services body that administers cantonments. I checked the record's 61 footprint entries. States: UP 13 (Agra, Prayagraj, Bareilly, Ayodhya, Fatehgarh, Kanpur, Meerut, Lucknow, Shahjahanpur, Varanasi, Babina, Jhansi, Mathura). Uttarakhand 9 (Almora, Chakrata, Clement Town, Dehradun, Landour, Lansdowne, Nainital, Ranikhet, Roorkee). HP 6 (Bakloh, Dagshai, Dalhousie, Jutogh, Kasauli, Subathu). Maharashtra 7. Bihar 1 (Danapur). The total is 61. DGDE prints commands, not states, so state assignment depends on the PIB 2023-03-20 state-wise list, which is in the record but missing from the claim's srcs. RGI Table 8, 2026 row ('000): India 14,23,435; HP 7,579; Uttarakhand 11,993; UP 2,42,859; Bihar 1,32,265; Maharashtra 1,29,308. All match. The ratios recompute: 0.79, 0.75, 0.054, 0.054, 0.0076, 0.043.
verdicts.baseRate: This is a density ranking, not a property shared across peers. 19 of 36 states/UTs have a cantonment. Next after HP and Uttarakhand are Meghalaya (1/3.31m = 0.30) and J&K (2/13.9m = 0.14). HP and Uttarakhand lead by a wide margin, so the ranking holds. Symmetry: HP (Congress-run) and Uttarakhand (BJP-run) are both at the top, and UP (BJP) and Bihar sit at the bottom with West Bengal and Tamil Nadu in between. Party does not explain the pattern, so the claim reads the same under either control.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable. This is an analytic claim that alleges no wrongdoing and accuses no party, so nobody needed to be asked. The only official statement on point (DGDE historical perspective, 56 pre-1947 + 6 post-1947, none after 1962) supports the claim's reading.
verdicts.innocentReading: The claim's own reading is the innocent one and is primary-sourced. Cantonments are a pre-1962 legal category, and 55 of the present 61 predate Independence (DGDE). Since 1962 MoD has set up military stations by executive order instead of notifying cantonments. The current government's only change to the map is subtractive: Khasyol (HP) was excised in 2023 under the policy of phasing out cantonments. Low density in UP and Bihar reflects their population size, not fewer installations: UP has the most cantonments of any state.
verdicts.reason: Every number checks against the primary sources: 61 cantonments per DGDE, state counts from PIB 2023, and 2026 populations from RGI Table 8. HP (0.79) and Uttarakhand (0.75) really are the densest. The causal clause "colonial … not present allocation" goes beyond the sources the claim cites, since the record admits notification dates are not printed. But DGDE's historical-perspective page supports it directly: six of the 61 were created after Independence and none after 1962. The claim survives as analytic. Its srcs and wording need fixing, and it is not refuted.
verdicts.corrections: (1) Add to srcs: the DGDE historical perspective page (https://dgde.gov.in/en/about-department/historical-perspective/; "Out of 61 Cantonments, six were created after Independence"; "In 1962, Ajmer was the last to be notified"), and the PIB 2023-03-20 RS list (PRID=1908805), since states come from it, not from DGDE. (2) Reword the causal clause to "55 of 61 predate 1947 and none has been notified since 1962 (DGDE); the distribution reflects pre-1962 garrison geography, not present allocation." Avoid "hill-station" as a blanket label: Roorkee, Clement Town and Dehradun are not hill stations, and which six are post-1947 is not established. (3) In text, give UP as 0.054 and India as 0.043, or label the figures as rounded. Give Uttarakhand's population as 11.99m (RGI 11,993 thousand). (4) "16 states/UTs have none" uses RGI's 35-unit universe, with J&K counted with Ladakh. On the current 36-unit map, 17 have none. State which universe is used. (5) Add the runners-up (Meghalaya 0.30, J&K 0.14) so "highest" can be checked. (6) Update upgradeIf: the post-1947 pattern is already partly answered by DGDE (6 created after Independence, last in 1962). What is still missing is which six they are.

verdicts.dateTest: Restated, the claim says DRDO technology-cluster pages, as they stand now, put 25 of 42 addressed labs/centres in Bengaluru, Delhi and Hyderabad. No actor or tenure is involved, and this is a point-in-time count. I fetched all eight URLs on 2026-10-04. All returned HTTP 200 and each shows "Last Updated: 01/10/2026", so the pages are current. Most of these labs were set up before 2014 (for example LRDE 1958, GTRE and ADE 1959, DRDL 1961, RCI 1988). The DYSLs date from 2020. Their siting therefore reflects decisions spread over decades, not one government, so dating does not undercut the claim. The arithmetic does.
verdicts.identityTest: The entity (DRDO) and the cluster pages are correct. The counting unit is not. The seven pages number 42 labs/centres: Aero 5, ACE 7, ECS 6 (including the MTRDC centre), MCC 5 addressed (DYSL-AI has no address), MSS 6, NS&M 7, SSS 6. The file's own footprint rows contain exactly those 42 entries, and by city they give Bengaluru 8 (ADE, GTRE, CABS, CEMILAC, LRDE, MTRDC, CAIR, DEBEL), Delhi 7 (CFEES, ISSA, SAG, SSPL, DIPAS, DIPR, INMAS), Hyderabad 7 (DLRL, ASL, DRDL, RCI, DYSL-AT, DMRL, DYSL-SM) and Pune 4 (ARDE, HEMRL, R&DE(E), DYSL-QT). That is 22 of 42 (52%), not 25 of 42 (60%). The claim's 9/8/8 and Pune 5 match a count that also includes the Director General cluster-headquarters offices printed on the same pages: DG ECS at LRDE Campus, Bengaluru; DG MSS at Kanchanbagh, Hyderabad; DG ACE at ARDE Campus, Pune; DG SSS or MCC at DRDO Bhawan, New Delhi. Those offices are counted in the numerator but left out of the denominator of 42. The claim's own figures also do not add up: 25 + Pune 5 + four cities at 2 each = 38, leaving 4 rows for the 8 single-lab cities in the data (Agra, Ahilyanagar, Kanpur, Jodhpur, Ambernath, Kochi, Visakhapatnam, Gwalior).
verdicts.baseRate: This kind of concentration does not single DRDO out. Central R&D bodies cluster in a few metros where public-sector users and universities sit: ISRO in Bengaluru, Thiruvananthapuram and Ahmedabad, and the DPSUs HAL, BEL and BDL in the same three cities. The correct figure, 22 of 42 (52%), is a concentration well below the 80% non-discrimination threshold. As a descriptive fact it is meaningful, but it implies no allocation choice by any current government. On symmetry, no party-political control applies: siting decisions span every government since 1958, and the three cities sit in states run by different parties (Karnataka INC, Telangana INC, Delhi BJP). The scope is incomplete in both directions. The HR corporate-cluster page addresses further DRDO centres, mostly in Delhi: DESIDOC, CEPTAM and RAC in Delhi, and ITM in Mussoorie. Labs found on neither set of pages are mostly outside the top three cities: DIAT Pune, DFRL Mysuru, DIHAR Leh, DRL Tezpur and DIBER Haldwani. The ECS page text also names DARE and LASTEC, but neither has an address there.
verdicts.denialFound: None found, and no one was asked. This is a descriptive count of DRDO's own published addresses and alleges no wrongdoing, so no response is needed.
verdicts.innocentReading: Labs are placed next to their users and suppliers. Aeronautics and radar sit with HAL, ADA and BEL in Bengaluru. Missiles sit with BDL and the Kanchanbagh complex in Hyderabad. Delhi's labs (Metcalfe House, Timarpur) hold the headquarters-adjacent functions: analysis, cryptology, physiology and psychology. Most of this siting was set in the 1950s–80s. The claim's own innocent reading is adequate.
verdicts.reason: The source pages do not support the numbers. Counting the cluster pages, and the file's own 42 footprint rows built from them, gives Bengaluru 8, Delhi 7, Hyderabad 7, which is 22 of 42, with Pune at 4. The claim's 9/8/8 (25) and Pune 5 come from also counting the DG cluster-headquarters offices in the numerator while keeping a denominator of 42 that excludes them. The claim's own totals also exceed 42 (25+5+8 = 38, leaving 4 rows for 8 single-lab cities). Separately, the killIf as written is already met: the claim itself says DIAT, DFRL, DIHAR and DRL are missing from the pages, so it states its own kill condition. That is a framing defect, not a fact against the pattern, because the missing labs are mostly outside the top three cities. Analytic is the right tier for a corrected count; the figures as written are wrong.
verdicts.corrections: 1) Change the text and lab field to: "22 of the 42 labs/centres addressed on DRDO's seven technology-cluster pages sit in Bengaluru (8), Delhi (7) and Hyderabad (7)". 2) Change the d field to: "Pune 4; Chennai, Dehradun, Chandigarh, Balasore 2 each; Agra, Ahilyanagar, Kanpur, Jodhpur, Ambernath, Kochi, Visakhapatnam, Gwalior 1 each (sum 42). DG cluster-HQ offices (Bengaluru ECS, Hyderabad MSS, Pune ACE, Visakhapatnam NS&M, New Delhi SSS/MCC) and DIT&CS are excluded; DYSL-AI has no printed address." 3) Turn the killIf into a scope note plus a real falsifier. Scope note: "Excludes HR-cluster centres (DESIDOC, CEPTAM, RAC Delhi; ITM Mussoorie) and labs on no cluster page (DIAT Pune, DFRL Mysuru, DIHAR Leh, DRL Tezpur, DIBER Haldwani; ADA Bengaluru is a separate society)." Falsifier: "a complete DRDO establishment list puts the three-city share below 45%". 4) Add the corporate-clusters HR page as a source if those centres are mentioned. 5) Keep tier analytic, pred analytic, s/t force:drdo.

verdicts.dateTest: Restated: NCRB reports that Delhi's central jails held 19,362 inmates against capacity 9,346 on 2023-12-31. The table title is "Capacity, Inmates Population and Occupancy Rate of Central Jails as on 31 December, 2023" (Table 1.4, PSI 2023, p.24). It is a single snapshot date, so no tenure window needs to overlap and the date test passes. The claim names no officeholder or government, so no tenure is attributed.
verdicts.identityTest: The Table 1.4 row reads: "32 DELHI 14 | 9346 0 0 9346 | 19357 0 5 19362 | 207.1 - - 207.2". The all-India row reads: "TOTAL (ALL-INDIA) 152 ... 198150 ... 239136 ... 120.7". Table 1.1 gives Delhi 16 jails in all: 14 central and 2 others (the women's jails, capacity 680, occupancy 105.1% in Table 1.6). So "14 central jails" is the right entity. The capacity is entirely the male column, because the women's jails are classed separately. The edge target force:dl-prisons (the Delhi prisons administration) matches the row. The source URL https://www.ncrb.gov.in/uploads/files/PSI-2023.pdf returns HTTP 200 (application/pdf, 20.6 MB). The local copy in scratchpad/psi2023.txt was checked line by line.
verdicts.baseRate: 23 states/UTs have 2 or more central jails. Delhi (207.2%) is the highest. Next are Maharashtra 175.4% (9 jails) and MP 170.5% (11 jails), then 26 points or more below. The national rate is 120.7%. Because this is a ranking claim, the property singles Delhi out rather than describing most states. The ≥2 cutoff conveniently removes Mizoram (one jail of 438 at 215.8%) and Uttarakhand (one jail, 143.1%). The record's d-field discloses Mizoram, so the cutoff is stated, not hidden. Overcrowding in Delhi is shown even without the cutoff: all Delhi jails together run at 200.2% (Table 1.3), the highest of any state/UT on the all-jail measure. Undertrials are 88.8% of Delhi's inmates against 73.5% all-India (Table 2.2), which supports the innocent reading.
verdicts.denialFound: None found, and not asked. The claim alleges no wrongdoing, so no response is needed. The figures are self-reported by the Delhi Prisons Department to NCRB ("As per data provided by States/UTs").
verdicts.innocentReading: Delhi's prisons (Tihar, Rohini and Mandoli) serve a metropolitan court system with a very high undertrial share: 88.8% against 73.5% nationally (PSI 2023 Table 2.2). Capacity has not grown with remand inflow. Prisons are run by GNCTD, while Delhi Police reports to the MHA, so the occupancy figure does not attribute blame to either authority. Tihar has run above 150% for well over a decade under governments of different parties. On symmetry, the same lens puts BJP-run Maharashtra and MP next in line. No party-political reading follows.
verdicts.reason: Every number checks against PSI 2023 Table 1.4: 14 jails, capacity 9,346, inmates 19,362, 207.2%, national 120.7%. The ranking among states/UTs with 2 or more central jails holds; the runner-up is Maharashtra at 175.4%. The claim implies no impropriety, and the source URL is live. The one flaw is in the text field: "not policing" overstates the innocent reading. The record's own innocentReading says "as much as of policing", and the evidence does not exclude policing (arrest and remand volume). Analytic is the right tier for a rank built from a primary table. The underlying figures are themselves documented.
verdicts.corrections: text: change "Innocent reading: undertrial load and court throughput, not policing" to "Innocent reading: undertrial load (88.8% of Delhi inmates vs 73.5% national, PSI Table 2.2), capacity additions and court throughput, as much as policing". This aligns it with the record's innocentReading field. d: optionally add "all-jail occupancy 200.2% (Table 1.3), also highest of any state/UT" so the ranking does not depend on the ≥2-central-jail cutoff. srcs label: add Table 2.2 if the undertrial share is cited. No change to tier, amounts, date or nodes.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim has no date. It is read as CRPF's training institutions listed on crpf.gov.in as of 2026-10-04. The site footer shows "last updated 02-02-2023", but the homepage carries news from 14-06-2026, so the menu is current enough to test against. The claim is a snapshot, so there is no tenure overlap to check.
verdicts.identityTest:
The 16 force:fp-crpf-* rows in footprint.json do match 16 entries in the Hindi menu: CTC Neemuch, Coimbatore, Mudkhed and Gwalior; RTC Jodhpur, Neemuch, Avadi, Rajgir, Amethi, Latur and Lethpora; CIAT Silchar, Shivpuri and Kalikiri; IED Management Institute Pune; and CIT Bengaluru. They fall in 10 states, 4 of them in MP. But the same Training menu (/hi/Training) also lists institutions the file leaves out:
- Internal Security Academy. Its page /hi/Training/Internal-Security-Academy describes "टीम ISA CRPF ... माउंट आबू" (Mount Abu, Rajasthan).
- CRPF Academy. Its page /hi/Training/CRPF-Academy says "के रि पु बल अकादमी गुरुग्राम" (Gurugram, Haryana).
- CTC (T&IT), CSJWT, DBTS and RAPO.
- RTC Peringome (Kerala). It appears as a tile ("पेरिंगोम") on /hi/Training/Recruit-Training-Centres, and the homepage news says "महानिदेशक केरिपुबल ने 14-06-2026 को RTC पेरिंगोम का दौरा किया".
So the record undercounts the institutions its own source names.
verdicts.baseRate: Concentration in MP does not single the state out. Maharashtra hosts 3 (Mudkhed, Latur, Pune) and Tamil Nadu 2. Once the omitted institutions are added, Rajasthan has 2 (Jodhpur, Mount Abu), and Haryana and Kerala enter the map. Training sites of central armed police forces (CAPFs) cluster where land, firing ranges and historic raising stations are, and this is true of every CAPF (BSF Tekanpur, also in MP; ITBP Mussoorie and Bhanu). No party-control comparison applies, because these sites were set up decades ago.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable. This is an analytic count that alleges no wrongdoing, so there was no party to ask. None found; not asked.
verdicts.innocentReading: The record's innocent reading holds. CRPF came into being in 1939, and the record names Neemuch as its raising station (the homepage gives the date but not the place). Central India also has large tracts of land for firing ranges. The claim fails on the count, not on any inference.
verdicts.reason: The record's own killIf condition is met: the menu the claim relies on turns out to be incomplete. The cited site names at least three more placeable training institutions: the Internal Security Academy at Mount Abu (Rajasthan), the CRPF Academy at Gurugram (Haryana) and RTC Peringome (Kerala). It also names four more that the claim does not place: CTC (T&IT), CSJWT, DBTS and RAPO. So "16 institutions in 10 states" is wrong. Counting only what the source places gives at least 19 in 12 states. "4 in MP" still holds, but the headline denominator does not.
verdicts.corrections:
Kill footprint:c014 as written. If it is rewritten, here are the fixes:
- Add force:fp-crpf-isa-mount-abu (st rj, city Mount Abu), force:fp-crpf-academy-gurugram (st hr, city Gurugram, Kadarpur) and force:fp-crpf-rtc-peringome (st kl, city Peringome, Kannur).
- Placing CTC (T&IT), CSJWT and DBTS needs a source that gives their cities. Until one is found, record them as a void, not as rows.
- Rewrite the lab as "at least 19 named training institutions in at least 12 states; MP hosts 4 (Neemuch x2, Gwalior, Shivpuri); 3 more menu entries unplaced".
- Change the d field: the English sub-pages are 404, but the Hindi sub-pages (/hi/Training/...) open and give places.
- Change upgradeIf to "the CTC (T&IT), CSJWT and DBTS locations are sourced".
- Keep the tier at analytic and keep the innocentReading.

verdicts.dateTest: Restated as: MoD de-notified one cantonment (Khasyol, HP) between the 2023-03-20 RS reply (62) and the DGDE page updated 2025-10-21 (61). The dates line up, but the record never fixes the date and calls the mechanism unconfirmed. PIB PRID 1942023 (24 Jul 2023, RS written reply by RRM Ajay Bhatt) prints it: "One Cantonment namely, KhasYol has already been de-notified w.e.f. 27.04.2023." The Tribune reported a ministry notification dated April 27. So the drop happened in April 2023, five weeks after the 62 list, under a stated policy. It was not a lone event spread across 'thirteen years'. The '2012 to 2025, one drop' framing turns a 2023 policy start into a thirteen-year average.
verdicts.identityTest: The entity matches. The PIB 2012 list (relid 90277, Antony LS reply) prints 'KhasYol' under Western Command. The PIB 2023 state-wise list prints '10 Khasyol' under Himachal Pradesh (7). On the DGDE page I counted Central 24, Eastern 4, Northern 1, Southern 19, Western 12 and South Western 1, which is 61. Khasyol is absent. 'Khasyol' and 'Yol' (Kangra) are the same cantonment, and the press calls it Yol. There is no confusion with any other unit.
verdicts.baseRate: The 'abolition' premise covers almost every cantonment, so it cannot single any one out. PIB 1942023 says modalities to excise civil areas from 58 cantonments went to the state governments. With Khasyol already de-notified, that is 59 of the 62 counted in 2023 (about 95%). The three left off the list are Badamibagh, Jammu and Chakrata. A land-to-builders story about any one cantonment needs a record for that cantonment, not this programme. Symmetry: the excision list includes cantonments in opposition-run states, among them Secunderabad (Telangana), Cannanore (Kerala), Belgaum (Karnataka), Barrackpore, Jalapahar and Lebong (West Bengal), and the HP cantonments. Khasyol itself is in Congress-run Himachal (since Dec 2022). The Tribune says civilian residents and state governments had long asked for excision. I did not run a UPA-II comparison. The 2012 list shows 62 and no excision programme then.
verdicts.denialFound: No denial addressed to the 'handed to builders' allegation was found, and I found no record that MoD was asked about it. MoD's stated reason, PIB 1942023 (24 Jul 2023): "In order to bring uniformity in municipal laws governing civil areas of Cantonments and adjoining State Municipal areas, it has been decided to consider to excise civil areas of certain Cantonments and merge them with neighbouring State municipalities." https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=1942023
verdicts.innocentReading: This is municipal normalisation, not a sale. Civil areas of colonial-era cantonments go to state municipalities so residents can use state welfare schemes and MoD stops paying for civic upkeep. Military areas become 'exclusive military stations' under Army control. For Khasyol, the Tribune (2023) reports that "the military area within the cantonment will be converted into a military station and the civil area will be merged with the municipality" (Dharamshala MC). Under the third modified proposal (Deccan Chronicle, 9 Aug 2024), proprietary rights over civic assets go to states and municipalities "at no cost", and "ownership of vacant land parcels will remain with the MoD". In this reading the transferee is the state or municipality, not a private builder. The one opening for the narrative is in the same report: if transferred land is sold or leased, 50 per cent of the income goes to a share. That is a monetisation clause, not a record of any transfer to a builder.
verdicts.reason: The three cited sources do say 62, 62 and 61, so the numbers are right. The framing is refuted. 'One documented drop in thirteen years, no land-transfer record opened' leaves out a primary PIB record (PRID 1942023, 24 Jul 2023). That record confirms the abolition half of the narrative as stated policy: civil areas of 58 cantonments are to be excised, and Khasyol was de-notified w.e.f. 27.04.2023. A March 2024 MoD notification (Tribune, 8 Mar 2024) then listed areas in 10 cantonments for excision. So 'cantonments are being abolished' is documented in substance: cantonment status is being dissolved, the civil areas are merged and the military areas are kept as military stations. Only the motive clause ('so defence land can be handed to builders') lacks support. The available records name states and municipalities as transferees and say MoD keeps vacant land. The record's own falsifier ('a record that Khasyol's land remains with the Army as a military station') is already met by public reporting, and the record did not look. Calling the whole narrative 'speculative' on 'one drop' understates the premise and overstates our ignorance of the mechanism. The narrative should be split: the excision programme as documented (PIB 1942023), and the builders motive as unsupported or speculative. The assessment itself is our own analysis, so it should carry an innocentReading.
verdicts.corrections: 1) narrative:0 strongestCase: replace 'the Government has for years discussed excising civil areas' with the documented record. Third modified proposal: if transferred land is sold/leased, 50% of income shared [reported, Deccan Chronicle 2024-08-09]." 2) narrative:0 strongestCounter: delete 'One de-notification in thirteen years'. verdicts.dateTest: The claim reads: India (SIPRI country series) had a military burden of 2.3% of GDP in calendar year 2024, the median of the top 15 spenders, and ranked 5th in dollars. Every figure comes from the same SIPRI April 2025 release, so there is no window mismatch. The 'from: 2024' field is correct. The PRS source is out of window. It cites SIPRI 2023 data (India 4th, $84 bn, 2.4%) and the MoD budget-to-GDP ratio for 2025-26 (1.9%), not 2024.
verdicts.identityTest: The subject 'min:ministry-of-defence' is a loose fit. SIPRI's India figure is a national total that includes paramilitary forces: PRS says 'This includes spending on paramilitary forces', and SIPRI's methodology is the same. So the 2.3% is not the MoD budget. PRS puts the MoD's own figure at 'India is estimated to spend 1.9% of its GDP on defence' (2025-26). The peer set is exactly SIPRI Table 1, ranks 1-15. No entity is mismatched.
verdicts.baseRate: SIPRI 2024 Table 1, ranks 1-15, burden sorted: 1.4 (Japan), 1.6 (Italy), 1.7 (China), 1.9 (Germany), 1.9 (Australia), 2.1 (France), 2.3 (India), 2.3 (UK), 2.6 (South Korea), 3.4 (USA), 4.2 (Poland), 7.1 (Russia), 7.3 (Saudi Arabia), 8.8 (Israel), 34 (Ukraine). The 8th of 15 is 2.3, so the median is correct. India is tied with the UK at that value. Seven of the other fourteen spend a larger share and six a smaller one; the record text is correct. The world burden is 2.5%. By construction, being at the median does not single India out from its peers. That is the claim's point, and it alleges nothing.
verdicts.denialFound: None found, and none was asked for. The claim is a neutral benchmark that alleges nothing, so no party has anything to respond to.
verdicts.innocentReading: India spends close to the peer-group norm. The 2.3% includes paramilitary spending, so it overstates the MoD-only burden, which PRS puts at about 1.9% for 2025-26. The Standing Committee's 3% figure is a domestic target, not a peer norm. These benign readings are already the claim's own reading. Nothing in it implies under- or over-spending or wrongdoing.
verdicts.reason: The SIPRI fact sheet, which I opened, confirms every number. Table 1 lists 'India 86.1 ... 2.3', rank 5. The text says 'India, the fifth biggest military spender in the world in 2024, increased its spending to $86.1 billion'. The world burden is 2.5%. Recomputing the median of the 15 burden figures gives 2.3. The claim does not chain facts into an implication. It is a pure comparison, so analytic is the right tier. The weak point is the second source: PRS does not support the 2024 figures. It uses 2023 SIPRI data (India 4th, 2.4%) and a different measure (MoD budget, 1.9% of GDP). It supports only the context about the Standing Committee's 3% figure.
verdicts.corrections: (1) Label the PRS source as context only: '2023 SIPRI comparison and Standing Committee 3% recommendation; PRS gives 1.9% MoD budget/GDP for 2025-26, a different measure'. Alternatively, drop it from the srcs of the 2.3%/fifth claim. (2) Add to d: 'SIPRI's India figure includes paramilitary forces; MoD-budget-only burden is lower (PRS: 1.9% in 2025-26).' (3) Add to d or lab: 'tied with the UK at 2.3%'. (4) Optionally re-point s from min:ministry-of-defence to a national 'India (SIPRI)' node, or note that the SIPRI total goes beyond the MoD. (5) The citation 'table 1 and p. 5' is fine. The 'fifth biggest' sentence is in the India paragraph on p. 4-5.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim restated: the Ministry of Defence's 2025-26 BE allocates about 24% to pensions and about 50% to pay plus pensions (PRS, 4 Feb 2025), and in 2022-23 P&A plus pension were 79% of MoD revenue expenditure (ORF Issue Brief 567, 16 Aug 2023). Each figure sits in the right fiscal year in its own source. One caveat: ORF's 2022-23 figure is a budget estimate, not actuals. ORF says "In 2022-23, P&A and Pension will add up to INR 287,040 crore, or 79 percent of the MoD's total revenue expenditure", and its Figure 1 note reads "Figures for 2021-22 and 2022-23 are revised and budget estimates". The claim should label 2022-23 as BE. Edge from:'2025' is fine for the PRS half. The ORF half dates from 2023.
verdicts.identityTest: The actor is the Ministry of Defence, the same body both sources name. One wording problem: Rs 6,81,210 crore is the MoD's total allocation across all its demands (MoD Civil, Defence Services Revenue, Capital Outlay, Defence Pensions), not a single "defence demand". PRS says: "the central government has allocated Rs 6,81,210 crore for the Ministry of Defence". PRS also notes that "Salaries include pay and allowances of the armed forces, auxiliary forces, civilians, research and development, and salary expenditure of the civil estimates." So "pay" includes civilians and R&D staff, not only the armed forces. PRS adds that salaries "could be an underestimate as detailed breakup for revenue expenditure on Rashtriya Rifles, National Cadet Corps, and the Agnipath cadre is not available."
verdicts.baseRate: Not discriminating, and the claim makes no accusation. A large personnel and pension share is structural for the MoD under every government. From ORF's own numbers, pensions were about 18% of MoD spending in 2013-14 under UPA-II (Rs 45,500 crore). PRS reports 24% in 2025-26 under the NDA. The rise is put down to OROP and the 7th CPC. The same lens applied to the UPA-II years gives the same descriptive reading: a high committed share. No rival, state or vendor control applies, because this is a budget-composition statistic, not conduct.
verdicts.denialFound: None found, and none was sought. The claim imputes no conduct to any party, so no response is owed. The figures are the government's own budget numbers as transcribed by PRS.
verdicts.innocentReading: Pensions are deferred pay owed under service contracts. Their share rose because of policy choices about people: OROP (2015) and the 7th CPC (2016). It does not show waste. PRS also notes that the 2025-26 pension line is inflated by a one-off Rs 8,000 crore recovery from a deposit account. One error in the record's innocentReading: it says "about 26.8 lakh pensioners", but ORF gives 32,94,181 pensioners as of 1 April 2021 (26,79,645 military veterans or dependents plus 6,14,536 defence civilians). The pension line covers both groups.
verdicts.reason: Every number checks out against the sources, which I opened and quoted. In the PRS PDF, Table 2 has Pension 1,60,795, Salaries 1,77,923 and Total 6,81,210 for 2025-26 BE. The text says "In 2025-26, 24% of the total defence budget is estimated to be spent on pension" and "Salaries and pension account for 50% of the estimated spending on defence in 2025-26." The ORF brief says "79 percent of the MoD's total revenue expenditure" for 2022-23, and gives pension growth of 163% against 107% for MoD overall between 2013-14 and 2022-23. My arithmetic: 23.6% and 49.7%. The claim does not combine facts to imply wrongdoing, names no individual and contains no operational detail. Analytic is a conservative tier. Because both outlets state these exact percentages themselves, 'reported' would also be defensible. The fixes needed are wording only: say BE, say "MoD total allocation", and correct the pensioner count.
verdicts.corrections: 1. text/lab: replace "the 2025-26 defence demand" with "the MoD's total 2025-26 BE allocation (Rs 6,81,210 crore, all demands)". 2. text/d: change "79% of revenue expenditure 2022-23" to "79% of MoD revenue expenditure, 2022-23 BE (ORF, Aug 2023)". 3. d: add PRS's caveats that "salaries" includes civilians, R&D and civil estimates but leaves out Rashtriya Rifles, NCC and the Agnipath cadre, and that the 2025-26 pension line includes a Rs 8,000 crore deposit-account recovery. 4. innocentReading: change "about 26.8 lakh pensioners" to "about 32.9 lakh pensioners (26.8 lakh military veterans or dependents plus 6.1 lakh defence civilians, as of 1 Apr 2021, per ORF)". 5. Optional: the tier could be raised to 'reported' with note 'reported: PRS transcription of Union Budget 2025-26', because the percentages are stated verbatim by PRS and ORF, not computed by us. Keeping 'analytic' is acceptable.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim reads: PRS Legislative Research reported, on 4 Feb 2025, that the Ministry of Defence is 13% of central expenditure in 2025-26 BE, down from 17% in 2014-15, and that defence is 1.9% of GDP against the Standing Committee on Defence's 2018 recommendation of about 3%. The PDF is dated February 4, 2025, which matches the record's from=2025-02. The 2025-26 figures are Budget Estimates. The 17% for 2014-15 comes from PRS's time series, which mixes actuals and BE/RE, so the comparison is actual against BE. PRS states this mix in its own note ("BE is budget estimate and RE is revised estimate"). Neither the dates nor the ministers involved have an overlap problem, because the claim is purely descriptive.
verdicts.identityTest: The entity is correct: the Ministry of Defence demand as a whole, Rs 6,81,210 crore including pensions and civil. It is not the narrower "Defence Services" figure. Quoted from p.1: "In 2025-26, the Ministry has been allocated Rs 6,81,210 crore ... The allocation towards the Ministry is the largest across all ministries and accounts for 13% of the total expenditure of the central government." And: "In 2014-15, the Centre spent 17% of its total budget on defence which reduced to 13% as per the budget estimates of 2025-26. Between 2013-14 and 2025-26, compared to an annual increase of 9% in defence spending, total central government expenditure increased at an annual rate of 10%." And: "The Standing Committee on Defence (2018) had recommended that the Ministry of Defence should be allocated a fixed budget of about 3% of GDP ... In 2025-26, India is estimated to spend 1.9% of its GDP on defence." Rough cross-check: 6.81 lakh crore against Budget at a Glance total expenditure of about 50.65 lakh crore gives about 13.4%. Against nominal GDP BE of about 357 lakh crore it gives about 1.9%. Every number, the fiscal year, the stage and the actor match the source.
verdicts.baseRate: The figures are not discriminating, and the claim alleges no wrongdoing. No Indian government since the early 1990s has met the 3%-of-GDP level. PRS's own chart shows a steady decline from 2013-14 onward. The UPA-II control (FY2009-14) had defence also falling as a share of GDP and of central spending, and also below 3%. Defence's share shrinking as the overall budget grows faster is the normal pattern for India. The 2014-15 starting year happens to be the first NDA budget. That could be read as a partisan baseline, so a UPA-II comparison should sit next to it.
verdicts.denialFound: The Ministry of Defence's position appears inside the same PRS PDF (p.2), citing the Standing Committee report: "According to the Ministry of Defence, spending 3% of India's GDP on the defence sector will lead to much higher allocations which the defence services may not be able to absorb." This is the Ministry's own documented response on the 3% benchmark. No denial of the share figures exists, and none is needed because they are arithmetic from budget documents.
verdicts.innocentReading: The defence budget is growing in absolute terms (9% a year) while total central spending grows faster (10% a year), so defence's share falls without any cut. The Ministry itself says the services could not absorb 3% of GDP. The GDP ratio counts MoD pensions; leaving pensions out lowers it by about 0.5 percentage points. It also excludes MHA's paramilitary forces (CAPFs).
verdicts.reason: I could not refute the claim. The PRS PDF states each figure word for word: 13% in 2025-26 BE, 17% in 2014-15, 1.9% of GDP, and the Standing Committee on Defence (2018) recommendation of about 3%. The figures also roughly reproduce from Budget at a Glance totals. "Reported" is the right tier: PRS is one credible outlet doing analysis from published documents. It would move to "documented" once the ratios are rebuilt directly from indiabudget.gov.in. The claim is fair only if three things are added: that 2025-26 is BE, that the committee report is from 2018, and the Ministry's absorption-capacity response that PRS itself quotes.
verdicts.corrections:
1. text: change to "Defence 13% of Union expenditure in 2025-26 BE (17% in 2014-15); 1.9% of GDP vs Standing Committee on Defence (2018) recommendation of about 3% (PRS)."
2. d: add "MoD stated 3% of GDP would produce allocations the services may not be able to absorb (PRS p.2, citing the Standing Committee report)." Also add that the 1.9% includes pensions; excluding them gives about 1.4-1.5%.
3. Add a symmetryCheck noting the decline began before 2014. Report the UPA-II FY2009-14 share and GDP ratio from the same Budget documents, so the 2014-15 baseline is not read as partisan.
4. upgradeIf: keep as is. When the union-defence domain reproduces 6,81,210 / total expenditure and / nominal GDP from Budget at a Glance 2025-26, raise to documented.
5. Leave tier=reported and pred=analytic as they are.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim restated: PRS Legislative Research reported, in its Feb 2025 DFG analysis, that MHA's police allocation in the 2025-26 Budget Estimate was Rs 1,60,391 crore, 69% of the ministry total. The figure is a BE for FY 2025-26. The record's "from: 2025-02" matches the date the PRS note was published. Nothing about tenure or ownership needs to overlap, because the actor is the Union Budget. One caveat: the 2025-26 Revised Estimates were published in the Feb 2026 Union Budget, so this BE figure may since have been revised. The claim names the stage as BE, so it is not wrong, but it is not the latest figure.
verdicts.identityTest: The entity is right. The PDF is "Demand for Grants 2025-26 Analysis — Home Affairs" (PRS, Niranjana S Menon). Table 1 gives "Police 1,24,715 / 1,46,833 / 1,60,391 / 9%" and "Total ... 2,33,211 / 6%". The "85%" figure refers to the police head, not the whole MHA, and the claim's wording "85% of it" reads it the same way.
verdicts.baseRate: Not applicable. This is a descriptive budget-share figure with an 'analytic' predicate. It implies no wrongdoing and does not single out any actor, so there is no discriminating property to test against a base rate. Symmetry check: the same arithmetic run on a UPA-II-era MHA DFG would give a similar result, with CAPFs dominating the police head. The claim does not depend on which government is in power.
verdicts.denialFound: None found, and none was sought. The claim alleges nothing, so no party has anything to deny.
verdicts.innocentReading: The Union's police demand pays for forces the Union itself runs: CAPFs, Delhi Police, J&K Police after 2019, and border infrastructure. State police are paid for from state budgets and are not in this number. The 85% concentration is therefore structural and does not reflect a policy choice. The record already carries this reading.
verdicts.reason: I could not refute the claim. Every number matches the source PDF text. Quotes: "In 2025-26, Rs 1,60,391 crore has been budgeted for police expenditure. A majority of this expenditure (85% of total allocation) is towards the Central Armed Police Forces (CAPF), the Delhi and J&K police, and border infrastructure." Table 1 is headed "69% of the Ministry's expenditure in 2025-26 will be towards police". "Rs 21,258 crore has been allocated to Delhi police and J&K police together ... 13% of the total allocation towards police." The arithmetic checks out against the BE column of Table 2: CAPF 1,09,037 + Delhi Police 11,932 + J&K Police 9,326 + Border Infrastructure 5,597 = 1,35,892, which is 84.7% of 1,60,391. 11,932 + 9,326 = 21,258. 1,60,391 / 2,33,211 = 68.8%. The claim does not combine separate facts to suggest something none of them says. The tier is 'reported' because it rests on a single credible secondary analysis built from published Budget documents. 'Documented' would be justified once the figure is reproduced from the Union Budget Expenditure Profile or from the MHA demand itself.
verdicts.corrections: 1. Optionally make "85%" exact in field d: "CAPF 1,09,037 + Delhi Police 11,932 + J&K Police 9,326 + Border Infrastructure 5,597 = 1,35,892 crore (84.7% of police, BE)". 2. Note in d that "border infrastructure" is the PRS Table 2 line 'Border Infrastructure' (5,597), which is separate from 'Police Infrastructure' (4,379). 3. Add the PRS HTML page as a second source link if one exists. To meet the upgradeIf condition, reproduce the figures from the Union Budget 2025-26 MHA police demand (indiabudget.gov.in, sbe48 or the equivalent demand number), not from 'Demand 48' as the record assumes; check the demand number. 4. Add a note that the 2025-26 RE (Union Budget, Feb 2026) may supersede the BE figure; record it in 'supersededBy' if the RE differs materially. No change to the tier.

verdicts.dateTest: As written: "Ministry of Defence denied c006 from 2019-03." The two parts of the claim come from different dates. (1) The privilege argument was made by the Attorney General for the Union in the review proceedings (March 2019) and rejected on 2019-04-10. So 2019-03 fits that part. (2) The price defence predates c006 by months. Jaitley's 9%/20% statement and M.J. Akbar's Times of India op-ed (₹538 to ₹737 crore, ₹670 crore, 9%, 20%) are from the 2018 controversy. Ravi Shankar Prasad's €100.85m vs €91.75m comparison was made in the July 2018 Macron row (Wikipedia places it just after the no-confidence debate of 20 July 2018). Modi's "liars" remark was on 2018-12-16. None of these statements can be a response to a 2019-04-10 ruling. The price material also does not contradict c006 at all, since c006 is only about whether the documents are admissible. The `contra` edge holds only for the privilege part.
verdicts.identityTest: This test fails. The record says "the then Defence Minister said the 2007 bid (₹526 crore per aircraft, escalating to ₹737 crore by 2015) and the 2016 IGA basic price (~₹670 crore) were not comparable and the IGA saved about 20%". Wikipedia gives the ₹737 crore, 9% and 20% figures to two other people. First, M.J. Akbar, Minister of State for External Affairs, in an op-ed: "Dassault's bid had been accepted at ₹538 crore along with a price escalation formula that would have increased the price to ₹737 crore in 2015... IGA price of ₹670 crore for each basic aircraft represented a 9% decrease... the IGA price was 20% lower". Second, Finance Minister Arun Jaitley: "the basic aircraft was 9% cheaper and the overall agreement was 20% cheaper". The Defence Minister, Sitharaman, said only that "the prices could not be compared" and that "the figure of ₹526 crore quoted by Congress represented the cost of basic aircraft". The ~₹670 crore figure came from MoS Defence Subhash Bhamre in Parliament. The record also merges ₹526 crore (Congress's figure) with Akbar's ₹538 crore base. The subject `min:ministry-of-defence` is wrong for most of the content. The privilege argument was made by the Attorney General for the Union of India (SC order: "The learned Attorney General contends that ... three documents unauthorizedly removed from the office of the Ministry of Defence"). The price defence came from the Finance Minister, the Law Minister, the MoS External Affairs and the PM.
verdicts.baseRate: The test barely applies: this is a single case, and the claim records a respondent's position. On symmetry, governments of both alliances claim secrecy over defence pricing. Wikipedia records Jaitley citing 15 UPA-era refusals to disclose arms expenditure, and the 2008 security agreement was signed by UPA minister A.K. Antony. For Bofors, the control case, the same lens would record the Rajiv Gandhi government's denials as contra in the same way. Recording the government's case is evenhanded and should stay.
verdicts.denialFound: This record is itself the government's response. Contrary material exists. (a) The SC order of 2019-04-10 (https://indiankanoon.org/doc/126750916/) rejected the privilege argument, saying s.123 covers "unpublished public records", while "the three documents have been published in different editions of 'The Hindu'". (b) The CAG report of February 2019 is reported to have found the IGA about 2.86% cheaper, not 9–20%. literature.json line ~1010 records this as not opened because cag.gov.in was unreachable. (c) Congress (Surjewala, Rahul Gandhi) disputes the comparison (Wikipedia).
verdicts.innocentReading: The government's case is that a basic-aircraft price cannot be compared with a fully loaded, India-specific package. On that view, the 2007 bid with its 3.9% escalation is the right baseline, and on that basis the IGA came out cheaper. This reading is internally coherent and is the defence the record should carry. The record's errors are attribution errors, not a slant.
verdicts.reason: The headline survives: the privilege claim was rejected by the SC, and a 9–20% saving was claimed. The SC order confirms the privilege part verbatim, and Wikipedia confirms the 9%/20% figures. But the `d` field puts figures in the mouth of "the then Defence Minister" when the source gives them to M.J. Akbar and Arun Jaitley. It also uses ₹526 crore where that chain started at ₹538 crore. And the subject is MoD for statements made by other ministers and the AG. Putting a statement in the mouth of an office-holder who did not make it fails the identity test. The 2019-03 date and the `contra` target also fit only the privilege part. Treat the record as refuted until it is corrected; once corrected it stands at `reported`.
verdicts.corrections: 1) d: replace "the then Defence Minister said the 2007 bid (₹526 crore ... ₹737 crore by 2015) ... saved about 20%" with: "Defence Minister Sitharaman said the prices were not comparable and that Congress's ₹526 crore was the basic-aircraft cost. MoS Defence Bhamre told Parliament the IGA cost was ~₹670 crore per aircraft. Finance Minister Jaitley said the basic aircraft was 9% cheaper and the package 20% cheaper. MoS External Affairs M.J. Akbar wrote that the bid accepted at ₹538 crore would have escalated to ₹737 crore by 2015." 2) s: the privilege argument should be `Union of India / Attorney General`. Best fix is to split into two records: c007a (privilege, subject Union/AG, from 2019-03, contra c006, with the SC order as source) and c007b (price defence, 2018, contra to the Congress overpricing narrative, not to c006). 3) from: 2019-03 holds only for the privilege part; the price statements belong to the 2018 controversy, with Modi's remark on 2018-12-16. 4) Add to d: "CAG (Feb 2019) reported as 2.86% cheaper — not opened". 5) text: "like-for-like saving 9–20% claimed" should read "9% (basic aircraft) to 20% (package) claimed by ministers Jaitley/Akbar/Prasad".

verdicts.dateTest: I tested three dated parts. (1) Swiss documents: the Delhi HC judgment (indiankanoon 561739) says "the second set of documents was received in January 1997 from the Swiss authority". It also lists Swiss tranches received in December 1990, December 1999, 2 June 2000 and 4 October 2000. The McIntyre/Hinduja payments were "revealed" by the December 1999 set, not the 1997 set. So "1997" is one tranche among several, and Wikipedia's "some 500 documents" figure carries no citation. (2) Closure: Wikipedia says that on 4 March 2011 a Delhi court allowed CBI to close the case against Quattrocchi (citing ET, 5 March 2011, and TOI). That matches the claim. (3) SC dismissal: Hindustan Times (7 August 2026) says "A Supreme Court bench on Thursday dismissed the last existing appeal against the 2005 Delhi high court judgment". 6 August 2026 was a Thursday, and DNA and Republic (7 August 2026) agree. The dates hold.
verdicts.identityTest: The claim fails on who filed the plea. The record's d-field says "CBI's later attempts to revive ended with the Supreme Court dismissing the final plea on 2026-08-06". HT says the dismissed appeal was filed by "advocate Ajay K Agrawal, who had challenged the high court verdict as a private appellant". It adds that the SC "had already dismissed the Central Bureau of Investigation's appeal against the same high court judgment in November 2018 ... delay of 4,522 days". The 2026 order is therefore not CBI's. It is also about the 2005 Delhi HC discharge of the Hindujas and AB Bofors, not the 2011 Quattrocchi closure. The killIf condition ("2026 order concerns a different petition") is not triggered, because this is the last surviving plea. But the claim and its framing must not attribute it to CBI. The other names match the sources: Italian agent = Ottavio Quattrocchi / AE Services; agents = Svenska/Win Chadha, AE Services/Quattrocchi, McIntyre/Moresco (Hindujas).
verdicts.baseRate: Not a cohort property, so a base-rate test does not apply. This is a single-case enforcement chronology. The SPEC symmetry control is Rafale. The SC dismissed the Rafale petitions (Dec 2018) and the review petitions (Nov 2019), CBI never registered an FIR, and a French PNF judicial inquiry opened in 2021. The Rafale record should carry identical fields: agency action, closure, final SC disposal, and whether recipient-side evidence exists. Bofors has a documented agent-payment trail but no recipient trail. Rafale has neither in an Indian court record.
verdicts.denialFound: The exculpatory record is in the cited source itself. Delhi HC, 4 February 2004 (https://indiankanoon.org/doc/561739/): the ASG for CBI conceded that, as to bribe receipt by public servants, "till date there was none". The court held the late PM "is entitled to be seen as innocent". BBC, 25 April 2012 (cited on Wikipedia): Swedish investigator Sten Lindstrom said there was "No evidence Rajiv Gandhi took bribe". The JPC report (1988) found no evidence that the payments violated Indian law. I found no separate 2026 statement from the Hindujas or Bofors, and none appears to have been sought. Both Hinduja respondents who died (Srichand and Gopichand) are deceased.
verdicts.innocentReading: Bofors paid commissions to agents. That breached its assurance to the Government of India that it used no middlemen, and the HC judgment documents those payments. But a payment to an agent is not a bribe to a public servant. In 2004 the prosecution conceded it had no evidence of receipt by officials. The 2011 and 2026 disposals reflect evidentiary failure, deaths, and a 4,522-day CBI delay rather than a finding of either guilt or innocence. The claim's wording "recipient side never established" already states this reading correctly.
verdicts.reason: The core conjunction survives. Payments to agents are confirmed by a primary court record: the Delhi HC says CBI "succeeded in tracing the Swiss accounts of 'Commission Agents' employed by M/s A.B. Bofors wherein illegal payments received by them from Bofors as commission were deposited". The same judgment records the ASG's concession that there was no evidence of public servants receiving bribes. The 4 March 2011 Quattrocchi closure and the 6 August 2026 SC dismissal are reported by multiple outlets (HT, DNA, Republic, NewsX). Two errors need fixing. First, the d-field attributes the 2026 plea to CBI, but it was the private appellant Ajay K Agrawal's appeal; CBI's own appeal died in November 2018 on delay. Second, "Swiss documents (1997)" understates the timeline: the documents came in tranches from 1990 to 2000, and the 1997 tranche is not shown to be the one that "establishes" the payments. As sourced, the record rests on Wikipedia for 2011 and 2026, so it stays at reported. It becomes documented once the HT and DNA URLs (or the SC order itself) are added; the agent-payment and no-recipient elements already rest on a court order.
verdicts.corrections: 1. d-field: replace "CBI's later attempts to revive ended with the Supreme Court dismissing the final plea on 2026-08-06" with "The SC dismissed CBI's own appeal against the 2005 HC discharge in November 2018 for a 4,522-day delay. verdicts.dateTest: The claim reads: MoD (UPA-II, Defence Minister A.K. Antony) terminated the 8 Feb 2010 AWIL contract on 2014-01-01 and had recovered ₹2,068 crore by June 2014. Both the actor's tenure and the contract window overlap the action. The MoD statement dated 1 January 2014 is reported by CNBC and Business Standard on 2014-01-01. Wikipedia says "in January 2014", and its cited NIE article is dated 2014/01/01. Wikipedia gives the June 2014 total recovery date: "in June 2014, the Indian government encashed ₹18.18 billion, taking the total amount recovered so far to ₹20.68 billion." The date test passes.
verdicts.identityTest: The actor is the Ministry of Defence, Government of India. The counterparty is AgustaWestland International Ltd (AWIL), a Finmeccanica subsidiary. The contract is the one signed 8 Feb 2010 for 12 AW101 VVIP helicopters, about €556–560m or ₹3,600 crore. The source names this same entity and contract. Units are correct: ₹20.68 billion = ₹2,068 crore, made up of ₹250 crore encashed in India in January 2014 plus ₹1,818 crore from Italian bank guarantees in June 2014.
verdicts.baseRate: This does not apply in a discriminating sense. The edge records a single enforcement act, not a shared property. Termination plus bank-guarantee encashment under an integrity pact is rare among Indian defence contracts, so the claim is not swept up in a ≥80% base rate. On symmetry: the government that awarded the contract (UPA-II) also cancelled it. The edge says nothing about which party benefits, so applying the same lens to NDA-era contracts creates no asymmetry.
verdicts.denialFound: No denial of the cancellation or of the recovery figure was found. AgustaWestland/Finmeccanica disputed that it had breached the contract and sought arbitration in 2013. In Italy, the first-instance court rejected India's bid on the guarantees on 2014-03-17 (Indian Express/NDTV, 18 Mar 2014), and the Milan appellate court reversed that. NDTV reported on 2016-04-29 that AgustaWestland had kept €106 million for the three delivered helicopters (https://www.ndtv.com/india-news/agusta-hasnt-returned-106-million-euros-for-3-choppers-sources-to-ndtv-1400632). In the May 2016 Rajya Sabha debate, the government restated the ₹2,068 crore recovery and said the three helicopters remained confiscated (http://www.mainstreamweekly.net/article6400.html; https://m.thewire.in/article/economy/rajya-sabhas-agustwestland-debate-counter-arguments-probe-delays-and-the-six-foot-tall-ghulam-nabi-azad). AgustaWestland was not asked by us; its position is that of a party in arbitration.
verdicts.innocentReading: This was routine contractual enforcement. Once bribery allegations surfaced in February 2013, the pre-contract integrity pact required the MoD to terminate the contract and encash the guarantees. The edge records enforcement and implies no further wrongdoing by the MoD. The ₹2,068 crore is gross encashment, not net loss recovery: India paid about ₹1,620 crore (45%) and kept three aircraft, and Agusta disputes €106m of it.
verdicts.reason: The cited source confirms every load-bearing element. Wikipedia quotes the cancellation "on grounds of breach of the Pre-contract Integrity Pact and the agreement by AWIL". It gives ₹250 crore encashed in January 2014 and ₹1,818 crore in June 2014, "taking the total amount recovered so far to ₹20.68 billion". Independent outlets confirm the 1 Jan 2014 MoD statement: CNBC (https://www.cnbc.com/2014/01/01/india-cancels-560-million-euro-agustawestland-helicopter-order.html) and Business Standard (https://www.business-standard.com/article/current-affairs/govt-scraps-agustawestland-chopper-deal-114010100555_1.html). Reporting of the 2016 Rajya Sabha debate repeats the ₹2,068 crore figure. The claim is not built from separate facts that only imply something together; it is a single, directly sourced enforcement act. The tier stays "reported" only because the record's sole source is Wikipedia. Adding the CNBC/Business Standard and India Today/Indian Express items, or the PIB release / Rajya Sabha record, would meet the "documented" bar.
verdicts.corrections: 1) Add primary or independent sources. Use CNBC and Business Standard for the 1 Jan 2014 MoD statement, India Today (2014-06-07) "India recovers Rs 1818 crore from AgustaWestland" for the figure, and the PIB release / Rajya Sabha debate of May 2016 as the upgrade path to "documented". Do not cite Wikipedia alone. 2) In `d`, say that ₹2,068 crore is gross bank-guarantee encashment. Add a contra noting that AgustaWestland reportedly retained €106m for the three delivered helicopters (NDTV, 2016-04-29) and that the arbitration and Italian litigation were contested. Remove or qualify any implication that the full amount paid was recovered net. 3) Set `from` 2014-01-01 for termination and `to` 2014-06 for recovery. The Italian Cassazione upheld the 2018-01-08 Milan acquittal on 2019-05-22. All of these dates fall after the February 2010 contract and the CBI probe ordered on 2013-02-12, and all are in the right order (PE 2013-02-25, then FIR, then arrests, then extradition). The cited Wikipedia page gives the extradition date two ways: line 11 says "extradited to India on 4 December 2018" and line 24 says "On 5 December 2018 ... was extradited". He landed on the night of 4 December. The record's 2018-12-04 is defensible, but the d field should note the 4/5 Dec ambiguity. The "Indian trial pending" part still holds as of 2026-10-04. The Delhi HC rejected Michel's plea for release on 2026-04-08 (supremetoday.ai). In May 2026 the SC asked the Centre to respond to his plea against continued detention, listed for July 2026 (barandbench.com). I found no verdict in an Indian court. Tyagi's tenure as IAF chief was 2004–07. The 2003 change to the helicopter specifications came before his tenure, under the NSA/PMO (Tyagi's defence). That does not affect the enforcement edge.
verdicts.identityTest: The source names each entity: "The FIR named 13 persons including: former Indian Air Force Chief, Air Chief Marshal S. P. Tyagi, his three brothers ... Satish Bagrodia, and Pratap Aggarwal ... The FIR also named four companies - Italy-based Finmeccanica, UK-based AgustaWestland and Chandigarh-based IDS Infotech and Aeromatrix." The middleman is Christian Michel James, a British national. The edge's subject "s":"agencies" is a generic bucket, not the specific agency. The actor of the FIR, the 2016 arrests and the CBI case is the CBI, and the ED runs the parallel PMLA case. The subject should point to the CBI node. The claim names nobody below public rank; it names no person at all.
verdicts.baseRate: This is a single dated enforcement record about one case, not a comparison, so no property is shared across a peer set and a base rate does not apply. Symmetry check: the paired control in SPEC/CONTRACT-force is Tatra/BEML. Its node exists but is a Wikipedia stub with no FIR, no chargesheet status and no outcome. So the identical-fields comparison cannot be run yet. That is a gap in the control, not a defect in this claim. A slow, unresolved Indian trial (more than 12 years since the FIR, no verdict) is the norm for high-profile CBI corruption cases: Bofors never reached trial, and the Tatra outcome is not recorded. So the delay does not single out this case.
verdicts.denialFound: Tyagi has repeatedly denied the allegations. He says the decision to change the specifications was taken by a group of senior officials before his tenure, and his counsel argued in court that "CBI in the last four years has never been able to establish any evidence against ex-air chief regarding receipt of any bribe" (https://www.india.com/news/india/sp-tyagi-granted-bail-in-agustawestland-chopper-scam-case-1724022/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shashindra_Pal_Tyagi). The UPA government initially said it had "nothing to hide" (Wikipedia, citing the JPC debate). Michel contests his detention and the added charges (Bar and Bench, 2026). The edge carries none of these as contra; it carries only the Italian court record as counter-record.
verdicts.innocentReading: An FIR and arrests are steps in an investigation, not findings of guilt. Twelve years with no Indian verdict fits ordinary CBI and trial-court delay, plus extradition-specialty litigation, as well as it fits a weak case. The Italian acquittals were for insufficient evidence. They do not prove the absence of a bribe, and they do not prove a bribe either. The claim as worded does not overreach toward guilt.
verdicts.reason: I opened the single cited source (the raw text of the Wikipedia article). It states every element of the claim. The FIR line reads: "registered an FIR on 13 March 2013. The FIR named 13 persons ... The FIR also named four companies". It reports the CBI arrests of 9 December 2016, Michel's extradition in December 2018, the Milan acquittal of 8 January 2018 "upheld by the Supreme Court of Cassazione on 22 May 2019", and Michel remaining "an accused in the separate CBI corruption case" in December 2025. 2026 reporting (Delhi HC 2026-04-08, SC hearings May–July 2026) confirms there is still no Indian verdict. Neither lens refutes the claim. One sentence is incomplete: "Italian courts ended in acquittal" leaves out that in August 2014 AgustaWestland SpA and AgustaWestland Ltd took a plea bargain (patteggiamento) in Busto Arsizio. That deal involved confiscation of EUR 7.5 million as proceeds of the alleged international corruption, plus administrative fines of EUR 80,000 and EUR 300,000. A patteggiamento is not a finding of guilt, but omitting it makes the claim read more exculpatory than the Italian record is. That calls for a correction, not a kill. The claim rests on one tertiary source whose underlying news reports (The Hindu, TOI) were not opened, so it stays "reported". That fits the contract, but it is not "documented".
verdicts.corrections: 1) Text/framing: change "Italian courts ended in acquittal (2018, upheld 2019)" to "Italian proceedings against the individual executives ended in acquittal (Milan appeal 2018-01-08, upheld by the Cassazione 2019-05-22); the two AgustaWestland companies took a 2014 Busto Arsizio plea bargain (EUR 7.5m confiscation plus administrative fines), which is not a guilt finding; consultant Haschke was acquitted on appeal in Brescia 2025-06-30". Add sources: Il Fatto Quotidiano 2014-08-28 (https://www.ilfattoquotidiano.it/2014/08/28/finmeccanica-agustawestland-patteggia-7-milioni-e-mezzo-per-tangenti-in-india/1101205/) and the Reuters 2025-07-01 report on the Haschke acquittal. 2) Subject node: replace "s":"agencies" with the CBI node (and add a separate ED edge for the PMLA case if one is wanted). 3) d field: note the 4/5 December 2018 extradition-date ambiguity in the source. 4) Update the status line: Delhi HC 2026-04-08 rejected Michel's plea for release; SC issued notice in May 2026 on his specialty/continued-detention challenge; no Indian verdict as of 2026-10. 5) Add a contra: Tyagi's denial and his counsel's statement in court (india.com, 2016). 6) Upgrade path: open the TOI FIR report and The Hindu PE/arrest reports cited by Wikipedia. Two independent outlets would meet the contract's bar for "documented". 7) The Tatra control node needs a matching FIR, chargesheet and outcome record before the SPEC symmetry check can be run.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim, put as actor-did-thing-when: on 2022-08-25 the CJI N.V. Ramana bench (with Surya Kant and Hima Kohli JJ) read out in open court the findings of the technical committee supervised by Justice R.V. Raveendran. The committee was set up by the order of 2021-10-27. Its report was filed in sealed cover before the hearing. So 2022-08-25 is the date the findings were disclosed in court, not the date the report was written or filed. The dates fit together, and the label should say "disclosed in court on 2022-08-25" rather than imply the committee acted that day.
verdicts.identityTest: The node is right: it is the Technical Committee constituted in paragraph 59 of Manohar Lal Sharma v Union of India (2021-10-27), with Naveen Kumar Chaudhary, Prabaharan P. and Ashwin Anil Gumaste as members and Justice Raveendran overseeing. One caution: the Wikipedia article (line 107) wrongly calls CJI Ramana the "head of the Supreme Court appointed committee". The record should not inherit that error. Ramana headed the bench. Raveendran supervised the committee.
verdicts.baseRate: Does not apply. This is a single factual report of a court-appointed inquiry's findings, not a claim about how common a property is. No comparison set is implied. On symmetry: the claim says nothing about wrongdoing, and it states that Pegasus was not conclusively shown.
verdicts.denialFound: In court, SG Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Union, answered the CJI's remark that the government had not cooperated with "I am not aware of that" (LiveLaw live-tweets, quoted by The Wire, 2022-08-25, https://thewire.in/law/supreme-court-pegasus-technical-committee). The Union's earlier position was the IT Minister's statement of 2021-07-19 that the reports had "no factual basis", plus its refusal on national-security grounds to file a detailed affidavit. The record already carries the second point but not the SG's in-court reply.
verdicts.innocentReading: Finding malware on 5 of 29 voluntarily submitted phones fits ordinary commercial malware or poor device security, and the committee itself said it could not attribute the malware to Pegasus. The Union's non-cooperation fits the national-security stance it had already taken before the Court. That is not proof that it procured or used the spyware. The claim, read as written, does not assert either point, so this reading does not contradict it.
verdicts.reason: The substance holds. The Wire (2022-08-25) says: "had found 'malware' in five out of the 29 devices submitted to it. The bench also noted that the Union government 'did not cooperate' with the expert committee... the committee found no conclusive proof of whether Pegasus was the malware used". Scroll says the same: "some malware was found on five of the phones... The committee had examined 29 mobile phones... took note of a finding by the panel that the Centre did not co-operate". Wikipedia also states it, citing Indian Express, Scroll and The Wire. The problem is the source chain in the record. Of its two sources, the indiankanoon link (doc 39021018) is the 2021-10-27 order that set up the committee. It contains nothing about 29 devices, malware on 5, inconclusive findings or non-cooperation, so it cannot support the claim. The other source is a tertiary Wikipedia page. The claim survives on retrieved press reporting, not on the sources the record actually cites. Two independent outlets (The Wire and Scroll, both also cited by Indian Express) would meet the contract's bar for "documented". Only upgrade once those outlets are attached. With the record's current sources, "reported" is the ceiling.

Name the findings as the committee's, relayed by the bench. (3) d: add the in-court response "SG Tushar Mehta: 'I am not aware of that'" (via LiveLaw/The Wire). verdicts.dateTest: Bombay HC ordered demolition on 2016-04-29. Wikipedia: "the Bombay high court on 29 April 2016, ordered the demolition of the building." That passes. HC quashed the Governor's Feb-2016 sanction to prosecute Ashok Chavan on 2017-12-22. Wikipedia: "Dec 22, 2017: HC allows Chavan's petition and quashes and sets aside Governor's order granting sanction to prosecute him." That passes. Patil commission report submitted April 2013 and tabled/rejected December 2013. That passes. "SC stay 2018" FAILS. The SC order is dated 22 July 2016, not 2018. Deccan Chronicle, 22-07-2016: the Centre was told to take possession and ensure no demolition, and the Solicitor General said "We will secure the building and there will be no demolition." ThePrint (2024-04-20) says the same: "The apex court did not pass any interim order, but directed the Centre to take possession ... The Army took possession of the building in July 2016." Wikipedia's "2018" comes from a mis-dated citation. The ET article it cites (articleshow/53464339) is from July 2016, and its "issue=18 July 2018" field is wrong.
verdicts.identityTest: The former CM is Ashok Chavan (CM 2008-2010), and the claim does not name him. The governor who granted sanction was C. Vidyasagar Rao (Feb 2016). The governor who refused it in Dec 2013 was K. Sankaranarayanan. The four indicted ex-CMs were Ashok Chavan, Vilasrao Deshmukh, Sushilkumar Shinde and Shivajirao Nilangekar Patil. The two ministers were Rajesh Tope and Sunil Tatkare, both former urban-development ministers. All of these match the source. The source URL redirects to "Adarsh Housing Society scandal", which is the same article. The edge's subject 'bombay-hc' is right for the HC orders, but the SC possession order is a Supreme Court act and not a Bombay HC one.
verdicts.baseRate: This does not discriminate as evidence of anything unusual. Large Indian corruption cases involving politicians very commonly run more than a decade with no trial verdict (2G, Bofors, CWG). Courts quashing prosecution sanction, and governors refusing or granting it, is routine litigation. The claim implies no wrongdoing beyond what the commission found, and it is a factual chronology rather than an inference, so this is acceptable.
verdicts.denialFound: Chavan has called the scandal a "political accident" (ThePrint, 2024-04-20, https://theprint.in/india/demolition-regularisation-pleas-pending-chavan-moves-on-but-mumbais-adarsh-society-languishes/2048404/). The HC quashed the sanction because the CBI "failed to furnish fresh evidence" ("In the absence of fresh material, the sanction cannot be sustained"). The Maharashtra cabinet first rejected the Patil report in Dec 2013 and then partially accepted it. The society's position is that the building is legal, and its appeal against the demolition order is pending in the SC. The record carries no denial or response from Chavan or the society. One should be added.
verdicts.innocentReading: Quashing the sanction was a procedural ruling: a second sanction needs fresh material, so the ruling is not a finding of innocence. The SC order keeps the status quo while the appeal is pending and is not a judgment on the merits. "No verdict" reflects the pace of the courts, and the case is still pending, not dropped. On symmetry: a UPA-era governor refused sanction (2013), an NDA-era governor granted it (2016), the HC quashed it (2017), and Chavan joined the BJP in Feb 2024. Reading the same facts under both governments gives the same result: an unresolved prosecution under both. Any framing should note the 2024 party switch so the record does not read as targeting one party.
verdicts.reason: The claim's own killIf says "Orders differ in date or scope", and the SC element triggers it. The claim says "SC stay 2018". Primary-adjacent reporting (Deccan Chronicle 22-07-2016; ThePrint 2024) puts the SC order on 22 July 2016 and says it was not a formal stay. It was a direction to the Centre to take possession and not demolish while the appeal is pending, and the Army took possession in July 2016. The rest of the claim checks out against the single Wikipedia source: the 2016-04-29 demolition order, the 2017-12-22 quashing of sanction, and the Patil commission's indictment of 4 ex-CMs, 2 ministers and 12 bureaucrats with 25 illegal allotments and 22 benami. As written, the claim is refuted on the date. With the date corrected and a non-Wikipedia outlet added, it can stay "reported". It would reach "documented" if the HC orders (2016-04-29, 2017-12-22) and the SC order of 22-07-2016 are opened on indiankanoon or the court portals.

Name Ashok Chavan as the former CM. Add "report partially accepted by the state cabinet after Dec 2013 rejection". Add a contra/response: Chavan calls it a "political accident" (ThePrint 2024-04-20), the HC quashed for want of fresh evidence, and the society's SC appeal is pending.
