verdicts.dateTest: Passes for the headline. The contention is that the petitioners (IESM, WP(C) 419/2016) challenged the 7 Nov 2015 MoD letter as 'one rank multiple pensions'. The SC bench of Chandrachud, Surya Kant and Vikram Nath JJ decided this on 16 Mar 2022. Judgment para 49(iv): 'Since the OROP definition is not arbitrary, it is not necessary for us to undertake the exercise of determining if the financial implications...'. Para 51 directs: 'a re-fixation exercise shall be carried out from 1 July 2019... paid over accordingly within a period of three months.' The Cabinet approved the 2019 revision on 23 Dec 2022 (PIB 1886168), about 9 months after the judgment and later than the three months the Court allowed. So 'happened only after the SC ordered it' is right on dates. But the record leaves out a later event. A third revision took effect from 1 Jul 2024 by MoD letter of 10 Jul 2024, with 19.65 lakh beneficiaries and Rs 6,703.24 cr a year (MoS Sanjay Seth, LS written answer, 6 Dec 2024). That cycle ran on schedule without a court order. As of 2026-10-04 the narrative implies a pattern that the 2024 cycle does not bear out.
verdicts.identityTest: Passes. The petitioner is Indian Ex Servicemen Movement in WP(C) 419/2016, and the respondent is the Union of India through MoD. The order is MoD letter 12(1)/2014/D(Pen/Pol)-Part-II of 7 Nov 2015. All of these match indiankanoon doc 160389977. One misattribution: the Rs 42,776.38 cr figure belongs to the Union, not IESM (see corrections).
verdicts.baseRate: Not a discriminating property. Pension-equalisation disputes are routine: Nakara (1983) and SPS Vains (2008) are the precedents the Court distinguished. Every CPC (4th, 5th and 6th) and the 2009 and 2012 Cabinet Secretary committees declined OROP under UPA and earlier governments, so the definitional contest predates NDA. Symmetry check: the 26 Feb 2014 UPA order fixed no base or periodicity. The UPA-II government never priced or implemented it, and the SC found that the 'automatically passed on' wording 'cannot be construed as a commitment with reference to any period of time'. Under the same test, neither government delivered annual or maximum-based equalisation. The narrative should say this. Otherwise 'betrayal' looks like an NDA-only property, when the gap between the 2014 promise and the 2015 definition is about pricing that UPA-II left undone.
verdicts.denialFound: The Government's answer is on record and was given in court. The Union said on affidavit, recorded in the judgment, that automatic revision 'would be impossible to implement' and that 'revising the rate of pension every year would cause administrative difficulty and is impracticable'. Its written submission, quoted in the judgment, called the petitioners' maximum-pension reading 'completely arbitrary'. Source: https://indiankanoon.org/doc/160389977/. The PIB e-booklet (Apr 2023) frames OROP as 'fulfilling long standing demand'. The 'betrayal' framing is attributable to Congress: Randeep Surjewala on 16 Mar 2022 said the government gave 'one rank, five pensions' and 'betrayed the interests of over 30 lakh ex-servicemen' (https://www.deccanherald.com/national/national-politics/not-giving-one-rank-one-pension-betrayal-of-soldiers-congress-1091968.html; https://inc.in/congress-sandesh/analysis/not-giving-one-rank-one-pension-is-cheating-the-army-and-betraying-the-interests-of-the-soldiers).
verdicts.innocentReading: OROP has to be defined so that it can be priced. Under the services' maximum-pension option (CGDA working committee option 4, 2013), the cost was Rs 14,898.34 cr a year and Rs 1,45,339.34 cr in arrears. Under the adopted average of minimum and maximum, it was Rs 7,123.38 cr a year. Five-yearly re-fixation follows the general practice for revising pay and pensions. The 'multiple pensions' within a rank come from MACP and different pre-2014 base pay, which the Court held is not arbitrary. On this reading the difference is a costed policy choice, not a reneged promise. The petitioners' reading is that the Government accepted 'automatic' pass-through in Feb 2014 and then narrowed it. Both readings fit the record, so 'contested' is the correct status.
verdicts.reason: The headline holds and is documented. There is a petitioners' contention of 'one rank multiple pensions' (judgment para 1: 'the principle of OROP has been replaced by "one rank multiple pensions"'), and the SC upheld the 7 Nov 2015 definition on 16 Mar 2022 (para 49). The status 'contested' is correct. However, two statements in the narrative body are attributed to sources that do not say them, so the record cannot be published as written. (1) strongestCase says the IESM petition 'showed the fiscal difference (its arithmetic: Rs 42,776 cr additional arrears)'. The judgment says the opposite. 'According to the Union Government, if non MACP personnel are grouped with MACP personnel for the payment of OROP, the total financial outflow from 2014 would be in the range of Rs 42,776.38 crores... submitted by the Union Government on affidavit'. It is the Government's figure, and it concerns MACP matching, not average-versus-maximum or annual revision. (2) strongestCounter says the Congress 2024 manifesto 'promises OROP "in letter and spirit", i.e. accepts the frame'. The cited Business Today article does not contain 'letter and spirit'. It quotes: 'One Rank One Pension (OROP) will be implemented in accordance with the order of the UPA government dated 26 February 2014. Anomalies that have arisen in the implementation of OROP by the BJP/NDA government will be rectified.' That contests the definition outright, so it belongs in strongestCase, not strongestCounter. A third problem: 'the base was shifted from the maximum' presents the petitioners' contention as fact. The judgment shows the maximum was the services' proposal (CGDA option 4), and the Government never adopted it.
verdicts.corrections: 1) strongestCase: replace '(its arithmetic: Rs 42,776 cr additional arrears)' with the Union's own figures from judgment C.2.2–C.2.3: matching non-MACP to MACP would add Rs 42,776.38 cr in arrears to 2021 (Union affidavit), and the services' maximum-pension option would have cost Rs 14,898.34 cr a year against Rs 7,123.38 cr, with Rs 1,45,339.34 cr additional arrears (CGDA working committee, 2013). Attribute both to the Union, not IESM. 2) claim text: change 'because the base was shifted from the maximum to the 2013 average' to 'because the base is the average of the 2013 retirees' minimum and maximum rather than the maximum the services proposed, and revision is five-yearly rather than automatic (petitioners' contention)'. 3) strongestCounter: delete the manifesto clause ''in letter and spirit', i.e. accepts the frame'. Move the manifesto to strongestCase with the exact Business Today quote ('implemented in accordance with the order of the UPA government dated 26 February 2014. Anomalies... will be rectified'). Also fix line 1163 of pay-pensions.json, which carries the same unsourced 'in letter and spirit' wording. 4) srcs: add the Congress source for 'betrayal' (Surjewala, 16 Mar 2022: https://www.deccanherald.com/national/national-politics/not-giving-one-rank-one-pension-betrayal-of-soldiers-congress-1091968.html or https://inc.in/congress-sandesh/analysis/not-giving-one-rank-one-pension-is-cheating-the-army-and-betraying-the-interests-of-the-soldiers). Otherwise 'betrayal' is our word, not a party's. 5) strongestCounter: add that the SC read 'automatically passed on' in the 26 Feb 2014 documents as not 'a commitment with reference to any period of time' (para 37), so the UPA order fixed neither base nor periodicity. Also add the third revision w.e.f. 1 Jul 2024 (MoD letter 10 Jul 2024; 19,64,973 beneficiaries; Rs 6,703.24 cr a year; MoS Sanjay Seth, LS written answer 6 Dec 2024), which ran without a court order. This also partly closes the gap at line 2430. 6) whatWouldChangeThis: keep it, and add 'a Court finding on the 2024 cycle or a fresh challenge'.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim reads: Defence Pensions (Demand 22) actual spending rose from FY2013-14 to FY2024-25. Both endpoints are actuals, and both cabinets (UPA-II in 2013-14, NDA in 2024-25) fall inside the window. The window spans the 7th CPC (constituted under UPA-II in 2014, implemented under NDA in 2016), OROP (2014/2015, revised 2022-23) and dearness relief. The narrative assigns no cause to either government. The figures are right for the window but depend on where it starts: 2013-14 comes before both OROP and the 7th CPC, so 3.47x is close to the largest multiple a recent base year can give. The 2009-10 actual (Rs 34,999.45 cr) is inflated by 6th CPC arrears and would give about 4.5x. 2022-23 carried OROP arrears. The text should say the multiple depends on the base year.
verdicts.identityTest: Every figure matches the demand it is attributed to. Expenditure Budget 2015-16, Demand 22 Defence Pensions, 'Actual 2013-2014 ... Grand Total 45499.54' (net of recoveries). Expenditure Budget 2026-27, Demand 22 Defence Pensions, 'Net 157653.65' for Actual 2024-2025. 157653.65/45499.54 = 3.465, which rounds to 3.47. Demand 20 (2026-27): '1.01 Pay and Allowances of the Army 113801.21', '2.01 ... Navy 9313.73', '3.01 ... Air Force 20196.29', total 143,311.23. Expenditure Budget 2015-16 Demand 23: '1. Pay and Allowances of the Army ... 49647.95'. 143311.23/61625.32 = 2.33. Demand 21 (2026-27) Capital Outlay 'Grand Total 159768.40'; Demand 28 (2015-16) 'Grand Total 79125.05'. The ratio is 2.02. The 24.8% share also checks out: civil 27,616.45 + revenue 290,964.51 + capital 159,768.40 + pensions 157,653.65 = 636,003.01, and 157,653.65/636,003.01 = 24.79%. The BE 2020-21 peak also checks out: 133,825 out of the MoD BE total of roughly Rs 4.71 lakh cr is 28.4%. Source-chain gap: the 2024-25 pension actual comes from Expenditure Budget 2026-27 Demand 22 (https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/doc/eb/sbe22.pdf), and that file is NOT in the narrative's srcs. The srcs list sbe20 and sbe21 only. The 24.8% figure is credited to union-defence:c043, but c043 only gives BE shares up to 2026-27 and never states 24.8%. The 32,94,181 pensioners (Standing Committee 1st Report) include 6,14,536 defence civilian pensioners and 26,79,645 armed forces pensioners. The Demand 22 rupee totals likewise include civilian pensions, so these are not soldiers alone.
verdicts.baseRate: Not discriminating: pension growth has hit the whole Union, not just defence. All Union pensions were Rs 2,43,296 cr in BE 2024-25 (PRS). I did not re-verify the 2013-14 Union total in a primary document, but by my recollection the 2013-14 actual is about Rs 74,000 cr, which would give roughly 3.3x, against 3.47x for defence. The 7th CPC fitment (x2.57) and dearness relief apply to all central pensioners, so most of the defence growth is the general central-government pension rule. Only the OROP increment is specific to defence. Nominal GDP grew about 2.9-3x over the same years. Symmetry: union-defence:c042 shows the pension share rising under both governments (average BE share 15.6% under UPA-II, 23.3% under NDA), with step changes at 6th CPC arrears (UPA-II), OROP (both) and the 7th CPC (NDA). Run on the UPA-II window, the same lens reads the same way, so it says nothing about party.
verdicts.denialFound: No accused party, so no denial is expected. The narrative accuses no one of wrongdoing. Contrary reporting cuts against the record's own counter-argument rather than against the share fact. Lt Gen Prakash Menon and Pranay Kotasthane (ThePrint, 12 Mar 2020, https://theprint.in/opinion/indias-defence-pension-bill-affecting-military-5-myths-busted/379289/), citing Laxman Behera, say 'the entire increase in the pension's share has come at the cost of capital procurement ... dwindled by 11 percentage points' (from 2011-12 to 2020-21). IISS (https://www.iiss.org/online-analysis/military-balance/2023/04/indian-defence-budget/) frames it as personnel versus capital. The opposite view comes from veterans and readers who argue that pensions are a contractual obligation and that modernisation should be funded by a bigger envelope rather than set against pensions. The Finance Minister presents defence spending excluding pensions separately (Deccan Herald, 'not counting pension'). I found no MoD statement that pensions crowd out capital. The government's official Agnipath aims (PIB, 14 Jun 2022) do not cite pension savings.
verdicts.innocentReading: The pension bill is a deferred-wage contract with about 26.8 lakh armed forces pensioners and about 6.1 lakh defence civilian pensioners. It grew because rules common to all central pensioners (7th CPC fitment, dearness relief indexation) and the defence-specific OROP were applied to a growing pensioner stock. Under both governments a manpower-heavy force pays these pensions out of the same MoD envelope. The pension share therefore rises mechanically and spikes in arrears years. That is an accounting fact about the envelope, not a transfer or a leak. How far pensions "eat" capital depends on whether the envelope is treated as fixed, which is a policy choice and not a finding.
verdicts.reason: The share fact survives. Every number (45,499.54, 157,653.65, 3.47x, 2.33x, 2.02x, 28.4% BE 2020-21, 24.8% actual 2024-25) matches the primary Expenditure Budget demands, so the underlying rows are documented and the narrative judgement is analytic. The narrative's counter-argument does not hold, though. A flat service-pay-to-capital ratio (0.78 to 0.90) shows that pay and capital grew together. It says nothing about pensions against capital. Pensions-to-capital moved from 45,499.54/79,125.05 = 0.58 in 2013-14 to 157,653.65/159,768.40 = 0.99 in 2024-25. The platform's own union-defence:c042 shows the capital share of the MoD total falling from an average of 33.8% under UPA-II to 26.6% under NDA. Read with Behera's finding, the record supports a share squeeze on capital, not "did not crowd out capital". The "framing contested" label is right, but for the wrong reason. What is contested is whether a share squeeze inside a fixed envelope is the right frame, not whether the squeeze happened. The pension growth is also mostly a Union-wide rule (7th CPC and DR), not specific to defence. The narrative also leaves out the primary source for its 2024-25 endpoint.
verdicts.corrections: 1) Add to srcs ["Expenditure Budget 2026-27, Notes on Demands for Grants, Demand No. 22 Defence Pensions (Actual 2024-25 Net 157653.65)", "https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/doc/eb/sbe22.pdf"], plus the 2015-16 Demand 23/24/25/28 files used for the 2013-14 pay and capital rows (https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/budget_archive/ub2015-16/eb/sbe23.pdf, ...sbe28.pdf). 2) In strongestCase, change "(union-defence:c043)" so it credits the 24.8% to a computation from the actual 2024-25 rows of Demands 19-22 (civil 27,616.45 + revenue 290,964.51 + capital 159,768.40 + pensions 157,653.65 = 636,003.01). c043 carries only BE shares. 3) Rewrite strongestCounter. Delete "so pensions did not crowd out capital in the budget actually spent", which is a non sequitur. Replace it with: "the pay-to-capital ratio is flat (0.78-0.90), so the squeeze fell on both pay and capital shares; pensions-to-capital rose from 0.58 (2013-14) to 0.99 (2024-25) and the capital share fell (c042), but whether that is 'eating' depends on treating the MoD envelope as fixed — pensions are a contractual liability and the FM reports defence spending ex-pensions separately". 4) Add to strongestCounter: "most of the growth is the Union-wide 7th CPC fitment and dearness relief common to all central pensioners; OROP is the defence-specific increment". 5) Change "a contract with 32.94 lakh people" to "32.94 lakh pensioners, of whom 6,14,536 are defence civilians and 26,79,645 armed forces (Standing Committee 1st Report 2024-25)". 6) Note that the base year matters: the 3.47x multiple starts before OROP and the 7th CPC, and a 2009-10 base inflated by 6th CPC arrears would give about 4.5x. 7) Add the Menon/Kotasthane (ThePrint, 12 Mar 2020) and Behera crowding-out finding to srcs as contrary reporting. 8) Keep status "well-supported" only if the claim sentence is narrowed to "the pension share of the defence budget has risen sharply, under both governments". The literal claim "eating the defence budget" should carry status "contested".

verdicts.dateTest: Restated as a claim: "CAPF, Assam Rifles and NSG suicide counts rose from 2016 to 2021 and were flat from 2020 to 2024." Both windows match the Parliament answers that cover them. LS UQ 4187 (29 Mar 2022, Annexure-I) gives 118, 113, 125, 108, 92, 125, 96, 129, 143, 156 for 2012-2021, total 1205. RS UQ 1036 (4 Dec 2024) gives 144, 157, 138, 157, 134 for 2020-2024, total 730. There is a date flaw: the 2024 figure of 134 is a partial-year count, because the answer is dated 4 Dec 2024. (PRS Table 5 says "as of December 12, 2024", which cannot be right for an answer given on 4 Dec. The c023 field "to 12 Dec" copies that error.) A Lok Sabha reply of 16 Dec 2025 by MoS Nityanand Rai, reported by Millennium Post and Northlines, gives 438 suicides for 2023-25 and says the count "declined from 157 in 2023 to 133 in 2025". That implies a full-year 2024 figure of about 148, not 134. The Ministry's own series also disagree for the years they share. For 2020: 143 (LS 4187), 142 (Report 242 Table 4.4), 144 (RS 1036). For 2021: 156, 157, 157. For 2022: 130 (Report 242) against 138 (RS 1036), with 136 in a later reply. The claim text uses 156 for 2021 from LS 4187 and 157 from RS 1036, so it mixes revisions.
verdicts.identityTest: This passes. Every source counts the same group: "Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs), Assam Rifles (AR) & National Security Guard (NSG)" (LS 4187 and RS 1036), and Report 242 Table 4.4 also includes AR and NSG. "Paramilitary forces" is a fair lay name for this group. One caveat: RS 1036 / PRS counts include missing-in-action cases ("Suicides include those missing in action", PRS Table 5).
verdicts.baseRate: The relevant base rate is the trend in the rate, not a cross-section of entities. Five-year averages from the Ministry's own figures: 2012-16 = 111 a year, 2017-21 = 130 a year, 2020-24 = 146 a year (148 if the implied full-year 2024 figure is used), and 2023-25 = 146 a year. Actual strength was about 9.20 lakh in Jan 2017. PRS gives a sanctioned strength of 10,78,514 with 1,58,591 posts (15%) vacant: https://prsindia.org/theprsblog/central-police-forces-overview-and-issues. Actual strength was 9,50,118 on 1 Jul 2024 (six forces, LS UQ 2426 via PRS). That is about 3% growth in the denominator while the five-year count rose about 12-30%. So the crude rate rose from about 10-12 per lakh in the mid-2010s to about 15 per lakh, and has stayed on a plateau since 2020. The comparison with the general population (14 against 12.4 per lakh, which PRS computes on 2022 figures, not 2024) is not adjusted for age or sex in a force that is overwhelmingly young men, so it does not tell CAPFs apart from comparable groups. On the symmetry control: the UPA-II years in the series (2012-13: 118 and 113) sit below the NDA-era average. That reflects a time trend in a single series, and the narrative does not attribute it to any party, so the control does not apply.
verdicts.denialFound: The Ministry's position is on record and the narrative uses it. LS UQ 4187 (29 Mar 2022, MoS Nityanand Rai): "Domestic problems, illness and financial problems are some of the contributory factors among others behind the incidents of suicide." https://sansad.in/getFile/loksabhaquestions/annex/178/AU4187.pdf. RS UQ 1036 (4 Dec 2024): "Generally, the working hours in the Central Armed Police Forces are 8 hourly shifts," and the Task Force report "has been circulated to all CAPFs & AR". https://www.mha.gov.in/MHA1/Par2017/pdfs/par2024-pdfs/RS04122024/1036.pdf. The Ministry has not denied that the counts rose. The Dec 2025 reply presents 2023→2025 as a decline (157→133).
verdicts.innocentReading: There is a boring explanation that also fits. Counts in a group of about 9.5 lakh fluctuate by ±20 a year by chance; 2016 (92) and 2018 (96) are low outliers. The general Indian male suicide rate also rose over the same decade. Reporting and classification may have improved after the Task Force was set up in Oct 2021, and the inclusion of MIA cases inflates the counts. On this reading, the 2016→2021 rise is partly a matter of where the comparison starts and partly a society-wide trend. The 2020-25 plateau (133-157) suggests a stable rate, not an escalating crisis.
verdicts.reason: Every number in the claim text matches the primary Parliament answers word for word: 92 for 2016 and 156 for 2021 in LS UQ 4187, and 144/157/138/157/134 in RS UQ 1036. Report 242 confirms 654 for 2018-22, with CRPF at 230 and BSF at 174. The "contested" status is a fair reading: the count rose over the decade and has held at about 133-157 a year since 2020. The record survives, but its framing has three faults. (1) Starting the rise at 92 picks the lowest year in the series; the five-year averages (111 → 130 → 146) make the case more honestly and more strongly. (2) The counter-case's "the force grew, so the rate did not rise" has no source in the file. The file's own void entry says no year-wise strength was found, and the strength that is available was roughly flat (about 9.2 lakh in 2017, 9.5 lakh in 2024). So the 2016-21 rise is a rise in the rate too. (3) "Flat to falling" leans on the partial-year 2024 figure of 134, while the Dec 2025 reply implies about 148 for 2024 and gives 133 for 2025. The status is an inference from documented counts, so the record belongs in the analytic tier.
verdicts.corrections: text: replace "2016→2021 rose 92→156" with "five-year averages rose 111 (2012-16) → 130 (2017-21) → 146 (2020-24); the single-year low was 92 in 2016". Change "2020-24 flat 134-157" to "2020-25 flat at 133-157 (2024's 134 was a partial-year count to early Dec; the Dec 2025 LS reply gives 438 for 2023-25, implying about 148 for 2024)". strongestCounter: delete "the force grew, so the rate did not rise", which has no source and is contradicted by about 9.20 lakh actual strength in Jan 2017 (PRS) against 9,50,118 on 1 Jul 2024. Replace it with "the rate has been flat since 2020 on a roughly constant strength". Change "flat to falling" to "flat". strongestCase: note that PRS's "14 per lakh" is computed on 2022 suicides, not 2024. Add a note that the Ministry's series disagree by up to 8 a year (2022: 130 in Report 242 against 138 in RS 1036). Add sources: Lok Sabha written reply of 16 Dec 2025 (MoS Nityanand Rai; 438 suicides 2023-25; 157 in 2023 and 133 in 2025), reported at https://www.millenniumpost.in/nation/capfs-saw-438-suicides-seven-fratricides-in-three-years-says-govt-640011 and https://thenorthlines.com/capfs-report-438-suicides-7-fratricides-in-3-years-over-23000-resignations-since-2014-govt-data/ (find the primary MHA PDF to upgrade the source). Add the PRS blog for the Jan 2017 strength. c023 d: change "2024, to 12 Dec" to "2024, partial year to the 4 Dec 2024 answer". Set the tier/status to analytic, with the underlying counts tagged documented.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim: retired officers told The Tribune in July 2024 that Agnipath was flawed. The article is by Vijay Mohan, datelined Chandigarh 27 July 2024 and published 28 July 2024 (datePublished 2024-07-28T11:07:27+05:30). It was written after the PM's Kargil Vijay Diwas speech of 26 July 2024. The scheme has run since the Cabinet approved it on 14 June 2022 (c008), so the objections come after the scheme started. "Jul 2024" and from=2024-07 are correct. The article itself says the "first cycle of Agniveer intake was still not complete", so the objections are forecasts, not measured outcomes.
verdicts.identityTest: The objectors are named retired officers, not nodes. Maj Gen IP Singh (retd), former director of the Mai Bhago Armed Forces Preparatory Institute, made the tenure point and the "double-edged weapon" remark. Brig IS Gakhal (retd), former Commandant of the Sikh Regimental Centre, made the 66% and training points. Both are public figures quoted on the record, so no below-public-rank issue arises. The 66% figure is attributed to veterans in general: "According to veterans, in about 10-12 years, about 66 per cent of the force will comprise Agniveers." The scheme is correctly identified as force:agnipath. There is one problem with the "double-edged weapon" attribution. The source applies it to "The uncertainty of getting absorbed after four years", not to "25% retention" as such. The paraphrase is close but not exact.
verdicts.baseRate: Veteran criticism of Agnipath has been widespread in Indian media since June 2022, so the record does not single anyone out. That is acceptable, because it is a contra or opinion record and alleges no wrongdoing. The 66% figure is a veterans' projection, not an official one. It follows roughly from 1.75 lakh a year intake with 75% leaving after four years, but the article gives no working, and that is why it should stay at reported.
verdicts.denialFound: No ministry rebuttal to these specific veterans was found. Ministry of Defence (MoD) comment on this article: none found; the article does not say MoD was asked. The government's side is the PM's 26 Jul 2024 Kargil Vijay Diwas defence of the scheme, which the article cites as its news peg. The Ministry's stated case (younger profile, tech-savvy force) is already in c008 (PIB 1833747). The article also notes the scheme's purpose "was to keep the age profile of the armed forces young, and also to reduce the burgeoning pension bill."
verdicts.innocentReading: Retired officers from the old long-service model naturally prefer longer training and tenure. These are policy and professional judgements made before the first four-year cycle had ended, not evidence of failure. The 66% projection depends on the intake really rising to 1.75 lakh, and on retention staying at 25%, which the government may change.
verdicts.reason: The Tribune article (28 Jul 2024) contains every element of the claim. Training: "The training of Agniveers is of about six months... It took seven to eight years for an individual to be an effective soldier." Tenure: "the initial tenure needs to be increased." Double-edged: "The uncertainty of getting absorbed after four years can also be a double-edged weapon." The 66% figure: "According to veterans, in about 10-12 years, about 66 per cent of the force will comprise Agniveers." Intake: "46,000... will go up to 1.75 lakh." The claim rests on one credible outlet with named, on-record sources, which meets the reported tier. It is labelled as opinion and not raised to documented. Neither lens finds a decisive refutation.
verdicts.corrections: (1) Change "25% retention a double-edged weapon" to "uncertainty of absorption after four years (25% retained) 'a double-edged weapon' (Maj Gen IP Singh, retd)". (2) Credit the 66% projection to "veterans (Brig IS Gakhal, retd, quoted on it)" and mark it as a projection that assumes intake reaches 1.75 lakh a year. (3) Add the dateline 27 Jul 2024 (published 28 Jul 2024) and the author, Vijay Mohan. (4) Fix the predicate framing. Under the CONTRACT, contra runs from the denier to claim:<id>, so s=force:agnipath (the scheme objecting to its own terms) is the wrong way round. Also, the veterans do not dispute the facts in c008, only whether the policy is sound. Either make s a veterans/commentators node, or keep s as the scheme and say explicitly in d that this contradicts the Ministry's stated case (youthful, effective force), not the documented terms. (5) Add an innocentReading, quoting "first cycle ... still not complete", and record that MoD was not shown to be asked: "denial: none found — not asked in source".

verdicts.dateTest: The claim reads: Agniveers made up about 11% of Army JCO/OR held strength and 16% of Navy sailors plus Agniveers by March 2025. The cited source is the Standing Committee on Defence 18th LS Eighth Report (DFG 2025-26), presented 17.3.2025. The three counts come from different dates. (1) The Army numerator comes from oral evidence taken on 17-18 Feb 2025 (para 1.34): "Currently, 1,23,000 Agniveers are enrolled in the Agnipath Scheme." (2) The denominator comes from a written reply giving strength as on 01 Oct 2024 (para 1.31): "Held Strength 11,05,110". (3) The Navy figures come from the same Feb 2025 deliberations (para 22): "the Indian Navy has 10,045 officers, 59,828 sailors, 11,634 Agniveers and 32,171 defence civilians." So the numerator and denominator are about 4.5 months apart, and "Mar 2025" is the report date, not the date of the figures. Agniveer batches that joined between Oct 2024 and Feb 2025 sit in the numerator but not in the denominator. The record's 'd' field admits the dates differ, so this is a framing correction, not a refutation.
verdicts.identityTest: The entities match the source. The Army figure was given by "a representative of Army". The JCO/OR figure is for the Indian Army as on 01 Oct 2024 (authorised 11,97,520, held 11,05,110, deficiency 92,410 or 7.72%). The Navy figure was given by a Navy representative. One ambiguity remains. The source does not say whether Army held strength of 11,05,110 includes Agniveers, or Agniveers still in training. For the IAF, the same report says outright that airmen strength of 1,39,876 includes Agniveervayu and excludes 2,317 trainees, of whom 1,982 are Agniveervayu. If the Army figure follows the IAF convention, part of the 1,23,000 "enrolled" (trainees) is outside the denominator. If Agniveers are outside held strength altogether, the right denominator is 11,05,110 + 1,23,000 and the share is 10.0%, not 11.1%. The Navy calculation (Agniveers / (sailors + Agniveers)) treats Agniveers as additive. The Army calculation treats them as included. The two denominators are built inconsistently.
verdicts.baseRate: Not a discriminating-property claim. It is a descriptive share computed from government figures, so the ≥80% test does not apply. The arithmetic checks out: 1,23,000 / 11,05,110 = 11.13%; 11,634 / 71,462 = 16.28%. With officers in the Navy denominator the share is 14.3%. With Agniveers treated as additive to Army held strength it is 10.0%. For comparison, the IAF figure in the same report does not give an Agniveervayu sub-count of in-post airmen, so no comparable IAF share can be computed from this source.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable. No party is accused of anything. All figures are the Ministry's or Services' own statements to the Committee. No correction from the Ministry was found. None was sought.
verdicts.innocentReading: The scheme started in 2022 and fills from zero at roughly 40,000 Army intakes a year. Three batches by early 2025 mechanically give about 1.2 lakh, which is roughly 10-11% of a JCO/OR body of about 11 lakh. The share must keep rising until the first four-year exits in 2026-27. It says nothing about quality, readiness or policy intent. The record's own innocentReading already says this.
verdicts.reason: All four numbers appear verbatim in the cited source, 18_Defence_8.pdf: para 1.31 (held 11,05,110 as on 01 Oct 2024), para 1.34 (1,23,000 Agniveers enrolled, oral evidence), and Navy para 22 (59,828 sailors, 11,634 Agniveers). Both ratios are calculated correctly, and the record labels the share as a calculation with a mixed-date caveat. Analytic is the right tier. It survives, but with corrections. The source does not say whether the Army held strength includes Agniveers or trainees. That makes the Army share between 10.0% and 11.1%, and the Navy share is built on an additive denominator while the Army share is built on an inclusive one. The phrase "by Mar 2025" is also wrong for the denominator (Oct 2024) and imprecise for the numerators (17-18 Feb 2025 oral evidence).
verdicts.corrections: (1) Text/lab: change "by Mar 2025" to "1,23,000 enrolled (oral evidence 17-18 Feb 2025) against JCO/OR held strength of 11,05,110 as on 1 Oct 2024". Change "~11%" to "~10-11% (11.1% if Agniveers are counted inside held strength, 10.0% if additive; the source does not say which)". (2) The 'd' field wrongly attributes the 11,05,110 denominator to the 2nd Report "via SPEC". It is in the cited 8th Report itself, para 1.31, p.15. Cite the 8th Report para 1.31 for the denominator, para 1.34 for 1,23,000, and para 22 for the Navy figures. (3) Navy: state that the 16% excludes officers (14.3% of officers + sailors + Agniveers). (4) Set 'from' to 2025-02, the evidence date, or leave 2025-03 explicitly as the report date. (5) The node t=force:indian-army is right for the Army ratio. The Navy half of the claim is about the Indian Navy and should be a separate edge, or the text should say the edge covers both.

verdicts.dateTest: Passes. Claim: the Agnipath Scheme sub-heads of Demand 20 (MoD) cost ₹7,459.75 cr (actual 2024-25) and are budgeted at ₹17,396.18 cr (BE 2026-27). sbe20.pdf (Notes on Demands for Grants 2026-27, Demand No. 20, "(In ₹ crores)") has the columns Actual 2024-2025 | Budget 2025-2026 | Revised 2025-2026 | Budget 2026-2027. The stages are labelled correctly: actual for 2024-25 and BE for 2026-27. The scheme dates from June 2022, so both years fall inside it. The ratio compares an actual with a BE, which is a mixed-stage comparison and should be stated. The intermediate figures (BE 2025-26 ₹11,039.51 cr; RE 2025-26 ₹11,466.92 cr) are left out but do not contradict the claim.
verdicts.identityTest: The figures match the source exactly. Actual 2024-25 sub-heads: 1.12 Army 6216.74, 2.08 Navy 544.65 and 3.06 Air Force 698.36, which sum to 7,459.75. BE 2026-27: 15173.68 + 1150.50 + 1072.00 = 17,396.18. Service pay actual 2024-25 is 113801.21 + 9313.73 + 20196.29 = 143,311.23. BE 2026-27 is 118167.91 + 9662.50 + 20536.83 = 148,367.24. All amounts are in ₹ crore as printed. Node mismatch: the edge target is force:indian-army, but the numbers are the sum of all three services. Only ₹6,216.74 cr and ₹15,173.68 cr are Army figures. The target should be the Ministry of Defence/Demand 20 node, or the edge should be limited to the Army figures.
verdicts.baseRate: The share is of a single scheme, so no cross-entity base rate applies. The SPEC control (UPA-II beside NDA) cannot be applied because the line has existed only since 2022-23. The growth is not discriminating evidence of anything: a new recruitment channel naturally grows its share as each annual intake is added and the regular-cadre intake it replaced runs off.
verdicts.denialFound: The Ministry/DMA position is on record. In June 2022 Lt Gen Anil Puri (DMA) and the three services said pension savings were 'most definitely' not a consideration and that the scheme was not about cutting costs (ThePrint, https://theprint.in/defence/agnipath-not-new-development-govts-ideating-for-decades-says-top-officer-in-charge-of-scheme/1005804/; India TV, https://www.indiatvnews.com/news/india/agnipath-scheme-explained-point-by-point-lt-general-anil-puri-on-army-air-force-navy-recruitment-agniveer-agnipath-protests-2022-06-19-785750). Against that, The Wire (https://m.thewire.in/article/security/agnipath-scheme-pension-savings-military-denial) reports that DMA calculations showed a 'prospective life-term saving' of ₹11.5 crore per Agniveer compared with a 17-year pensioned jawan. That is a reported, secondary account; I did not verify it against a primary record. The MoD was not asked about this claim's specific framing.
verdicts.innocentReading: The Agnipath sub-head is not wholly an additional cost. It is the pay of the soldiers who replace the regular sepoy intake, and that pay would otherwise sit inside 'Pay and Allowances'. As the cohorts build up from 2022, the line has to grow while regular-cadre pay grows more slowly. A rising share therefore shows a channel substituting for another, not a new burden. Whether there is a net saving depends on career-long and pension costs that Demand 20 does not print.
verdicts.reason: The headline percentage is wrong. Using the claim's own denominator (service pay plus Agnipath, the same basis that gives the correct 10.5% for BE 2026-27), the 2024-25 share is 7,459.75 / 150,770.98 = 4.9%, not 5.5%. Taking Agnipath over service pay alone gives 5.2%. 5.5% matches neither basis. Every underlying amount is confirmed in sbe20.pdf, so the claim can be fixed, but as written its central number is false. Two further problems: the edge target names the Army while the totals cover all three services, and 'saving uncosted' overstates the record, since a DMA per-recruit saving estimate (₹11.5 cr) has been reported even though no costed projection has been published.
verdicts.corrections: 1) Change '5.5%' to '4.9%' (7,459.75 of 150,770.98 cr, pay plus Agnipath), the same basis as the 10.5% (17,396.18 of 165,763.42 cr). Alternatively, state both bases: 5.2% and 11.7% of service pay alone. 2) Change the target from force:indian-army to the MoD/Demand 20 node (the three-service total), or restrict the edge to the Army figures (₹6,216.74 cr actual 2024-25 and ₹15,173.68 cr BE 2026-27, which is 11.4% of Army pay plus Agnipath at BE). 3) Replace 'saving uncosted' with 'no costed pension-saving projection published in the Budget documents; the DMA and services said in June 2022 that savings were not the motive (ThePrint), and a DMA per-recruit life-term saving of ₹11.5 cr has been reported (The Wire) but not verified'. Add the ThePrint and The Wire URLs as a contra or note. 4) Note that the comparison is actual 2024-25 against BE 2026-27 (mixed stages), and optionally give RE 2025-26 (₹11,466.92 cr). 5) Soften 'a present cost' to say the line partly substitutes for regular-cadre pay rather than adding to it, in line with the innocentReading.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim restated: IESM, as first petitioner, contended in 2016 (letters of 25 Jan 2016 and 25 Mar 2016; WP(C) 419/2016) and in the hearing up to the judgment of 16 Mar 2022 that the MoD letter of 7 Nov 2015 changed OROP. The dates line up. The 7 Nov 2015 letter came before the 2016 objections, and the judgment came after them. The judgment says: "By its letter dated 25 January 2016 to the Defence Minister the first petitioner objected to the revision of the definition of OROP..." and "The first petitioner also wrote to Justice L. Narasimha Reddy on 25 March 2016". The edge's from = 2016 is correct.
verdicts.identityTest: Passes. The source is the Supreme Court judgment in Indian Ex Servicemen Movement & Ors. v. Union of India, WP(C) 419/2016, 16 Mar 2022 (Chandrachud, Surya Kant and Vikram Nath JJ). It names IESM as the first petitioner. The target, claim:pay-pensions:c014, is the 7 Nov 2015 OROP letter that the petition challenged. That is the right target.
verdicts.baseRate: This test does not really apply, because the claim is a party's recorded contention and not an inference drawn from a pattern. On symmetry: the "automatic" definition the petitioners relied on (Koshyari Committee in 2011, the UPA-II meeting and the letter to the CGDA of 26 Feb 2014, ₹500 cr provided) was never put into effect under UPA-II. The NDA's 7 Nov 2015 letter was the first implementation. So the contention targets the only implementation that existed. It is not a reading that singles out one government over another.
verdicts.denialFound: The Union's response appears in the same judgment, from its affidavit: "The Petitioner's interpretation is an attempt to equalize the pension of every defense personnel with the highest pension drawn by a defense personnel in the same rank with the same length of service. Such an interpretation is completely arbitrary definition..." It also said annual revision "would cause administrative difficulty and is impracticable" and that "The phrase 'automatically' does not mean the time period." The Court found no constitutional infirmity in the 7 Nov 2015 policy. It directed the five-yearly re-fixation from 1 Jul 2019 and disposed of the petition (https://indiankanoon.org/doc/160389977/).
verdicts.innocentReading: This is a policy dispute about how to define OROP. The government chose the average of the minimum and maximum 2013 pensions, protected anyone already above that average, and set re-fixation every five years for cost and administrative reasons. The CGDA working committee's maximum-pension option would have cost ₹14,898.34 cr a year against ₹7,123.38 cr. The Supreme Court held that the policy choice was within executive discretion. The claim makes no allegation of wrongdoing.
verdicts.reason: The core text is confirmed word for word. The judgment says: "The petitioners contend that in the course of implementation, the principle of OROP has been replaced by 'one rank multiple pensions' for persons with the same length of service." It also records the petitioners' objection to re-fixing on the 2013 retirees' average and to revision "every five years and not automatically". The alleged tier is right: a named party asserted this and lost on adjudication, and the Union's reply and the Court's holding are on the record. The edge's `d` field, however, attributes two figures to the petitioners that the judgment attributes to the government. That needs correcting but does not refute the contention itself.
verdicts.corrections: 1) In `d`, delete "the petitioners' arithmetic put the additional arrears of their definition at ₹42,776 crore and the alternative recurring cost at ₹14,898 crore a year". The judgment does not support it. ₹42,776.38 cr is the Union Government's affidavit figure, from 1 Jul 2014 to 31 Dec 2021, for matching non-MACP personnel with MACP personnel ("According to the Union Government, if non MACP personnel are grouped with MACP personnel..."). ₹14,898.34 cr a year is the CGDA working committee's 2013 costing of the maximum-pension option proposed by the services, with arrears of ₹1,45,339.34 cr. If kept, both should be credited to the Union or CGDA as the government's costings. 2) In the text and `lab`, change "annual revision" to "automatic revision". The petitioners argued that enhancements were to be passed on "automatically"; it was the Union that framed the alternative as yearly revision. 3) In `lab`, "base shifted from 2014 maximum to 2013 average" should read: "past pensioners re-fixed on the average of min and max 2013 pensions, below the rates of those retiring from 2014". The petitioners compared pre-2014 and post-2014 retirees; "maximum" is how the Union characterised their position. 4) "CGDA letter of 26 Feb 2014" should be "MoD (Dept of ESW) letter to the CGDA of 26 Feb 2014". 5) In killIf, "rejected on the merits" should read: "the Court upheld the 7 Nov 2015 definition and disposed of the petition with a direction to re-fix from 1 Jul 2019". 6) Set innocentReading to the policy-choice explanation above.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim structure: Defence Pensions (Demand 22) spent ₹157,653.65 cr in FY 2024-25, divided by 32,94,181 pensioners, with growth measured against actual FY 2013-14. The windows overlap. The pensioner count comes from the Standing Committee on Defence, 18th LS, First Report (Demands for Grants 2024-25), presented December 2024. The count itself carries no date. The SPARSH figures next to it are dated 26.09.2024, so the count is mid-FY 2024-25 and matches the year of the numerator. FY 2013-14 actual ₹45,499.54 cr is from EB 2015-16 Demand 22. FY 2024-25 actual is from EB 2026-27 Demand 22. Both are final actuals, so the stages match. 157,653.65/45,499.54 = 3.465, which rounds to 3.47x. ₹157,653.65 cr / 32,94,181 = ₹4,78,580, which rounds to ₹4.79 lakh. Both figures are nominal. Neither is adjusted for inflation.
verdicts.identityTest: The entity is right. Demand No. 22 'Defence Pensions' is the pension demand in both EB 2015-16 and EB 2026-27. Both books give the same scope: retired defence personnel 'including civilian employees' of Army, Navy and Air Force and Ordnance Factories. The scope covers service pension, gratuity, family pension, disability pension, commuted value and leave encashment. The denominator uses the same scope. SC report para 7.1 reads: 'The total number of Defence pensioners in the country is 32,94,181 including 6,14,536 Defence Civilian Pensioners and 26,79,645 Armed Forces Pensioners.' Para 7.2 confirms the demand includes defence civilians and Ordnance Factory staff, so numerator and denominator cover the same population. The 2013-14 and 2024-25 figures are on the same scope. Both are Grand Total net figures. EB 2015-16 prints 'Revenue ... 45499.54 Total 45499.54'. EB 2026-27 prints 'Net 157653.65 ... Grand Total 157653.65'.
verdicts.baseRate: This is a descriptive ratio, so a base rate does not discriminate anything. Every Union pension line grew several-fold over 2013-14 to 2024-25 because of the 7th CPC fitment (x2.57) and dearness relief. Defence also had OROP. Pay grew 2.33x and capital 2.02x over the same years (the record's own symmetryCheck), so pensions are the fastest-growing MoD line. A PIB release of Dec 2025 cross-checks the count: 31.69 lakh pensioners onboarded on SPARSH out of 'approx 32 lakh'. That is consistent with 32.94 lakh, so the killIf condition is not met.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable. The claim does not accuse anyone. It is a per-head ratio of two official figures. No party was asked and none needed to be.
verdicts.innocentReading: The record already carries the innocent reading, and it holds. Most of the 3.47x nominal rise comes from rule-based drivers: the 7th CPC from 2016, OROP from 2014/2015 with the 2019 and 2022 revisions, DR indexation, and growth in the pensioner stock. Policy choices under both governments contributed. The 7th CPC was constituted under UPA-II in 2014. OROP was budgeted ₹1,000 cr by the incoming government in 2014-15. Also, ₹4.79 lakh is spend per head, not a pension rate. The numerator includes one-time lump sums to new retirees (gratuity, commutation, leave encashment). The record's 'd' field says this.
verdicts.reason: Both inputs are verbatim in primary documents and the arithmetic reproduces exactly. The SC First Report 2024-25 para 7.1 gives 32,94,181. EB 2015-16 Demand 22 gives 2013-14 actual 45,499.54. EB 2026-27 Demand 22 gives 2024-25 actual 157,653.65. Numerator and denominator have the same scope, defence civilians included. The record discloses the spend-versus-rate caveat and says no 2013-14 per-head figure was derived. The claim is not refuted. One fault remains. Neither the claim's srcs nor the record's srcs cite the document that contains ₹157,653.65 cr, which is EB 2026-27 sbe22. The record lists EB 2026-27 sbe20 (Defence Services Revenue) instead, and sbe20 does not contain the pensions actual. So the listed sources confirm the denominator and the 2013-14 base but not the 2024-25 numerator, which makes the source check 'partially'. Analytic is the right tier. The inputs are documented, but the ratio and the growth multiple are derived.
verdicts.corrections: 1) srcs: add ["Expenditure Budget 2026-27, Notes on Demands for Grants, Demand No. 22 Defence Pensions (Actual 2024-25 Net/Grand Total 157653.65)", "https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/doc/eb/sbe22.pdf"]. Remove or relabel the EB 2026-27 sbe20 entry, because it does not support this claim. 2) text/lab: write '3.47x (nominal)' so the multiple is not read as a real increase. 3) d: note that the 32,94,181 count is undated in the SC report (presented Dec 2024; nearby SPARSH figures dated 26.09.2024). Note also that PIB Dec 2025 (PRID 2204165) puts the total at about 32 lakh, which is consistent. 4) The tier stays analytic. The edge pred 'analytic' from force:defence-pensions to force:defence-pensioners is acceptable.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim reads as: the MHA '(iii) Police' establishment spent ₹53,737.04 cr on pay and ₹61,185.82 cr on allowances in FY 2024-25 (actuals), against a strength of 11,01,452 on 1 Mar 2025. The source is Expenditure Profile 2026-27, Statement 22, p. 245. Its header reads 'Strength as on 1st March … Actuals 2025' and 'Actuals 2024-2025 Pay (Salary) / Allowances / Travel Expenses'. The row reads '1101452 1202988 1208445 (iii) Police 53737.04 61185.82 3628.99 …'. The stage (actual) and the FY (2024-25) are right. One small mismatch: the denominator is a single-day headcount taken one month before FY-end, while the numerator is spending over the whole year. With headcount rising (12,02,988 estimated for 2026), using an average strength would give a slightly higher per-head figure. This is a convention issue, not an error. The record's from=2024-04-01 is consistent with this.
verdicts.identityTest: The entity is Statement 22, item '25. Ministry of Home Affairs', sub-line '(iii) Police'. This is the MHA's Police establishment, separate from (i) MHA proper, (ii) Cabinet and the UT lines (A&N, Chandigarh, DNH&DD, Ladakh, Lakshadweep). The claim text names it correctly as 'MHA Police establishment'. The edge target t='force:capf' is narrower than the source line. '(iii) Police' covers more than the CAPFs: Statement 22 gives no breakdown, and the record itself says it includes IB, Delhi Police and others. The parenthetical in the record's 'd' field ('CAPFs, IB, Delhi Police and others') is our inference from how Demand 51 is structured. Statement 22 does not say it.
verdicts.baseRate: I used the Statement 22 GRAND TOTAL as the comparator. All-government establishment: 33,02,539 heads, pay actual 2024-25 ₹1,60,473.76 cr, allowances ₹1,66,226.32 cr. That works out to ₹4.86 lakh pay per head and ₹9.89 lakh with allowances. The MHA Police figures are ₹4.88 lakh and ₹10.43 lakh, so pay per head is almost exactly the government average and pay plus allowances is about 5% above it. Allowances exceeding pay is common across the large lines in the statement (e.g. Atomic Energy and MoD Civil are close to even, and the government-wide total has allowances above pay). The figure therefore flags nothing as unusual. It is a descriptive denominator, which is what the analytic tier is for. My recomputation: 53,737.04e7 / 1,101,452 = ₹4.8787 lakh; 114,922.86e7 / 1,101,452 = ₹10.4338 lakh. The arithmetic is correct.
verdicts.denialFound: None found. None is needed: this is a descriptive per-head division of an official budget statement and alleges no wrongdoing. The MHA was not asked.
verdicts.innocentReading: Pay and allowances are both average-sized for central government (pay per head is about the same as the all-government figure). Allowances exceed pay because DA, HRA, risk and hardship pay are booked as allowances for a force deployed away from home. The per-head figure is an average over constables and officers. The record's innocentReading field is adequate. It should add that the figure is in line with the government-wide average of ₹4.86 lakh / ₹9.89 lakh.
verdicts.reason: Every figure in the claim matches Statement 22 (stat22.pdf, p. 245, row '(iii) Police'), and the division is correct to two decimals. The claim is our own computation, carries an innocentReading, and implies no wrongdoing, so analytic is the right tier. It is not refuted. The weak points are the edge target and the framing, not the numbers. t=force:capf is narrower than the source's '(iii) Police' line. The claim also gives no comparator, although the source itself shows MHA Police pay per head is at the all-government average.
verdicts.corrections: 1) Change t from 'force:capf' to an MHA Police-establishment node (e.g. 'force:mha-police-establishment'). If force:capf must stay, add to lab: 'Statement 22 line (iii) Police covers more than the CAPFs'. 2) In 'd', mark '(CAPFs, IB, Delhi Police and others)' as inference from the Demand 51 structure; Statement 22 gives no breakdown. 3) Add the comparator to lab or innocentReading: 'All-government Statement 22 average: ₹4.86 lakh pay, ₹9.89 lakh pay+allowances per head (33,02,539 heads)'. 4) Clarify that '₹10.43 lakh with allowances' means pay plus allowances and excludes travel (₹3,628.99 cr). 5) Note that the denominator is the strength on 1 Mar 2025, not the average strength over FY 2024-25. 6) Cite the page: Expenditure Profile 2026-27, p. 245.

verdicts.dateTest: Passes. The claim is that UP Police (Grant 26, MH 2055) spent X% of the head on salary in actual 2024-25 and budgets Y% in BE 2026-27. The source is the Detailed Estimates 2026-27 for Grant 26, dated February 2026. I re-downloaded it from budget.up.nic.in (HTTP 200) and its md5 (73741e08...) matches the builder's cached copy. Its columns are Actual 2024-25, BE 2025-26, RE 2025-26 and BE 2026-27, so the FY and stage labels are right. The District Police 01 line wraps in the PDF text. Its actual 2024-25 value is 1,093,479.82 lakh, the figure the claim uses. I confirmed this because the sub-head lines add exactly to 'योग : 03' = 1,941,229.28, and RE/BE = 0.8 holds for that column.
verdicts.identityTest:
Fails on the numerator. The denominator is MH 2055 voted actual 2024-25, 2,812,757.60 lakh ('2055 - पुलिस मतदेय 2812757.60'), and BE 2026-27 is 3,788,057.98. The numerator of 1,509,056.42 lakh is not MH 2055 salary. It is the object head '01 - वेतन' summed over the whole grant's revenue account. It includes four salary lines that sit after 'योग : 2055' (text line 1813) under other major heads:
- 2070-108 Fire (34,551.12)
- 2070-800 (1,354.91)
- 2245-02-102 (2,777.83)
- 2251-090 Secretariat (520.31)
These add to 39,204.17 lakh, which is exactly the gap between the claim's numerator and the true MH 2055 sum (376,372.43 + 1,093,479.82 = 1,469,852.25 lakh). The BE numerator has the same fault: it is 61,831 lakh too high. The text says 'summed across every MH 2055 sub-head', but the arithmetic does not do that.
verdicts.baseRate: Non-discriminating. Pay plus allowances is the majority of revenue police spending in essentially every Indian state (well above 80% of comparable entities). The claim implies no wrongdoing, so a base rate is not needed for any inference. The SPEC control (BJP-run vs opposition-run states) cannot be run because only UP's grant opened. The file already records that asymmetry as a void and draws no comparison, which is correct.
verdicts.denialFound: None found, and the party was not asked. None is needed: the claim is analytic arithmetic on the state's own budget document and accuses nobody.
verdicts.innocentReading: A police force is mostly people, so personnel costs dominate MH 2055 in every state. When computed correctly, UP's personnel share is higher than the claim implies, about 84% once DA is included. That is the ordinary pattern, not an anomaly.
verdicts.reason:
The record misstates its own source in two ways.

1. Major-head mismatch. The numerator adds salary from MH 2070, 2245 and 2251 to MH 2055 salary, then divides by MH 2055 alone. The correct MH 2055 figures:
   - Object head 01 salary, actual 2024-25: ₹14,698.52 cr of ₹28,127.58 cr = 52.3%, not 53.7%.
   - With 06 other allowances (93,646.22 lakh) and 55 HRA (49,581.52 lakh): 57.3%, not 58.9%.
   - BE 2026-27: 01 = 1,857,002.44 lakh = 49.0% (not 50.7%); with 06 + 55, 54.6% (not 56.4%).

2. Dearness allowance claim is false. The 'd' field says 'Dearness allowance is not a separate object head in this grant, so the salary figure likely includes DA'. The PDF prints '03 - मंहगाई भत्ता' as a separate object head in every sub-head. Examples: 001-03 '1124.59 … 03 - मंहगाई भत्ता', and District Police '559512.45 … 03 - मंहगाई भत्ता'. MH 2055 DA totals 743,751.60 lakh (₹7,437.52 cr) in actual 2024-25, about 26% of the head. So '01' is pay without DA, and '01 + 06 + 55' leaves out the second-largest pay component. Pay with DA, other allowances and HRA is 83.8% of MH 2055 actual 2024-25 and 86.5% of BE 2026-27.

Analytic is still the right tier: the arithmetic comes from a primary state document and implies nothing. But every headline number and the DA note have to be corrected before publication.
verdicts.corrections:
text/lab: "Uttar Pradesh: pay (object head 01, excluding DA) is 52.3% of the Police head MH 2055, actual 2024-25 — ₹14,698.52 cr of ₹28,127.58 cr; 57.3% with other allowances (06) and HRA (55); 83.8% with DA (03) as well. BE 2026-27: 49.0% / 54.6% / 86.5%."

d: Replace 'Dearness allowance is not a separate object head in this grant, so the salary figure likely includes DA' with 'DA is object head 03 (MH 2055 actual 2024-25 ₹7,437.52 cr; BE 2026-27 ₹12,070.52 cr)'. State that only the lines between the 2055 header and 'योग : 2055' are summed. Exclude 2070-105/108/800, 2245-02-102 and 2251-090.

Ratio rows at build.py lines 369–370: numerator 1509056.42 → 1469852.25, and 1655336.25 → 1613079.99. Add a row for 01+03+06+55 = 2356831.59 over 2812757.60.

UP salary budget rows (build.py around line 306): recompute from MH 2055 only. Actual 2024-25 = 14,698.52 cr and BE 2026-27 = 18,570.02 cr, not 19,188.34.

force:up-police node 'd' (build.py line 146): make the same figure fixes. Also drop '[documented, derived]' in favour of analytic.

symmetryCheck: change '53.7%' to '52.3%'.

innocentReading: may add that personnel cost including DA is about 84% of MH 2055.

verdicts.dateTest: Restated, the claim is: "CAPFs+NSG+AR recorded 134 suicides in 2024, against 9,50,118 actual strength on 1 Jul 2024, a rate of 14.1 per lakh." The numerator and denominator dates overlap, so the claim passes the basic date test. Four problems remain. (1) The 2024 count covers only part of the year. RS UQ 1036 was answered on 4 Dec 2024, so 134 covers about 11 months. PRS Table 5 labels it "as of December 12, 2024", which is after the answer date and cannot be right. The record copies "to 12 Dec". (2) The comparator does not match the year. 12.4 per lakh is the NCRB ADSI 2022 rate, but it is set against a CAPF 2024 rate. (3) PRS's own "14 per lakh" was computed from 2022 suicides: "Based on the actual strength and the number of suicides among CAPFs in 2022, the suicide rate for CAPFs is 14 per lakh". It is not a 2024 figure, so the 14.1 for 2024 is the record's own arithmetic. That arithmetic is correct: 134/9,50,118 = 14.10, and 730/5 = 146, giving 15.37 per lakh. (4) The 15.4 figure uses 2024 strength as the denominator for every year from 2020 to 2024.
verdicts.identityTest: The numerator and denominator cover different groups. RS UQ 1036 covers "Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs), National Security Guard (NSG) and Assam Rifles (AR)". The denominator (LS UQ 2426 via PRS Table 4) covers six forces: CISF 1,51,925, CRPF 2,98,033, ITBP 90,000, SSB 91,922, BSF 2,55,663, with the residual of about 62.5k being AR. That totals 9,50,118 and excludes NSG. The record flags this mismatch correctly as a small upward bias. "Includes missing in action" comes from the note under PRS Table 5. It is not in the MHA answer and should be attributed to PRS.
verdicts.baseRate: This test defeats the comparison. NCRB ADSI 2022 reports 1,70,924 suicides with a male:female ratio of 71.8:28.2, and 66.4% of all suicides at ages 18-45 (34.6% aged 18-30, 31.8% aged 30-45). That gives roughly 1.23 lakh male suicides, a male crude rate of about 17 per lakh. Men aged 18-45, the CAPF demographic, come out at roughly 25 per lakh (my estimate from NCRB counts and Census-projected age shares). The CAPF crude rate of 14.1 (or 15.4 on the 5-year average) is therefore below the age- and sex-matched civilian rate, not above it. The record's own killIf ("NCRB's male 25-50 rate exceeds the CAPF rate") is met on the evidence available. NCRB does not print an age-sex-specific rate, but the published male all-ages count alone already puts the male rate above the CAPF rate. On symmetry: the identical lens applied to any male working-age uniformed force (Army, state armed police) would show the same "above general population" result. The property comes from the population's makeup and says nothing specific about CAPFs.
verdicts.denialFound: No denial is needed because no wrongdoing is alleged. The Ministry's stated position is in the same RS UQ 1036 answer (MoS Nityanand Rai): working hours are "Generally... 8 hourly shifts", leave and training reserves are built into battalions, and the annexure lists welfare measures, including that the "Task Force on the remedial measures for prevention of suicide and fratricide... has been circulated to all CAPFs". Source: https://www.mha.gov.in/MHA1/Par2017/pdfs/par2024-pdfs/RS04122024/1036.pdf. The Ministry was asked by Parliament (Mukul Wasnik).
verdicts.innocentReading: The record's own innocent reading is correct and decisive. CAPF personnel are overwhelmingly men aged 18-50, the group with India's highest suicide rate. Their crude rate exceeds the all-ages, both-sexes national rate only because of who serves, and it sits below the matched male working-age rate. The 2024 numerator is also a partial year, which lowers the 2024 rate rather than raising it.
verdicts.reason: The arithmetic and the primary numbers check out. The RS 1036 answer gives 144/157/138/157/134 = 730, PRS Table 4 gives 9,50,118, and PRS gives 12.4 per lakh from NCRB 2022. But the claim's informational content is the contrast "vs 12.4 general population", and that contrast fails the base-rate test. Using NCRB 2022's published male share (71.8%) and age share (66.4% at 18-45), the male crude rate is about 17 per lakh and the rate for men aged 18-45 is about 25. Both exceed the CAPF 14.1, which triggers the record's own killIf. The source chain is also only partial. PRS's "14 per lakh" was derived from 2022 suicides, not 2024. The "to 12 Dec" date postdates the 4 Dec answer. The 2024 count covers part of the year. As written, the label implies an excess that the matched comparison does not support. The number can survive as analytic only if it is reframed. If the "vs general population" contrast is kept without the matched rate, kill it.

This is above the all-ages, both-sexes NCRB 2022 rate of 12.4 but below the male rate (~17, derived from NCRB 2022: 71.8% of 1,70,924) and the estimated rate for men aged 18-45 (~25)."

6. killIf: the falsifier as written is met on derived NCRB figures. Either restate the claim as above, or kill the comparison.
7. upgradeIf: keep "age-sex-standardised comparison", and add "full-calendar-2024 count".
