verdicts.dateTest: Restated: "MHA (MoS Nityanand Rai) told the Rajya Sabha on 4 Dec 2024 (RS UQ 1036) that CAPFs+NSG+AR had 11,185 VR+resignations in 2024 and 55,555 over 2020-24. The RS Standing Committee on Home Affairs (Report 242, presented to the RS on 17 Mar 2023, laid in the LS on 20 Mar 2023) printed MHA's 'attrition due to other reasons' figure of 50,155 for 2018-22." The dates fit: the minister was in office and the data windows sit inside the answer dates. Two date faults. (1) The 2024 row only runs to some point before 4 Dec 2024. The answer gives no cut-off date, and the press read it as "has touched 8,751". So 11,185 is a year-to-date count, and 11,185/9,50,118 = 1.18% understates a full-year rate (simply scaling up 11 months gives about 1.28%). The record's innocentReading calls it "a 1.2% annual exit rate", which is not supported. (2) Report 242 is dated 20 Mar 2023 in the record. It was presented to the Rajya Sabha on 17 Mar 2023 and laid in the Lok Sabha on 20 Mar.
verdicts.identityTest: The entities differ between the numerator and the denominator. RS 1036 covers "Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs), National Security Guard (NSG) and Assam Rifles (AR)". The 9,50,118 denominator (PRS Table 4, from LS UQ 2426, 6 Aug 2024) covers CISF, CRPF, ITBP, SSB, AR and BSF and leaves out NSG. The effect is small but should be stated. The bigger problem is the 2018-22 series. Report 242 Table 4.5 is headed "Attrition due to other reasons data". The table never says it means VR+resignations, and it leaves out NSG. It also does not match the VR+R series for the years both cover: 2020 is 7,033 here against 7,684 in RS 1036, 2021 is 11,785 against 12,013, and 2022 is 11,884 against 12,371. The like-for-like VR+R figure for 2018-22 is 53,336 (47,000 VR and 6,336 R). MHA gave it in a Lok Sabha written answer on 1 Aug 2023 to Manickam Tagore, as reported by the Sentinel and ANI. The BSF (23,553) and CRPF (13,640) totals match in both sources, but CISF does not (5,876 against 5,151). Putting "50,155 in 2018-22" next to "55,555 in 2020-24" invites a trend reading across two series that do not match.
verdicts.baseRate: Across forces the rate is uneven, and that can be shown. Using the 2018-22 VR+R figures against 1 Jul 2024 strength: BSF lost 23,553 out of 2,55,663, about 1.8% a year. The other forces lost about 29,800 out of about 6,94,000, about 0.9% a year. BSF is 27% of strength but about 44-47% of exits. That is close to the record's own killIf ("rate driven by one force's ... profile"), though nothing in hand shows the cause is BSF's service-length profile. The record gives no source for its comparison with civilian employers ("low beside most civilian employers"), and the SPEC's UPA-II control (pre-2014 CAPF VR/resignation counts) was not run. PIB PRID 1522728 (2017) is a possible source for earlier years.
verdicts.denialFound: No denial applies, because this is the Ministry's own data. The Ministry's account is on the record in the RS 1036 Annexure, quoted: "Generally, the working hours in the Central Armed Police Forces are 8 hourly shifts. This, however, varies depending on operational exigencies. Necessary leave/training reserve is built in the structure of Battalions", plus item xiv on the circulated Task Force report on suicide and fratricide. https://www.mha.gov.in/MHA1/Par2017/pdfs/par2024-pdfs/RS04122024/1036.pdf. The Committee's view, Report 242 para 4.5.4: "such a level of attrition may affect the working conditions in the CAPFs". Para 4.5.5 recommends exit interviews. Neither one disputes the figures.
verdicts.innocentReading: Voluntary retirement after 20 years' qualifying service is a pension right. Forces that grew fast in the 2000s (BSF and CRPF raised many battalions) now have large groups of staff reaching that point. Most exits are VR, not resignation (47,891 against 7,664). BSF's higher share fits a long-service, hard-posting force. Resignations still rose from 793 in 2020 to 2,434 by part of 2024. That rise is the part of the data the innocent reading does not explain.
verdicts.reason: The figures are correct. RS UQ 1036 prints 6,891/10,764/11,211/10,274/8,751 VR and 793/1,249/1,160/2,028/2,434 R, totalling 55,555, with 2024 at 11,185. Report 242 Table 4.5 prints 50,155 for 2018-22, with BSF 23,553, CRPF 13,640 and CISF 5,876. Both readings are quoted accurately, and 11,185/9,50,118 = 1.177%. The claim is analytic and alleges no wrongdoing, so it survives. Its framing has three faults, all fixable. First, the 2024 count is year-to-date as of the 4 Dec 2024 answer, so it is not an annual rate. Second, the 2018-22 figure is a different MHA series ("attrition due to other reasons") that does not match VR+R in the overlapping years; the like-for-like 2018-22 figure is 53,336 (LS answer, 1 Aug 2023). Third, the numerator includes NSG and the denominator does not. The 9,50,118 denominator comes from PRS/LS UQ 2426, which is not among the edge's two srcs.
verdicts.corrections: text/lab: change "in 2024 = 1.18% of strength" to "in 2024 up to the 4 Dec 2024 answer (partial year) = 1.18% of 1 Jul 2024 actual strength (9,50,118; excludes NSG; numerator includes NSG)". Change "50,155 in 2018-22" to "50,155 'attrition due to other reasons' in 2018-22 (Report 242 Table 4.5; a separate series that does not match VR+R in 2020-22). The VR+R figure for 2018-22 is 53,336 (47,000 VR, 6,336 R), LS written answer, 1 Aug 2023." srcs (edge): add PRS DFG 2025-26 Home Affairs (https://prsindia.org/files/budget/budget_parliament/2025/DFG_Analysis_2025-26-Home_Affairs.pdf), or LS UQ 2426 of 6 Aug 2024, for the denominator. Add the 1 Aug 2023 LS answer (e.g. https://www.sentinelassam.com/topheadlines/over-53000-capf-personnel-quit-jobs-in-5-years-centre-660821 until the primary MHA PDF is found). Report 242 date: 17 Mar 2023 (RS), laid in the LS on 20 Mar 2023. innocentReading: drop "annual" and the unsourced "low beside most civilian employers", or add a sourced comparator. d: add the BSF concentration (about 1.8%/yr against about 0.9%/yr for the other forces, 2018-22 VR+R against 2024 strength). symmetryCheck: add pre-2014 CAPF VR/R counts, or record the gap. upgradeIf: keep it, and add the "2024 full-year figure (later Parliament answer)".

verdicts.dateTest: Restated: "MoD (UPA-II, Antony / NDA, Rajnath Singh) spent service pay against Capital Outlay at ratio X in FY Y." UPA-II ran from 22 May 2009 to 26 May 2014. It presented the full 2009-10 budget in July 2009 and ran all of 2013-14, so both of those years belong to it. FY2024-25 belongs to NDA and BE 2026-27 to NDA-III. Every year overlaps the right government. Stage problem: the headline puts BE 2026-27 (0.68) beside actuals. Capital BE and actual can differ a lot (2013-14 BE 86,740.71 against actual 79,125.05), so a BE ratio is not a like-for-like point. The headline also gives BE 2026-27 without Agnipath (0.68), while the lab gives 0.76 with it. The like-for-like figure is 0.76.
verdicts.identityTest: Every printed figure checks against the PDFs, in Rs crore as printed. EB 2011-12 sbe22/23/24 (Actual 2009-10): Army 1. "Pay and Allowances of the Army 2076 ... 36196.47", Navy 2656.90, AF 6247.48. sbe27: "Grand Total ... 51112.37". EB 2015-16 sbe23/24/25 (Actual 2013-14): Army 49647.95, Navy 3463.35, AF 8514.02. sbe28: "Grand Total ... 79125.05". EB 2026-27 sbe20: Army 1.01 113801.21 / BE 118167.91; Navy 2.01 9313.73 / 9662.50; AF 3.01 20196.29 / 20536.83. Agnipath 1.12+2.08+3.06 = 6216.74+544.65+698.36 = 7459.75 actual and 15173.68+1150.50+1072.00 = 17396.18 BE. sbe21: Grand Total 159768.40 actual / 219306.47 BE. The arithmetic reproduces as 0.882, 0.779, 0.897, 0.944, 0.677 and 0.756. The edge srcs list omits the pay demands (2011-12 sbe22-24, 2015-16 sbe23-25), though the full record carries them. The denominator's scope is broadly the same in both years: R&D capital and OF/DPSU lines are in the 2009-10 and the 2024-25 Grand Totals alike.
verdicts.baseRate: I read the same series in the same Expenditure Budget demands for the years the claim skips. UPA-II actuals: 2009-10 0.88 (6th CPC arrears year); 2010-11 0.70 (43,278.28/62,055.98, EB 2012-13 sbe22-24, 27); 2011-12 0.72 (48,606.98/67,902.38, EB 2013-14); 2012-13 0.79 (55,984.87/70,499.12, EB 2014-15); 2013-14 0.78. NDA actuals: 2015-16 1.04 (74,200.30/71,675.43, EB 2017-18 sbe20/21); 2016-17 1.01 (86,944.68/86,356.93, EB 2018-19); 2017-18 1.13 (102,000.18/90,438.40, EB 2019-20); 2024-25 0.90 (0.94 with Agnipath). Every NDA year checked is 0.90-1.13. Every UPA-II year without arrears is 0.70-0.79. The claim takes its UPA-II starting point (0.88) from the one year inflated by 6th CPC arrears. From 2013-14 to 2024-25 pay rose 2.33x and capital 2.02x, so on that base the ratio rose about 15% (21% with Agnipath). The flatness is an artefact of which years were picked, not a property of the series.
verdicts.denialFound: None needed. This is an analytic comparison with no accusation, so no party was asked and no response exists. The record's own innocentReading names the 6th CPC arrears (2009-10) as a one-off but then uses that year as the comparison point.
verdicts.innocentReading: The ratio follows the pay commission cycle, not the party in power. It jumps when a CPC is implemented: 6th CPC arrears in 2009-10 and the 7th CPC in 2016, which takes it to 1.01-1.13 in 2015-16 to 2017-18. It then falls as capital catches up with the new pay base, back to 0.90 by 2024-25 and 0.76 in BE 2026-27 with Agnipath. Neither government chose to favour pay over capital in a way the ratio shows. The 7th CPC was set up under UPA-II and carried out under NDA, as the cycle requires. Read this way, the platform's neutral stance still holds, but "flat" is the wrong word for the series.
verdicts.reason: The figures are right and the conclusion is not. All 20+ line items match the printed demands exactly, but "flat across UPA-II and NDA" holds only for the four chosen points. The UPA-II reading of 0.88 comes from the arrears year. Same-source actuals for the omitted years show UPA-II at 0.70-0.79 and NDA at 0.90-1.13 (2015-16 1.04, 2016-17 1.01, 2017-18 1.13, 2024-25 0.90). The 3.18x vs 3.13x growth match is an endpoint effect. The real pattern is a hump driven by the pay commission cycle. The edge also mixes BE with actuals and drops Agnipath from the BE point. The flaw is in the conclusion, not the data, so the claim should stay analytic with the framing rewritten. The downstream strongestCounter text ("ratio is flat ... pensions did not crowd out capital") also needs revising.
verdicts.corrections: 1. Replace "flat" in text/lab/d with the series: "Service pay ÷ Capital Outlay actual: UPA-II 0.88 (2009-10, 6th CPC arrears), 0.70 (2010-11), 0.72 (2011-12), 0.79 (2012-13), 0.78 (2013-14); NDA 1.04 (2015-16), 1.01 (2016-17), 1.13 (2017-18), 0.90 (2024-25; 0.94 with Agnipath); BE 2026-27 0.76 with Agnipath (0.68 without). The ratio rises with each pay commission and falls as capital catches up." 2. Remove "Pay grew 3.18x ... capital 3.13x: the ratio is flat across both governments" from d. Or add the 2013-14 base (pay 2.33x, capital 2.02x) and call the 2009-10 base arrears-inflated. 3. Headline BE point: give 0.76 (with Agnipath) first, or label 0.68 "BE, excl. Agnipath, not comparable to actuals". 4. Add the intermediate-year sources to srcs: indiabudget.gov.in/budget_archive/ub2012-13, ub2013-14 and ub2014-15 eb/sbe22, 23, 24, 27; and ub2017-18, ub2018-19 and ub2019-20 eb/sbe20, 21. Also restore the edge srcs for the pay demands (ub2011-12 sbe22-24, ub2015-16 sbe23-25). 5. Make matching edits to symmetryCheck ("the ratio is flat"), the narrative strongestCounter ("pay-to-capital ratio is flat across UPA-II and NDA (0.78-0.90)") and the baseRates rows. 6. Set innocentReading to the pay-commission-cycle reading above. Tier stays analytic.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim is that Rajnath Singh held the post of Minister of Defence on 14 Jun 2022 (Agnipath Cabinet approval), 23 Dec 2022 (OROP revision) and in 2025 (8th CPC approval announced 16 Jan 2025, terms of reference notified Nov 2025). His tenure is 30 May 2019 to the present, a window taken from union-defence:c010, which is itself sourced to Wikipedia. Coverage from September 2026 (The Week, 29 Sep 2026, Navy Commanders' Conference; a Sri Lanka visit 8-10 Sep 2026) shows he is still in office, so `to: null` is correct. All three events fall inside the window, so the overlap test passes. The PIB source independently fixes him in office on 16 Jan 2023, which falls between the 2022 events and 2025.
verdicts.identityTest: PIB Release ID 1891550 (Ministry of Defence, "Posted On: 16 JAN 2023 2:33PM by PIB Delhi") names "Shri Rajnath Singh" and calls him "Raksha Mantri". That matches pol:rajnath-singh and min:ministry-of-defence. No other person of that name held the office, so there is no identity ambiguity.
verdicts.baseRate: The test does not apply. This is a neutral role edge, and every sitting Defence Minister holds this property for decisions taken during their tenure. The edge implies nothing beyond holding the office. The same lens applied to UPA-II (A.K. Antony as Raksha Mantri during the 2009-14 personnel decisions) would produce the same kind of edge. Nothing here singles anyone out, and none is claimed.
verdicts.denialFound: None found, and none was asked for. This is a factual record of office tenure that nobody disputes, so a response is not required.
verdicts.innocentReading: The edge only places the minister in office when ministry-level decisions were taken. It does not claim he personally decided them. In particular, the 8th CPC is a Ministry of Finance (Department of Expenditure) instrument, not a Defence Ministry one, so "during" is purely about timing.
verdicts.reason: The claim survives. The cited PIB release (fetched with curl after WebFetch got a 403) says: "Raksha Mantri describes the scheme as a pioneering step towards building a strong & prosperous 'New India'… Strengthening the country's security apparatus is Government's top priority…: Shri Rajnath Singh. Posted On: 16 JAN 2023". That confirms he held the office on 16 Jan 2023. The PIB source does not itself give the tenure dates (30 May 2019 to present) or mention OROP or the 8th CPC. Those dates come from union-defence:c010, which rests on Wikipedia, so the reported tier is correct and the record is honest that the dates are borrowed from c010. Current 2026 reporting confirms there is no end date. The claim does not chain facts together into any implication beyond holding the office.
verdicts.corrections: (1) The record has a duplicate JSON key: `"killIf": null` is followed by `"killIf": "an official record shows different dates"`. Remove the null entry. (2) Fill in `upgradeIf` (currently null) with: "PIB swearing-in/portfolio-allocation releases of 31 May 2019 and 10 Jun 2024 fetched with the same dates" (this would allow documented). (3) Optionally add PIB 1833747 (14 Jun 2022 Agnipath approval) as a second source to anchor the 2022 date directly. (4) Add a line to `d` saying the 8th CPC is a Ministry of Finance resolution and "during" is about timing only. (5) Set `innocentReading` to a role-only note (e.g. "holding office; implies no personal authorship of each decision").

verdicts.dateTest: Claim: MoD signed the CQB carbine contract with Bharat Forge and PLR Systems on 2025-12-30. PIB PRID 2209832 confirms that date. The ownership window overlaps: the file and trade press date Adani Defence's 51% of PLR to 2020, before the award. The narrative is dated as of 2026-10-04, but its "only PIB-named award" and "no sole-vendor award" statements carry no end date. They are already out of date. PIB PRID 2288009 (posted 22 JUL 2026) says: "A separate contract was inked with Adani Defence Systems and Technologies (ADSTL), Ahmedabad to engage with the company as Development Cum Production Partner (DcPP) for Mission Systems designed for the AEW&C MKII Programme." That is a PIB-named contract with ADSTL alone, signed with CABS/DRDO (Ministry of Defence) on 2026-07-22, ten weeks before the as-of date. It does not appear in the file. The ₹4.07 lakh crore denominator covers calendar 2021-25 only, so the 0.68% sits in a different window from the "only" statement.
verdicts.identityTest: PLR Systems Pvt Ltd is named in PIB 2209832: "signed with Bharat Forge Ltd and PLR Systems Pvt Ltd". The 51% Adani Defence link rests on trade press (Angel One), because MCA could not be reached. Chakra News, reporting on the day of signing, names the vendor as "Adani Defence" and says it will supply the IWI ACE carbines, so the identification as Adani-linked holds at the reported tier. The AEW&C contract names ADSTL, the same entity that signed the Air Works purchase agreement (Adani release, 2024-12-23: "Adani Defence Systems & Technologies Ltd. (ADSTL)", 85.8%, enterprise value ₹400 crore). That is the same Adani entity, and the narrative misses it.
verdicts.baseRate: The 2021-25 sample in this file has PIB-named awards to at least seven private Indian vendors: L&T (five, sole), Bharat Forge (two, joint), TASL (joint and consortium), PLR (joint), Chowgule, ICOMM and EEL (joint). Having one joint award is common among licensed private vendors and tells nothing apart. Arithmetic check: 2,770 / 407,145 = 0.680%. But ₹4.07 lakh crore is this file's sample of 45 award claims, not all PIB-named awards. The same PIB release says MoD signed ₹1,82,492 crore of capital contracts in FY2025-26 up to 30 Dec alone, so the full universe is much larger and the 0.68% is a share of a sample. Reported split: Bharat Forge was L1 with 60% (255,000 units) and Adani Defence L2 with 40% (170,000 units), which puts Adani's share near ₹1,100 crore if price per unit is equal (not printed by PIB).
verdicts.denialFound: None found for the narrative "Adani is being handed defence". Adani was not asked. No accusing party is named in the record, and the narrative quotes no Adani or MoD response.
verdicts.innocentReading: The carbine order was split between L1 and L2, a normal multi-vendor DAP quantity split after trials that go back to 2005, 2011, 2018 and 2022 (the 2018 Caracal fast-track was cancelled in 2020). Adani has a JV with IWI and an existing small-arms plant at Gwalior. The DcPP role on AEW&C Mk-II is DRDO's standard industry-partner route; it is used for other private and public firms too (e.g. VSHORADS). New entrants with foreign OEM tie-ups (IWI, Elbit) are expected to pick up first-generation orders. None of this shows favour, and it does not support "only one joint award" either.
verdicts.reason: Two factual parts of the narrative are false as of its own date. (1) "The only PIB-named award to an Adani-linked vendor is the 2025-12-30 CQB carbine contract": PIB PRID 2288009 (2026-07-22) names a separate contract signed by CABS/DRDO with ADSTL alone, as DcPP for AEW&C Mk-II mission systems, including integration and flight testing. (2) "No sole-vendor award to an Adani entity found": that PIB release is one, and the narrative's own cited source contradicts it too. The AEL Annual Report 2025 page lists deliveries to the Army (ULPGMs, UAVs, the first Drishti-10), to the IAF (micro UAVs, Type II NGARM), surface-to-air missiles to the Navy and IAF, and a counter-drone system to the BSF. Each delivery implies a contract, even though the ₹ is not printed. The 0.68% is arithmetically right but is a share of the file's 45-claim sample, and the text presents it as the whole PIB universe. Overall, "unsupported" may still be fair for "handed defence", but the counter-case is built on an incomplete search and is overstated. It needs rewriting at analytic tier.
verdicts.corrections: Text: replace "The only PIB-named award to an Adani-linked vendor is the 2025-12-30 CQB carbine contract" with "PIB-named contracts with Adani-linked vendors: the 2025-12-30 CQB carbine (₹2,770 crore joint with Bharat Forge; reported split 60/40, Bharat Forge L1, Adani L2) and the 2026-07-22 DRDO-CABS contract with ADSTL as DcPP for AEW&C Mk-II mission systems (sole vendor, amount not stated, PIB PRID 2288009)". Replace "of ₹4.07 lakh crore PIB-named awards 2021-25" with "of this file's ₹4.07 lakh crore sample of 45 PIB-named award claims, calendar 2021-25 (the PIB universe is larger; FY2025-26 capital contracts to 30 Dec alone were ₹1,82,492 crore per PRID 2209832)". Delete "no sole-vendor award to an Adani entity found", or change it to "no priced sole-vendor MoD capital acquisition in the sample; the AEL AR 2025 records deliveries of ULPGMs, UAVs, Drishti-10, SAMs and NGARM to the services and a counter-drone system to the BSF, with values not published". Add an award edge min:ministry-of-defence (or the DRDO/CABS node) → force:adani-defence, from 2026-07-22, a=null, void "amount not stated", src PIB PRID 2288009. strongestCounter: remove "the large Adani ventures ... are not shown as MoD orders in the opened records", which the AR page contradicts. Add the Chakra News L1/L2 60/40 split (reported) to the carbine edge. Keep status at "unsupported" only if the strongestCase is rewritten to include the AEW&C DcPP and the AR-listed deliveries. Tier: analytic, with innocentReading.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim, written out: the Government of India (Modi government, in office from May 2014) steered Dassault's offset partnership to Anil Ambani's Reliance group between the Paris announcement (10 Apr 2015) and the IGA and offset contracts (23 Sep 2016), with the JV formed in Feb 2017. The government's term covers that whole period, so the dates line up. The Supreme Court judgment confirms 10 Apr 2015 (joint statement), 23 Sep 2016 (IGA and the offset contracts with Dassault and MBDA) and the Feb 2017 JV. Reliance Aerostructure's incorporation on 24 Apr 2015 appears in the judgment as the petitioners' allegation ("the company itself had come into being only on 24th April, 2015"). The Court accepted it in substance ("It is no doubt true that the company ... has come into being in the recent past"). The Hollande quote is from Sep 2018 (Mediapart) and was reprinted by Gulf News on 2018-11-05. The CAG offsets audit was tabled 2020-09-24 (Scroll). The review dismissal on 2019-11-14 is correct, but no source in this narrative's srcs supports it. No date errors.
verdicts.identityTest: Pass, with care needed. The Supreme Court names "Reliance Aerostructure Ltd." and "Reliance Defence". Gulf News names "Reliance Defence" and DRAL. Scroll names "Dassault Reliance Aerospace". These are all Anil Ambani's group, and the narrative correctly separates them from Mukesh Ambani's RIL. One point to note: the judgment says Dassault's 2012 pact (under the MMRCA process) was with "Reliance Industries (Another business group)". The Court's line that "there was possibly an arrangement between the parent Reliance company and Dassault starting from the year 2012" therefore rests on a different group. Do not cite it as continuity of the Anil Ambani tie.
verdicts.baseRate: Under DPP 2013 clause 4.3, every foreign OEM picks its own Indian offset partner, so "the vendor chose a private IOP" tells you nothing on its own. Dassault's CEO said it had concluded partnerships with about 30 Indian firms out of about 100 in negotiation, and that DRAL is about 10% of the offsets. Scroll/HT say 20% of the offsets went to the private sector and the CAG found no discrepancy in that share. The features that do stand out are a partner incorporated days after the announcement, a JV with no aerospace track record, the Hollande statement and the Segalen document. These are specific facts, not base-rate artefacts. The symmetry control (Bofors beside Rafale, identical fields) has been run in symmetryCheck: neither case produced a conviction, and no audit or court found a payment to a public servant.
verdicts.denialFound: Yes, several. (1) Government of India, 'Clarification on Offset Policy' of 22 Sep 2018, as quoted by the Supreme Court: "the Government reiterates that it has no role to play in the selection of the IOP" (https://indiankanoon.org/doc/95183857/). (2) French government (Gulf News 2018-11-05): "The French government is in no manner involved in the choice of Indian industrial partners". (3) Dassault (same source): "Dassault Aviation has decided to make a partnership with India's Reliance Group. This is Dassault Aviation's choice." (4) Dassault's reply to Mediapart in Oct 2018: it "has freely chosen" Reliance, and Segalen's "imperative and mandatory" referred to the offsets (https://theprint.in/defence/picking-reliance-as-partner-was-our-choice-dassault-says-again-after-new-rafale-row/132659/). (5) PIB 2019-11-20 Lok Sabha reply: "Indian Government has not recommended any company". Hollande's own qualification to AFP: asked whether India pressured Dassault, he said he was unaware and "only Dassault can comment on this", while still standing by his claim that the Modi government proposed Reliance (https://scroll.in/article/895491/no-french-ex-president-hollande-did-not-deny-his-rafale-remarks-to-afp-heres-what-he-said).
verdicts.innocentReading: Dassault had to place 50% of the contract value in Indian offsets. It wanted a partner with land next to a runway (Nagpur MIHAN), a manufacturing JV it could control, and a group that was politically connected but commercially available. Having fallen out with HAL over MMRCA work-share and liability, it chose Reliance itself, as the offset guidelines allow. It spread the rest of the offsets across about 30 firms, and later took 51% of DRAL. On this reading, Hollande's "new formula" remark describes the sequence he saw (Reliance's name came up after the government changed), not a direction from the Indian government. He disclaimed knowing of any pressure.
verdicts.reason:
I checked all four sources. Each one supports what the narrative attributes to it.

- **Supreme Court (indiankanoon 95183857):** "We do not find any substantial material on record to show that this is a case of commercial favouritism to any party by the Indian Government, as the option to choose the IOP does not rest with the Indian Government." Clause 4.3 is quoted verbatim.
- **Gulf News:** carries the Hollande quote, the French government's "in no manner involved" and Dassault's "This is Dassault Aviation's choice."
- **CAG Report 3 of 2019 (CHRI PDF, text extracted):** contains no "Reliance", "DRAL" or "Ambani". "2.86 per cent lower" and "Offset contract with 50 per cent value" are present.
- **Scroll:** gives the 30% DRDO / 20% private split "including Dassault Reliance Aerospace", and says the auditor "had not detected any discrepancies as far as the 20% allocation to the private sector was concerned."

The narrative presents steering as contested, not as fact, and carries both case and counter. The core is not refuted. But the source check is only partial, for three reasons:

1. **Wrong figure.** "The offset is 50% of the contract (twice the policy floor)" is contradicted by the narrative's own Scroll source: the policy floor is "at least 30%", and 50% is about 1.67 times that.
2. **Misframing.** The claim text calls the "CAG 2020 offset findings" part of the case for steering. On Reliance specifically, that audit is exculpatory: it found no discrepancy in the private allocation. Its ToT shortfall concerns Dassault/MBDA and DRDO, not Reliance. Combining the two into one argument is a conjunction error.
3. **Material omissions on both sides.** The strongest case leaves out Mediapart's Oct 2018 internal Dassault document, in which Loïk Segalen (11 May 2017) called the Reliance JV "imperative and mandatory ... to get the export contract". The strongest counter leaves out Hollande's AFP qualification that he was unaware of any pressure.

On tier: a named party asserts the steering (Hollande, the petitioners, the opposition) and a contra exists, so `alleged` with contras is the right tier for the steering claim. The underlying court, CAG and statement facts remain documented.

2. **Claim text:** change "Hollande quote and CAG 2020 offset findings are the case for" to "the Hollande quote and the Mediapart-reported Dassault internal document are the case for; the CAG 2020 offsets audit found Dassault/MBDA had not confirmed ToT to DRDO (30% share) but found no discrepancy in the 20% private allocation that includes DRAL".
3. **strongestCase:** add, as [reported], Mediapart (Oct 2018): Dassault deputy CEO Loïk Segalen told staff representatives on 2017-05-11 that "it was imperative and mandatory for Dassault Aviation to accept this counterpart, in order to get the export contract from India". Add the contra: Dassault said it "freely chose" Reliance and that the remark referred to the offsets (ThePrint, https://theprint.in/defence/picking-reliance-as-partner-was-our-choice-dassault-says-again-after-new-rafale-row/132659/).
4. **strongestCounter:** add Hollande's own qualification to AFP (Sep 2018): asked whether India pressured Dassault, he said he was unaware and "only Dassault can comment on this" (Scroll article 895491).
5. **strongestCase:** mark the 24 Apr 2015 incorporation as cited by the Supreme Court from the petitioners' submission, which the Court accepted as "in the recent past". If a CIN or MCA record is not opened, note it as a gap.
6. **srcs:** add the 2019-11-14 review-dismissal judgment and the PIB 2019-11-20 reply, since the narrative relies on both. Add the Reuters/TradingView 2025 source for the "Dassault took 51% of DRAL" statement.
7. **whatWouldChange:** record that the French PNF judicial inquiry opened on 2021-06-14, and that India reportedly had not executed France's Nov 2022 request for judicial cooperation (The Wire, reported). Its outcome is still unknown.
8. **Tier:** carry the steering claim as `alleged` with the contras above, not as an unlabelled narrative.

verdicts.dateTest: Restated: "India's major-arms imports (SIPRI TIV, deliveries) did not fall under Make in India (2014 onward)". Window: Make in India runs from Sept 2014 and the NDA from FY2014-15. The SIPRI periods cited are 2015-19 to 2020-24 (−9.3%) and 2016-20 to 2021-25 (−4.0%). Both fall inside the NDA window, but they are OVERLAPPING five-year windows, not consecutive ones, so "−9.3% then −4.0%" invites a cumulative reading the data does not support. The earlier comparison that SIPRI also publishes is missing: 2010-14 to 2015-19, −32% (SIPRI fs_2003_at_2019: "Between 2010–14 and 2015–19, arms imports by India and Pakistan decreased by 32 and 39 per cent, respectively"). India's world share went from 14% (2010-14) to 9.2%, 8.3% and 8.2%. Deliveries lag orders by years, so 2010-14 deliveries are mostly UPA-era orders. The date test passes for the figures given, but the window was chosen selectively. Rafale-M IGA is 2025-04-28 (PIB). The MRFA and P-8I AoNs are 2026-02-12 (AIR). The domestic share is FY2024-25. All are correctly dated.
verdicts.identityTest: Pass. The importer is India (SIPRI Table 2, rank 2 in both sheets). The contract figures are the MoD's FY2024-25 contracts (PIB 2191937). The Rafale-M IGA is between the Governments of India and France for 26 Dassault aircraft (PIB 2124851). One unit mismatch is flagged correctly in the record itself: SIPRI measures TIV volume of deliveries, while the PIB 81% is ₹ contract value signed. These are not commensurable, so the 81% cannot rebut or confirm a volume claim directly.
verdicts.baseRate: The volume decline does not single out Make in India. In the 2010-14 to 2015-19 comparison Pakistan's imports fell 39% against India's 32%. In 2015-19 to 2020-24, Saudi Arabia fell 41%, Egypt 44% and Australia 27% (SIPRI fs_2503 Table 2), with no Make-in-India policy behind any of them. Procurement cycles explain much of it. Symmetry with the UPA-II control: on the same lens UPA-era deliveries (2010-14) gave India 14-15% of world imports with Russia at 72%. The NDA-era figures are lower on every SIPRI measure. The narrative never runs this control, although SPEC requires UPA-II beside NDA. Large foreign buys in the pipeline (Rafale-M, MRFA, P-8I, MQ-9B) also have UPA-era analogues (MMRCA, the original P-8I, C-130J, C-17), so the "pipeline" argument applies to both governments alike.
verdicts.denialFound: The government's position is on record in PIB 2191937: "At least 65% of defence equipment is now manufactured domestically, a significant shift from the earlier 65-70% import dependency" (no method printed). SIPRI's own reading partly contradicts the narrative. fs_2503: "The drop was at least partly the result of India's increasing ability to design and produce its own weapons, making it less reliant on imports." fs_2603: "The decrease can be partly attributed to India's growing ability to design and produce its own weapons—although there are often substantial delays in domestic production. However, India's recent orders or planned orders—including up to 140 combat aircraft from France and 6 submarines from Germany—indicate its continued and probably increasing reliance on foreign suppliers." No direct MoD response to this specific framing was sought.
verdicts.innocentReading: Imports have fallen in volume in every SIPRI comparison since 2010-14 (−32%, −9.3%, −4.0%), partly through domestic production and partly through procurement cycles and delays. India also remains the world's second-largest importer, because a small number of high-end platforms (fighters, submarines, MPA, engines) are still beyond domestic capability. Both statements are true together. "Has not reduced imports" is false as a past-tense volume claim. As a forecast about continued dependence on high-end platforms it is defensible.
verdicts.reason:
Every number in the claim checks against its source. SIPRI fs_2503 Table 2: "India 8.3 9.1 –9.3 Russia 36"; text: "Russia (36 per cent)... 2010–14 (72 per cent)". SIPRI fs_2603: "India 8.2 9.3 –4.0 Russia 40"; Russia's share 70% (2011-15) to 40% (2021-25). PIB 2191937: "193 contracts valued at ₹2,09,050 crore... 177 contracts, worth ₹1,68,922 crore, were awarded to the domestic industry" (80.8%). PIB 2124851 confirms the 26 Rafale-M IGA. AIR 2026-02-12 confirms the MRFA (Rafale) and P-8I AoNs. As a contested narrative with documented components it is therefore not refuted. The framing is defective, though:
- −9.3% and −4.0% come from overlapping windows.
- The SIPRI −32% (2010-14 to 2015-19) and the 14% UPA-era share are omitted, so the required UPA-II control is not run.
- AoNs are called "orders".
- SIPRI itself attributes part of the fall to domestic production, which cuts against the literal claim.
The past-tense claim is unsupported on volume. Only the forward-looking dependence claim is genuinely contested. The four claim-level srcs do not cover the MRFA/P-8I AoN items; those rest on AIR, which is in the narrative srcs but not the claim srcs.
verdicts.corrections:
1. text: replace "volume −9.3% then −4.0%" with "volume −32% (2010-14→2015-19), −9.3% (2015-19→2020-24), −4.0% (2016-20→2021-25; overlapping windows, not cumulative)". Add "world share 14% (2010-14) → 9.2% → 8.3% → 8.2%". Add src SIPRI fs_2003_at_2019 https://www.sipri.org/sites/default/files/2020-03/fs_2003_at_2019.pdf.
2. text: replace "large foreign orders (Rafale-M, Rafale MRFA AoN, P-8I)" with "a signed IGA (26 Rafale-M, 2025-04-28) and AoNs, which are not orders (MRFA Rafale and P-8I, 2026-02-12; the ministry says the majority of MRFA aircraft are to be manufactured in India)".
3. srcs: add https://www.newsonair.gov.in/dac-clears-proposals-of-nearly-3-60-lakh-cr-to-enhance-capabilities-of-armed-forces to the claim-level srcs, since it supports the MRFA and P-8I items.
4. status: split it. The past-tense volume claim is "unsupported on SIPRI volume" (decline in all three comparisons, with SIPRI attributing part of it to domestic production). The forward-looking claim is "contested" ("probably increasing reliance" per SIPRI 2026).
5. Add symmetryCheck: UPA-II deliveries (2010-14, 14% share, Russia 72%) beside NDA periods. Pakistan −39% and Saudi Arabia −41% show the volume decline does not single out the policy.
6. Keep the note that PIB's 81% is ₹ contract value signed and SIPRI's figure is TIV deliveries. They are not commensurable, and "domestic industry" contracts carry imported content (e.g. GE F404 in LCA Mk1A).

verdicts.dateTest: As a claim: "DPSUs (actor) hold a dominant share of award value and production (thing) FY2019-20 to FY2025-26 / calendar 2021-25 (when), while private firms won ATAGS (2025-03-26), K9 VAJRA-T (2024-12-20), HPR and CIWS (2024-03-01) and the CQB carbine (2025-12-30)." I opened every PIB release and the dates match. The private share of production also checks out: 20.9% in 2023-24 (DDP table, 26,675 of 127,434), then 22% in FY2024-25 and 24% in FY2025-26. PIB 2273824 (17 Jun 2026) says: "the private sector contributed 24%, which is a rise from 22% in FY 2024-25." The FY2024-25 figure was first published as about 23% (PIB Aug 2025) and later restated to 22%; the record carries both. The windows are not mixed in a misleading way, but the award share (calendar 2021-25, a sample) and the production shares (FY) use different periods and should not be read as one series.
verdicts.identityTest:
The vendors match the sources. PIB 2115365 names "Bharat Forge Limited and Tata Advanced System Limited" for ATAGS and the 6x6 towing vehicles "respectively", total about Rs 6,900 crore. PIB 2010528 names L&T for CIWS (Rs 7,668.82 cr) and HPR (Rs 5,700.13 cr). PIB 2086514 names L&T for K9 VAJRA-T (Rs 7,628.70 cr, "under Buy (Indian) category"). PIB 2209832 names "Bharat Forge Ltd and PLR Systems Pvt Ltd" for the CQB carbine (Rs 2,770 cr). PIB 1912309 says BDL Akash, Rs 8,160 cr: "Around 60% of the project cost will be awarded to the private industry, including MSMEs."

There is one class conflation. The text says DPSUs hold "~74-76% of production". The 74% (73.8%, 2023-24, MoD AR 2024-25 p.105 table: 74,434 + 19,551 of 127,434) counts DPSUs plus ex-OFB companies only. The 76% comes from PIB 2273824: "Defence Public Sector Undertakings and other PSUs accounted for approximately 76%". That figure includes non-DPSU PSUs, which were 6,774 cr (5.3%) in 2023-24. On a like-for-like basis, DPSU+PSU was 79.1% in 2023-24, falling to about 76% in 2025-26. The range mixes two definitions.
verdicts.baseRate: The 77% DPSU / 58% HAL figure is not a base rate of the procurement universe. It comes from a sample of 45 PIB-named awards chosen for this file (₹4.07 lakh crore, joint contracts counted once). I recomputed the HAL total from the file's award claims: ₹2,36,737 crore of ₹4,07,145 crore = 58.1%. That is arithmetically correct. The figure is driven by a few platform-designer mega-contracts (LCH ₹62,700 cr, LCA Mk1A ₹62,370 cr, LCA ₹48,000 cr, AL-31FP ₹26,000 cr). HAL is the only Indian maker of fighters and helicopters, so any vendor that is the sole design or licence authority would score the same way. The symmetric check shows this: K9 VAJRA-T 2024 is a repeat Buy (Indian) single-vendor order to a private incumbent (L&T), the same kind of "protection" the narrative attributes to DPSUs. Nearly every country with state arsenals concentrates platform awards in the design-authority firm, so concentration alone does not discriminate. The UPA-II control for the DPSU/private production split is a declared gap: the UPA-II class series was not collected, so the trend comparison runs only from 2019-20.
verdicts.denialFound: MoD has not denied the claim directly. Its official position is promotional: PIB 2273824 credits "increased private sector participation". Other sources argue both ways, and the narrative should cite them. Supporting the protection reading: the CVC April 2021 memo said "award of contracts/projects/procurements on nomination basis without adequate justification amounts to restrictive practice eliminating competition", and private-industry complaints are documented (Defense News 2022-08-08, https://www.defensenews.com/top-100/2022/08/08/indias-private-defense-firms-seek-level-playing-field-as-mod-preps-new-arms-embargo/; Bharat Shakti, https://bharatshakti.in/defence-procurement-not-a-level-playing-field-for-private-sector-pses-still-rule/). Against it: ThePrint 2026-05-27 reports that in the AMCA prototype tender "State-run Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) has been kept out of the bidding process", with TASL, a Bharat Forge consortium and an L&T consortium shortlisted (https://theprint.in/defence/5th-gen-fighter-amca-tender-issued-hal-sits-out-as-private-sector-takes-centre-stage/2943139/). HAL and the DPSUs were not asked for comment.
verdicts.innocentReading: DPSUs win most award value because they are the sole design or licence holders for the platforms being bought: HAL for LCA, LCH, ALH and Su-30/AL-31FP under Russian licence, and BDL for DRDO's Akash. Repeat orders go to the incumbent producer whatever its ownership, as the L&T K9 repeat order shows. DPSU primes also pass much of their contract value to private suppliers (about 60% on Akash). Where a new category opened (towed guns, high-power radar, CIWS, carbines, AMCA prototypes), private firms have won or been the only ones shortlisted.
verdicts.reason:
The narrative survives, but only as a contested analytic synthesis. Every quoted fact I opened is confirmed by the primary record: the PIB releases for ATAGS, K9, HPR/CIWS, CQB and Akash's 60%, PIB 2273824's 76%/24%/22%, and the MoD AR 2024-25 production table. The 58% recomputes exactly from the file's award claims. The status "contested" is the correct reading, and an adversarial reading cannot push it to "true" or "false".

Three faults remain, and none is fatal. (1) "~74-76% of production" joins a DPSU+ex-OFB figure to a DPSU+other-PSU figure. (2) None of the four cited sources states the 77%/58%; those are our own computation on a hand-picked sample, and "PIB-named award ₹" reads as the universe. (3) The strongest case leaves out the actual documented mechanism of protection (nomination-basis awards, the 2021 CVC memo). The strongest counter leaves out the reported 2026 AMCA tender that excluded HAL, which is inside the asOf window. "narrative" is not a valid tier; the closest valid tier is analytic.
verdicts.corrections:
1. tier: "narrative" → "analytic"; carry the innocentReading above.
2. text: replace "DPSUs hold … ~74-76% of production" with "DPSUs + ex-OFB companies produced 73.8% in 2023-24 (MoD AR 2024-25 table); 'DPSUs and other PSUs' ~76% in 2025-26 (PIB 2273824)".
3. text: replace "77% of PIB-named award ₹ (HAL 58%)" with "77% of the ₹4.07 lakh crore of PIB-named awards sampled in this file, 2021-25 (45 contracts; HAL 58%) — sample, not universe".
4. srcs: add PIB 2086514 (K9 VAJRA-T), PIB 2010528 (HPR, CIWS) and PIB 2209832 (CQB carbine), which the text names but the claim's srcs omit. Add the HAL award releases behind the 58% (1694844, 2116411, 2171108) or point to claim procurement-industry:c063.
5. strongestCase: add the nomination-basis mechanism (CVC April 2021 memo; private-industry level-playing-field complaints, Defense News 2022-08-08) as reported evidence.
6. strongestCounter: add "K9 VAJRA-T 2024 is a repeat single-vendor Buy (Indian) order to a private incumbent" (symmetry). Add the AMCA tender: ThePrint 2026-05-27 reports HAL "kept out of the bidding process" and TASL, BFL-led and L&T-led bidders shortlisted (reported; move it out of whatWouldChange).
7. Note the FY2024-25 private share restatement (23% → 22%) in the text, or cite "22-24%" as the PIB 2026 figures.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim, written out: Adani Enterprises Ltd (AEL) owns Adani Defence & Aerospace / ADSTL, as of 23 Dec 2024 (the release date) and still in 2025-26. The edge has no from/to dates. The ownership window covers both dates. Source 1 is dated 23 Dec 2024 and published on AEL's own newsroom. Source 2 is AEL's Annual Report for FY2024-25. Later AEL exchange disclosures (March 2026) still call ADSTL an AEL subsidiary, so nothing contradicts the dates.
verdicts.identityTest: The entity matches. Source 1 says: "Ahmedabad, 23 December 2024: Adani Defence Systems & Technologies Ltd. (ADSTL) has signed a share purchase agreement to acquire 85.8% shareholding in Air Works". It calls the brand "Adani Defence & Aerospace" and quotes Ashish Rajvanshi as its CEO. Source 2 says: "Adani Defence & Aerospace, driven by the vision of our Chairman Mr Gautam Adani, is a pioneer in defence design, development and manufacturing". It places that business under Adani New Industries Ltd inside AEL's report. Neither page uses the word "subsidiary" or gives a percentage, and source 2 never names ADSTL. One caution: the 'd' field says the defence business sits "under Adani New Industries Ltd", but AEL's exchange filings describe ADSTL as a wholly owned subsidiary of AEL. No intermediate holding company is named there. Treat the ANIL wording as a segment label in the report, not a holding chain.
verdicts.baseRate: Not applicable. This is a plain corporate-ownership edge, not a pattern or a property claimed to set one company apart. Every private defence vendor (L&T, Tata Advanced Systems under Tata Sons, Bharat Forge/Kalyani Strategic Systems, Mahindra Defence) sits under a listed or holding parent. The edge implies no wrongdoing.
verdicts.denialFound: None found. None is needed: the claim is an ownership fact that the company itself states, in its own newsroom and annual report, and in exchange filings reported by AngelOne and Scanx (March 2026) calling ADSTL "its wholly owned subsidiary". Not asked.
verdicts.innocentReading: The edge is neutral. A listed conglomerate holds its defence and aerospace business through a wholly owned operating company (ADSTL), which runs under the brand "Adani Defence & Aerospace". This is the normal structure.
verdicts.reason: The claim is true and the record states its limits honestly: it admits the holding chain and percentage are not printed in the opened pages. Both sources are AEL's own publications and present Adani Defence & Aerospace as an AEL business, with ADSTL as the acquiring entity. That is enough for an ownership edge at 'reported'. Independent reports of AEL's stock-exchange disclosures (AngelOne, Scanx, March 2026) confirm ADSTL is a wholly owned subsidiary of AEL. Nothing refutes the edge. The tier could go up to 'documented' if the AEL BSE/NSE filing or the subsidiaries list in the annual report is cited directly.
verdicts.corrections: 1) Add a primary ownership source: AEL's BSE/NSE disclosure of 23 Dec 2024 or the March 2026 Air Works disclosure, which calls ADSTL "wholly owned subsidiary" of AEL, or the subsidiaries list (Form AOC-1) in the FY25 annual report. Once one is cited, set the percentage to 100% (wholly owned), drop "(holding chain and % not stated in opened pages)" and consider tier 'documented'. Secondary confirmation: https://www.angelone.in/news/stocks/adani-enterprises-subsidiary-raises-stake-in-air-works and https://scanx.trade/stock-market-news/orders-deals/adani-enterprises-subsidiary-completes-14-2-air-works-acquisition-stake-rises-to-99-98/34781260. 2) In 'd', change "places the defence business under Adani New Industries Ltd, an AEL entity" to say the annual report lists it under AEL's Adani New Industries segment. As written, it reads like an intermediate holding company, and the filings do not show one. 3) Set from = 2024-12-23 at the latest (first source date) or leave it null. Do not suggest ownership began on that date. 4) Optionally add the Air Works stake (85.8% in Dec 2024, 99.98% by Mar 2026) as a separate ADSTL to Air Works edge, not inside this one.

verdicts.dateTest: Claim restated: Adani's land-defence subsidiary acquired 51% of PLR Systems on 2020-09-10 and still held it at the 2025-12-30 PIB carbine award. PTI (Devdiscourse, updated 2020-09-11) reports a BSE filing: "Adani Land Defence Systems and Technologies Ltd -- a step-down subsidiary of the company -- has acquired 51 per cent equity shares of PLR Systems Private Limited from Fouraces Systems India Private Limited on September 10, 2020". Business Today (2025-12-30) says "Adani Land Defence Systems and Technologies, owns a 51 per cent stake in PLR Systems." Angel One (2025-07-18) gives the same 51%. The edge's from=2020-09 is correct and the holding is still reported at the award date. The dates overlap and the test passes.
verdicts.identityTest: Partial mismatch. All three outlets name the holder as Adani Land Defence Systems and Technologies Ltd (ALDSTL), a step-down subsidiary of Adani Enterprises. The source node force:adani-defence is labelled "Adani Defence & Aerospace (Adani Defence Systems & Technologies Ltd)". Adani Defence & Aerospace is a brand, ADSTL is a separate company, and the holding sits one level down. The target is right: PLR Systems Private Limited, Malanpur, Gwalior, with IWI holding 49%. No CIN was verified for either company because MCA is unreachable. The node and edge text calls PLR a "joint venture of Adani Defence and Israel Weapon Industries", which reads as if Adani co-founded it. In fact Adani bought an existing shareholder's 51% (from Fouraces Systems India) in 2020, so PLR existed before Adani. Its original Punj Lloyd parentage is from memory and was not sourced.
verdicts.baseRate: Not applicable. This is a single, disclosed shareholding fact, not a discriminating pattern claim. For context, joint ventures with foreign OEMs are the normal entry route for Indian private small-arms makers.
verdicts.denialFound: None needed and none found (not asked). The holding was disclosed by Adani Enterprises itself in a BSE filing in September 2020. No party disputes it.
verdicts.innocentReading: This is a routine, exchange-disclosed acquisition with Ministry of Home Affairs approval: a conglomerate buying a licensed small-arms maker that already had an IWI technology partner. The ownership edge implies nothing beyond itself. Any inference from it combined with the carbine award is a separate claim, and the file's symmetry section already treats it as one (0.68% of the sample, joint with Bharat Forge).
verdicts.reason: The core claim holds. Several independent credible outlets state the 51% stake: PTI reporting a BSE regulatory filing (2020-09-11), Business Today (2025-12-30) and Angel One (2025-07-18). An exchange filing is a primary record, so the tier should go up to documented. Of the two cited sources, only Angel One says what the claim says. The Adani Enterprises FY25 annual-report page says only "Our Gwalior facility specialises in manufacturing a diverse range of small arms for both domestic and international customers". It does not mention PLR Systems or any percentage. The remaining problems are framing and identity, not substance: the holder is ALDSTL rather than ADSTL, and the "JV of Adani and IWI" wording is misleading.
verdicts.corrections: 1) Tier: reported -> documented. verdicts.dateTest: The claim as a sentence: Reliance (Anil Ambani group) held 51% of DRAL from Feb 2017 until 2025. verdicts.identityTest: This only partly matches. The direct shareholder in DRAL was Reliance Aerostructure Ltd (RAL), not Reliance Infrastructure Ltd. ConstructionWorld reports that "Reliance Aerostructure Ltd (RAL) will transfer 2 per cent equity in Dassault Reliance Aerospace Ltd (DRAL)" and calls RAL "its subsidiary", meaning a subsidiary of R-Infra. The SC judgment names the partner as "Reliance Defence" and "Reliance Aerostructure Ltd" (incorporated 24 April 2015). R-Infra's holding was therefore indirect, through RAL. DRAL was a subsidiary of R-Infra and becomes an associate after the deal. The record's description correctly separates Anil Ambani's group (ADAG) from Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Industries. The SC also mentions a 2012 Dassault pact with "Reliance Industries (Another business group)", so keeping these apart is essential.
verdicts.baseRate: Before the 2020 defence FDI change (49% under the automatic route, raised to 74% in Sept 2020), Indian-majority 51:49 was the standard structure for foreign-OEM defence joint ventures in India. Other examples are Tata-Lockheed, Tata-Sikorsky and Mahindra-Airbus-type arrangements. Majority Indian holding is therefore close to universal for these JVs and says nothing distinctive. The claim makes no inference of wrongdoing, so this is context, not a reason to refute.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable. This is a neutral ownership fact, and nobody contests the stake split. Reliance Infrastructure itself disclosed the transaction in an exchange filing, as Reuters reports ("Reliance Infrastructure said in an exchange filing"). I found no contrary report of the earlier split.
verdicts.innocentReading: The 51:49 split shows the defence FDI cap in force in 2017 (49% automatic route), which required an Indian majority. In 2025 Dassault bought 2% to take majority control, once the higher cap allowed it. Nothing in the ownership fact implies a favour or impropriety.
verdicts.reason: The holding is sound by arithmetic and supported elsewhere. Reuters (via TradingView) says Dassault buys 2% and becomes "a majority owner of the firm with a 51% stake", while Reliance "will hold a 49% stake". So before the deal Reliance held 51% and Dassault 49%. ConstructionWorld confirms that RAL transferred the 2% and that DRAL ceases to be an R-Infra subsidiary, which only works if the Reliance side had a majority. Neither cited source states the 51% figure directly, hence sourceCheck is "partially". The SC judgment gives only the Feb 2017 formation and the partner's identity, not percentages. The real flaws are about precision, not refutation: (1) the direct holder was Reliance Aerostructure Ltd, with R-Infra holding indirectly; (2) the end date is an expected close of 1 Nov 2025 that I could not confirm; (3) the claim is already superseded by c053, which is correct. "Reported" is the right tier. Citing R-Infra's BSE/NSE disclosure of 5 Sept 2025 or a DRAL/RAL MCA filing would justify "documented".

Note that the SC judgment (indiankanoon 95183857) supports only the Feb 2017 JV formation and the partner's identity, not the 51% figure. Keep supersededBy = c053.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim reads: CAG (Report No. 2 of 2020, "Management of Defence Offset", tabled in the Lok Sabha on 23 Sep 2020) observed that Dassault Aviation and MBDA had not confirmed the transfer of technology to DRDO under the 36-Rafale offset contract (signed Sep 2016). The dates line up. Dassault and MBDA proposed the DRDO tranche in Sep 2015. DRDO named its technologies in Apr 2016. MoD told CAG in Oct 2019 that the vendor had "not yet been able to confirm" the transfer. Scroll published on 24 Sep 2020. One caveat: offset discharge only began around Sep 2019, so the observation is about a pending commitment early in a 7-year discharge window. It is not a finding of default at term. The claim's wording ("had not confirmed") is accurate to that state.
verdicts.identityTest: The entities match the source. Scroll names "French aerospace major Dassault Aviation and European missile maker MBDA" and DRDO, and calls Dassault Reliance Aerospace "a joint venture with Dassault Aviation set up in Nagpur". The target force:dassault-aviation is correct. MBDA is a co-subject and is not separately targeted, which is acceptable. DRAL (Dassault Reliance Aerospace Ltd) is correctly identified.
verdicts.baseRate: The property is not specific to Rafale. The same CAG audit covered 46 offset contracts signed between 2005 and Mar 2018, worth Rs 66,427 cr. Vendors claimed only 59% of the offsets due by Dec 2018 (Rs 11,396 cr of Rs 19,223 cr), and MoD accepted only 48% of those claims. CAG used Rafale as one example of vendors not being "earnest" about meeting commitments. Under-performance on offsets is therefore close to the norm across UPA-era and NDA-era contracts. Failing to confirm a technology transfer does not single out Dassault, and the claim should not be read as Rafale-specific misconduct. The claim already flags it as an audit observation, which helps. The symmetry control (Bofors beside Rafale, UPA-II contracts beside NDA) gives the same reading: the same audit criticised offset contracts from both governments.
verdicts.denialFound: No direct response from Dassault or MBDA to the 2020 CAG observation was found; I did not ask them. MoD's earlier position, in a Sep 2018 statement, was that "the vendor is to provide the details of offset partners either at the time of seeking offset credit or one year prior to the discharge of offset obligation, which in this case will be due from 2020" (reported by The Week: https://www.theweek.in/news/india/2020/09/23/cag-accuses-rafale-manufacturer-of-violating-offset-agreement.html). The Congress response came from P. Chidambaram, who asked whether the first annual obligation (Sep 2019 to Sep 2020) had been met; it is quoted in the Scroll source.
verdicts.innocentReading: Offset discharge on the Rafale contract had only just begun. Dassault and MBDA declined five of the six technologies DRDO asked for because they were "not within the vendor's core competence". The replacement request, Kaveri engine assistance, was still being negotiated when the audit was done. Across all 46 contracts audited, vendors routinely lagged on offsets. The finding records a commitment not yet confirmed. It is not evidence of a breach or of favouritism, and CAG found no discrepancy in the private-sector (DRAL) allocation.
verdicts.reason: The claim survives. The Scroll source states each element. Quotes: "Dassault Aviation and European missile maker MBDA have 'till date' not confirmed the transfer of technology to the Defence Research and Development Organisation". "20% was allocated to the private sector, including Dassault Reliance Aerospace, according to the Hindustan Times". "The CAG report said the auditor had not detected any discrepancies as far as the 20% allocation to the private sector was concerned." The claim is hedged ("as reported", "audit observation, not a sanction") and does not imply a quid pro quo. Tier "reported" is right because the only source is a secondary report of a primary CAG document. It becomes "documented" only if the CAG report PDF is attached and the passages are quoted from it.
verdicts.corrections: 1. Attribution: the "20% incl. DRAL" breakdown comes from the Hindustan Times as relayed by Scroll, not from the CAG text quoted in Scroll. Reword to: "...CAG found no discrepancy in the 20% private-sector allocation (which HT reported includes DRAL)". 2. Name the report: CAG Report No. 2 of 2020, "Management of Defence Offset", tabled 23 Sep 2020. Add the cag.gov.in PDF as the primary source; with it the tier can go up to documented. 3. Add the date context: "MoD informed CAG in Oct 2019 that the vendor had not yet confirmed; offset discharge window began ~Sep 2019." 4. Add the base-rate context: "same audit: vendors discharged only 59% of offsets due across 46 contracts (2005–2018)". 5. pred "enforce" overstates a non-sanction audit observation. Use an audit/observation predicate if the schema has one.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim reads: NCLT Ahmedabad special bench approved the Hazel Mercantile / Swan Energy resolution plan for Reliance Naval and Engineering Ltd on 2022-12-23. The company entered CIRP in January 2020, and the Swan board took over on 2023-12-08 with management control on 2024-01-04. The approval falls inside the insolvency window, so the dates are consistent. The Business Today article is dated 2022-12-23 and says the plan "has been approved today". The renaming to Swan Defence and Heavy Industries came in January 2025, so "now" is correct as of 2026. One small point: by 2022 the "Anil Ambani group" was the former promoter only, because a resolution professional had control from January 2020. The label describes where the company came from, not who controlled it at the time.
verdicts.identityTest: Business Today names the company as "Anil Ambani's bankrupt Reliance Naval and Engineering Ltd, formerly known as Pipavav Shipyard". Its headline uses the older style "Reliance Naval Defence & Engineering". This is the same entity as the force:reliance-naval-engineering node, and the record correctly separates it from Reliance Industries. Wikipedia confirms the same company was renamed Swan Defence and Heavy Industries Ltd. The bidder is named as the "Swan Energy-led Hazel Mercantile consortium", which matches the claim. No CIN is cited. Adding one would close the identity test fully.
verdicts.baseRate: Not applicable as a discriminator. This is a factual record of a tribunal outcome and implies no wrongdoing. Most large IBC cases end in liquidation rather than a resolution plan, so "resolved by sale" is if anything the less common result. Nothing here depends on a pattern-based inference.
verdicts.denialFound: None found, and none was needed or asked for. The claim makes no accusation. The record notes that the tribunal rejected the challenges from Jindal Steel and Power and from Reliance Infrastructure, the parent of the former promoter. Those rejected challenges are the only contrary position on file.
verdicts.innocentReading: This is a routine IBC resolution. About 95% of the committee of creditors voted for the highest compliant bid, and the NCLT approved it under section 31. The claim itself is the plain reading, and it carries no implication of impropriety.
verdicts.reason: Both sources say what the claim says. Business Today: "The Swan Energy-led Hazel Mercantile consortium plan for Reliance Naval Defence & Engineering has been approved today by the Ahmedabad special bench of the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT)" (2022-12-23). Wikipedia gives the same date of 23 December 2022 and the renaming to Swan Defence and Heavy Industries in January 2025. Bench, date, bidder and entity all match, and no part of the claim is an inference built by joining separate facts. The tier is right. There is one credible outlet with a named tribunal outcome, and Wikipedia does not count as a second independent outlet, so the claim does not yet qualify as documented.
verdicts.corrections: 1. Change pred from "enforce" to an adjudication or approval predicate if the schema has one (for example "adjudicate" or "approve"). An NCLT approval under IBC section 31 is not an enforcement action against the company. 2. In the text, change "(Anil Ambani group)" to "(formerly Anil Ambani group; under a resolution professional since January 2020)". 3. upgradeIf: cite the NCLT Ahmedabad order of 2022-12-23, or the Swan Energy / RNEL stock-exchange disclosure of the approval, to reach documented. 4. Add the company's CIN to the target node.

verdicts.dateTest: The claim restated: "MoD signed L&T sole-vendor contracts worth ₹24,984.65 cr (2022-03 to 2024-12) and signed one split CQB-carbine award to Bharat Forge and PLR Systems (Adani Defence 51%) on 2025-12-30." Every signing date falls inside the stated 2021-25 window. PLR became Adani-linked before the 2025-12-30 signing, so the dates overlap and the date test passes. The L&T sum checks out against the PIB text: MPV ₹887 cr (YER 2022, signed March 2022), Cadet Training Ships "over Rs 3,100 crore" (YER 2023), CIWS ₹7,668.82 cr and HPR ₹5,700.13 cr (PRID 2010528, 2024-03-01), and K9 VAJRA-T ₹7,628.70 cr (PRID 2086514, 2024-12-20). These add to ₹24,984.65 cr. The denominator also reproduces: summing the file's 45 award claims plus the four joint totals counted once (9,781 + 10,147 + 6,900 + 2,770) gives ₹407,144.93 cr. That makes L&T 6.14% and the full carbine total 0.68%. All figures are in ₹ crore as printed, and they are contract-signing values, not budget figures.
verdicts.identityTest: The PIB releases name the entities as "M/s Larsen & Toubro Limited" and "PLR Systems Pvt Ltd". PRID 2209832 says: "The contract for over 4.25 lakh CQB Carbine along with accessories, worth Rs 2,770 crore, for the Indian Army and the Indian Navy were signed with Bharat Forge Ltd and PLR Systems Pvt Ltd." That PLR is Adani-linked (Adani Defence 51%, IWI 49%) rests on reporting, not on the PIB text, and the record's own claim correctly treats it that way. The identity is right, with one problem. Reporting says this was not a single joint contract. It was an L1/L2 split: Bharat Forge was L1 with 60% (2.55 lakh units) and Adani/PLR was L2 with 40% (1.70 lakh units). Sources: chakranewz.com/critical-technologies/mod-to-sign-cqb-contract-with-bf-and-adani-defence, plus several outlets reporting the 60:40 split. The PIB text gives no split for each vendor.
verdicts.baseRate: Among private vendors named in the 45-award PIB sample, a zero sole-vendor PIB award total is the normal case. Only L&T, ICOMM, Chowgule and Bharat Forge/TASL (in joint releases) appear at all. L&T, with decades of naval, radar and artillery lines, is the outlier. Adani's ₹0 sole share therefore does not single it out as either favoured or disfavoured. The comparison is useful because it applies the same lens to both firms, as the SPEC requires, not because either number is remarkable. The sample covers only part of the PIB universe. FY2025-26 capital contracts alone were ₹1,82,492 cr per PRID 2209832, so the shares describe the sample, not all MoD procurement.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable. The claim alleges no impropriety by either party, so there is nothing to deny. Neither L&T nor Adani Defence was asked. I found no statement from either company disputing the amounts.
verdicts.innocentReading: L&T has been a licensed defence prime for decades, building warships, radars and K9 guns. Adani Defence entered around 2015-18 and so far wins mainly through JVs (PLR with IWI) and development programmes (Netra Mk2 DcPP L1, which is DRDO, not a signed MoD contract). On the second-bidder rule: when the L2 bidder matches the L1 price, defence procurement rules allow the order to be split 60:40, which is ordinary procedure. A gap in PIB-named awards between the two firms is what entry dates and capability predict. PIB also does not publish emergency procurements (for example Drishti-10 UAVs), below-threshold orders or MRO awards (Air Works), so Adani-linked receipts may be understated. L&T's may be too.

verdicts.dateTest: Passes. The claim reads: the Ministry of Defence signed Pinaka rocket contracts with EEL (a wholly-owned Solar Industries subsidiary) and MIL (a DPSU, corporatised from OFB in October 2021) on 2025-02-06. The PIB release says "Posted On: 06 FEB 2025 ... The contracts were signed in the presence of Defence Secretary Shri Rajesh Kumar Singh in New Delhi on February 06, 2025." Rajesh Kumar Singh became Defence Secretary in November 2024, so he was in office on that date. The Business Upturn piece is dated 6 Feb 2025, 4:08 PM IST, the same day. Both entities existed in the forms named on that date.
verdicts.identityTest: Passes. PIB names "Economic Explosive Limited (EEL) and Munitions India Limited (MIL)". Business Upturn says "Solar Industries India Ltd, through its wholly-owned subsidiary Economic Explosives Limited (EEL)". These are the same entities as the nodes force:economic-explosives and force:munitions-india. PIB assigns the rockets explicitly: "procurement of Area Denial Munition (ADM) Type-1 (DPICM) and High Explosive Pre Fragmented (HEPF) Mk-1 (Enhanced) rockets respectively", meaning ADM goes to EEL and HEPF to MIL. The company disclosure says "This significant contract includes the supply of Area Denial Munition (ADM) Type-1 (DPICM) and High Explosive Pre Fragmented (HEPF) Mk-1 (Enhanced) rockets ... Contract Value: INR 6,084 Crores". The tension the claim describes is therefore real and accurately quoted. Wording error: PIB says "contracts totalling Rs 10,147 crore" (plural), and the total covers three counterparties (EEL, MIL and BEL's SHAKTI software upgrade). It is not "one ... contract", and the label's word "joint" is wrong.
verdicts.baseRate: This pattern does not single anyone out. Dual-sourcing Pinaka production between OFB/MIL and private firms (Solar/EEL for rockets; Tata and L&T for launchers) has been standard since the 2010s. Splitting one MoD announcement across a DPSU and a licensed private vendor is common in ammunition procurement. The DRDO nomination of EEL as a production agency is a routine design-to-production route. The claim alleges no wrongdoing, so no discriminating property is needed. It works as the SPEC control "a private vendor beside the DPSU competing in the same category, same years", and it is symmetric by construction.
verdicts.denialFound: None found; nobody was asked, and no response is required. The claim is analytic and implies no wrongdoing. Neither MoD nor Solar has published a per-vendor split. ThePrint, The Week and Projects Monitor repeat only the ₹10,147 crore total.
verdicts.innocentReading: MoD signed separate contracts in a single ceremony and PIB reported only the aggregate. EEL's ₹6,084 crore may include HEPF Mk-1(E) volumes under a DRDO production-agency nomination, or PIB's "respectively" may simplify a split order. Either way, this is a reporting mismatch, not evidence of favour. The ₹4,063 crore residual is arithmetic only, and it is unreliable because the BEL SHAKTI value is folded into the total.
verdicts.reason: Both sources say exactly what the claim attributes to them: PIB gives the ₹10,147 crore total and assigns ADM to EEL and HEPF to MIL "respectively", while the Solar disclosure reports ₹6,084 crore covering both rocket types. The claim correctly marks the split as unresolved and makes no inference beyond that. The analytic tier with an innocentReading is right. The individual facts would support documented, but the comparison is ours. The flaws are in wording only: "one ... contract" should be "contracts totalling", and "joint" should go.

Another ~₹1,700 cr is Lynx-U2 naval fire-control systems, ₹950 cr is DR-118 radar warning receivers and ~₹3,000 cr is the Himshakti EW system. Part of the ₹2,400 cr pair is Sarang ESM. verdicts.baseRate: This is not a wrongdoing claim, so a discriminating base rate does not apply. The relevant base is the universe the sample is meant to stand in for, and the claim's own source PRID 2116411 gives it for FY2024-25: "193 [contracts] with overall contract value exceeding Rs 2,09,050 crore ... contracts to domestic industry are 177 (92%) with contract value Rs 1,68,922 Crore (81%)". That puts foreign at about 19% of value. The sample has foreign at 0% in both 2024 and 2025 and 5.4% pooled. The sample is also not the full set of PIB-named awards. PIB releases name vendor and ₹ for at least these contracts the claim leaves out: WASS Submarine Systems (Italy) ₹1,896 crore, 30 Dec 2025 (PRID 2209832, which the record itself cites); Naval Group (France) EHWT integration ₹877 crore and MDL AIP plug ₹1,990 crore, 30 Dec 2024; BEL Ashwini LLTR ₹2,906 crore, 12 Mar 2025 (PRID 2110849); HVF Arjun Mk-1A ₹7,523 crore, 23 Sep 2021 (PRID 1757320). verdicts.denialFound: None found; not asked. None is needed: this is a descriptive split that accuses no one. The MoD's own counter-figure is the 81% domestic / 19% non-domestic value split for FY2024-25 in PRID 2116411, which should appear beside the sample.
verdicts.innocentReading: This matches the record's own innocentReading. A few mega-contracts go to the only domestic designer of each platform: LCA 2021 and 2025, LCH 2025, AL-31FP engines 2024, Su-30 2024. PIB releases leave out most foreign G2G/FMS deals or print no ₹ figure for them (Rafale-M IGA PRID 2124851 has no ₹; MQ-9B value not stated). DPSU primes pass much of the value on to private sub-suppliers. So a PIB-sampled split will over-state DPSU share and under-state foreign share, and that says nothing about how vendors are treated.
verdicts.reason: The arithmetic reproduces exactly, and the three cited PIB releases confirm the HAL amounts (₹48,000 crore, ₹62,700 crore and ₹62,370 crore). The claim still fails as written, for two reasons. (1) The label "PIB-named MoD awards 2021-25" describes a set that is exhaustive by definition, but the tally is a hand-picked subset. It leaves out a PIB-named foreign award with a printed ₹ figure that sits in a source the record itself cites: PRID 2209832, "48 Heavy Weight Torpedoes ... at an approximate cost of Rs 1,896 crore was signed with WASS Submarine Systems S.R.L." The file even lists it as a documented foreign contract. It also leaves out other PIB-named, priced awards (Naval Group ₹877 crore, MDL ₹1,990 crore, BEL Ashwini ₹2,906 crore, HVF Arjun ₹7,523 crore). (2) The headline "foreign 5.4%" sits beside a cited MoD universe figure (PRID 2116411: domestic 81% of ₹2,09,050 crore in FY2024-25) showing the sample under-represents foreign value by a factor of about 3-4 in the years it covers. The "sample, not universe" caveat says that coverage is partial. It does not say the sample is biased, or which direction the bias runs. The analytic finding that DPSUs dominate PIB-named value holds up, so this needs correcting, not killing.

The PIB export releases use a two-way DPSU/private split that sums exactly (15,209 + 5,874 = 21,083; 17,353 + 21,071 = 38,424). verdicts.baseRate: Not a discrimination claim. It describes the shares of a whole and implies no wrongdoing, so there is no comparison set to test. On symmetry, the same arithmetic applied to any year gives the same result, and the series shows the private production share flat at about 19-21% for five years both before and after the 2020-21 OFB corporatisation. verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable. Every figure is the Ministry of Defence's own published data, and the ministry presents it as a success ("DPSUs' exports soar by 151%, private sector contribution up by 14%", PIB 2248124). verdicts.innocentReading: The fall in the private export share is a denominator effect, not a private-sector decline. Private exports rose in absolute terms (₹15,209 cr, then ₹15,233 cr, then ₹17,353 cr), while DPSU exports went from ₹5,874 cr to ₹8,389 cr to ₹21,071 cr. The 177/193 contracts and Rs 1,68,922 cr of Rs 2,09,050 cr figures are for FY2024-25 (PIB 2191937, posted 20 Nov 2025). Production of Rs 43,746 cr in FY2013-14 rising to Rs 1.78 lakh cr in FY2025-26 is in PIB 2273824 (17 Jun 2026). Exports of Rs 38,424 cr in FY2025-26 are in PIB 2248124 (2 Apr 2026). verdicts.identityTest: Pass. The entity in every source is India, as a SIPRI importer (Table 2, rank 2 in both fact sheets) and as MoD/DDP in the PIB releases. One definitional caution: 'production' (Rs 43,746 cr to Rs 1.78 lakh cr, PIB 2273824) and 'indigenous defence production' (Rs 46,429 cr in 2014-15 to Rs 1,27,434 cr in FY2023-24, PIB 2191937) are different MoD series. verdicts.baseRate: India's import fall does not stand out from its region. SIPRI 2025 says imports by states in Asia and Oceania 'dropped by 21 per cent' from 2015-19 to 2020-24, mainly because China's fell. SIPRI 2026 says Asia and Oceania 'fell by 20 per cent' from 2016-20 to 2021-25. India's -9.3% and -4.0% are both smaller than its region's decline. Global volume in 2021-25 was 9.2% higher than 2016-20, so part of the share drop from 9.3% to 8.2% comes from a larger global total. Among the top 10 importers in 2020-24, 4 of 10 fell (India, Saudi Arabia -41, Australia -27, Egypt -44). Shrinking imports therefore do not single India out, and the claim should not be read as showing self-reliance working better than at peers.
verdicts.denialFound: Not applicable in the usual sense: this is an analytic comparison with no accused party, and no one was asked. Contrary reading inside the sources: SIPRI's 2026 fact sheet qualifies its own finding. It says the decrease is 'partly' due to domestic capability, 'although there are often substantial delays in domestic production', and that India's planned orders 'including up to 140 combat aircraft from France and 6 submarines from Germany—indicate its continued and probably increasing reliance on foreign suppliers' (https://www.sipri.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/fs_2603_at_2025.pdf). The claim text leaves this out.
verdicts.innocentReading: The record's own innocent reading holds. SIPRI TIV measures deliveries of major platforms, not rupee value, so large recent orders (Rafale-M, 114 MRFA, submarines) have not yet been delivered and will show up later. 'Domestic' contracts and 'production' can include imported engines and subsystems (F404, AL-31FP under licence). There are three more boring explanations. First, the whole Asia-Oceania region imported about 20% less, so India's smaller decline fits a regional pattern and needs no policy cause. Second, the production series is nominal: CPI roughly 1.7-1.9x over FY14-FY26 means real growth is about 2-2.3x, not 'almost four times'. Third, the 81% domestic share comes from MoD's own classification of who the vendor is, not from measured indigenous content.
verdicts.reason: Every number checks out against a primary source. SIPRI 2025: 'Indian arms imports decreased by 9.3 per cent between 2015–19 and 2020–24', share 8.3% vs 9.1%. SIPRI 2026: 'Indian arms imports fell by 4.0 per cent between 2016–20 and 2021–25', share 8.2% vs 9.3%. PIB 2191937: '193 contracts valued at ₹2,09,050 crore... Of these, 177 contracts, worth ₹1,68,922 crore, were awarded to the domestic industry', which is 80.8%, so 81%. PIB 2273824: 'increased almost four times from Rs 43,746 crore in FY 2013-14' to 'Rs 1.78 lakh crore in... 2025-26'. The tier is right: this is our own juxtaposition of data with different units and denominators, it implies no wrongdoing, and it carries an innocentReading. I cannot refute it. There are three defects to fix. (1) The claim-level srcs list only the two SIPRI sheets and PIB 2191937, and none of those contains Rs 1.78 lakh crore or Rs 43,746 crore. Those figures are only in PIB 2273824, which appears in the record but not in the claim's srcs. That is why sourceCheck is 'partially'. (2) The text leaves out SIPRI's explicit counter-caveat about 'continued and probably increasing reliance on foreign suppliers', which makes the juxtaposition one-sided. (3) The text gives the -9.3% and -4.0% volume changes from two windows but the share change from only one (9.1 to 8.3). It also leaves out the regional base rate of about -20%.
